places.notes: [Ramen · the 24-hour bowl under Dotonbori's giant dragon] Minami's famous all-night ramen stand, known for the huge dragon sculpture over the shop. There are only two choices, ramen (¥900 in October 2026, after a ¥200 rise) or chashu ramen, in a tonkotsu the listing describes as rich, made from pork bones and chicken feet with a secret tare. Most 2026 diners found it surprisingly light, with medium-thin, slightly curly noodles. The fun is the free kimchi, garlic and garlic chives to load in. Take a number and carry your bowl from the counter to tatami or counter seats. Queues are mostly overseas visitors late at night but move fast. Opinions vary: a nostalgic finish to a night out for many, lukewarm and thin for one critic.

places.notes: [Ramen · Kamukura's light cabbage ramen on its home street] The Dotonbori shop of Kamukura, now a nationwide chain that long-time fans still call a local treasure, with 71 seats and open from 10:00 to 08:00 the next morning. The signature "delicious ramen" (¥850 in October 2026) is a light, gently sweet, secret-recipe broth heaped with crunchy napa cabbage and thin-sliced pork. The most popular version adds small chashu and a soft-boiled egg (¥1,270); there's kara-age (¥430), gyoza and seasonal bowls such as a hot-and-sour soup with Zhenjiang vinegar and cilantro. Order on the table tablet. It's easy to eat and veg-heavy, though one diner found it too salty, and the noodles are soft, almost udon-like.

places.notes: [Ramen · Osaka Black, the jet-black shoyu, through the night] Since 2011 the Dotonbori branch of Kinkuemon, a shop famous for sharp shoyu ramen, set just off the main strip by the Kinryū queue. It has 41 seats over two floors and is open through the night (24 hours Friday to Sunday). The signature Osaka Black is a glossy jet-black soy broth with chicken stock and a seafood edge, buttery chicken-fat aroma and a faintly bitter soy finish. Choose thin noodles (most recommend them) or thick, topped with chashu, menma, green onion and a soft egg; extra noodles are extra. Also on the menu: Red Shoyu, King Shoyu, and Osaka Kinjou Shoyu, a clear chicken-and-light-soy broth that one 34-visit regular likes at 8 am. Buy a ticket at the machine outside; garlic on request. ¥1,000–1,200 a bowl; a few found it pricey for tourists or the service curt.

places.notes: [Ramen · Tokyo's Hayashida right under the Glico sign] The first Kansai branch, opened in 2022, of Ramen Hayashida, a Shinjuku shop famous for queues and run by INGS Co. It's a 16-seat counter one floor below the Glico running man, southwest of Ebisubashi. The signature is a clear shoyu broth of duck and Daisen-dori chicken (¥900; the special with a "Maximum Koitama" egg ¥1,200) on firm, thin whole-wheat noodles, with pork-shoulder and chicken-breast chashu. There's also a creamy chicken paitan, a refined tsukemen (special ¥1,250), mazesoba with truffle-sauce egg, and summer yuzu cold ramen (¥950) with yuzu jelly. Add a TKG or oyakodon (¥350–400). Buy tickets at the entrance machine. Light and quick, with friendly staff: a handy fast lunch when Minami's big names are queuing.

places.notes: [Ramen · Himeji back-fat tonkotsu, round the clock] The Dotonbori branch, opened 31 October 2025, of Zundōya, a Himeji-founded chain with over a hundred shops (about 106 in Japan and 4 in Shanghai, per a December 2025 visitor). It sits just east of Ebisubashi and is open 24 hours. The broth is pork bone with a slightly creamy soy seasoning and as much back fat as you choose (light, regular, rich or extra rich). Noodles are house-made: ultra-thin straight (recommended) or curly. The motomi (original) ramen is ¥860, ajitama ¥980, and all-toppings up to ¥1,360; summer brought a cold ramen with grated daikon. Season at the table with pepper, pickled ginger, garlic, chili oil, sesame and takana. Buy a ticket outside (transit IC accepted) and head upstairs. A Kansai-friendly tonkotsu with a hint of sweetness.

places.notes: [Gyoza · Osaka Ohsho's main shop on Dotonbori] The Dotonbori main shop of the Osaka Ohsho gyoza chain: 189 seats over two floors, with back tables upstairs looking over the canal, and touch-panel ordering and payment. The gyoza are the reason to come: juicy enough that one fan skips the dipping sauce. Sets pair them with fried rice (generous chashu), kara-age or a hoikoro set meal (¥1,320 with gyoza). The menu also has mapo tofu, green-pepper beef, chilled Chinese noodles and the punchy lu-su fried rice (¥1,200 as a gyoza set). Plain gyoza are ¥700 here, which one visitor found steep, and the service at the flagship disappointed another. Fast and easy, with a take-out counter.

places.notes: [Ramen · Ichiran's pork-free "no tonkotsu" shop] The one Ichiran operating under its "100% no tonkotsu used" concept: the familiar experience (booth counters with partitions, an order sheet, Arita-ware bowls) but a broth developed from beef bones and chicken, so people who can't eat pork can have Ichiran. Diners call it surprisingly rich and creamy, very like tonkotsu, with the signature red secret sauce. One found it lacked real tonkotsu's punch. Instead of pork chashu there's sweet-spicy seasoned beef (gyūyarō), plus soft salted egg, extra garlic and a matcha pudding. The 100% pork-free ramen was ¥1,280 in July 2026. Expect 30–80-minute waits (scan a QR code and return); a 9 am weekday arrival walked straight in. 25 seats, many overseas visitors.

places.notes: [Ramen · Kinryū's standing yatai on Midōsuji] One of Kinryū's several Namba shops, under a big dragon sign on Midōsuji. It's done in a food-stall style: buy a ticket, then mostly stand at the counter or use the tables by the pavement, with the kitchen in full view. Like the Dotonbori shop, it serves a simple tonkotsu ramen (¥900) that most find lighter than its strong pork aroma suggests, plus free kimchi, garlic and garlic chives to pile on. A seven-time visitor praises the old-school simplicity of a shop that has served for over 35 years; a first-timer was underwhelmed. Turnover is quick and it's open 24 hours, handy at 2 am. Smoking is allowed (Tabelog).

places.notes: [Ramen · Zundōya by Ebisubashi, all night] A bright, busy 24-hour branch, since 2021, of Himeji's back-fat tonkotsu chain Zundōya, a few steps south of Ebisubashi. The chain's site says its broth simmers pork heads, backbones and whole bones over high heat for about ten hours. Diners describe it as rich and creamy yet not overly heavy, deepened by back fat. You choose thin or curly house-made noodles, the back fat (light to extra) and firmness (soft to very firm). An ajitama large was ¥1,070 in 2026, with wood-ear mushroom extra. Regulars add the spicy HOT version with bean sprouts, half fried rice and spicy takana, or a summer chilled ramen. Popular with a younger crowd after drinks.

places.notes: [Ramen · Zundōya in Sōemonchō, the morning-after bowl] A Zundōya branch, since 2022, in Sōemonchō, Minami's all-night entertainment district, open round the clock except a Monday-morning pause. Regulars come for the rich back-fat tonkotsu and the table full of free extras: all-you-can-eat takana, grated garlic, pickled ginger and sesame. One morning visitor found free extra noodles. A negi ramen with curly noodles was ¥980 (bean sprouts +¥110), and a chilled ajitama with grated daikon was ¥1,200 for a large. There are juicy gyoza and fried rice too, plus spicy noodles. Friendly, attentive staff, many from overseas, even at a busy 6 am.

places.notes: [Ramen · Kamukura on Midōsuji] A newer Kamukura (opened January 2025) on Midōsuji beside Kinryū, open until 7 am on Friday and Saturday nights. Its heavy entrance door may be why it's often the one shop without a queue. The "delicious ramen" (¥820 in October 2026) is the chain's light pork-and-vegetable broth, not tonkotsu, sweet from crunchy napa cabbage, with pork belly, thick bouncy chashu and chewy medium-thin straight noodles. Sets add half fried rice and gyoza (¥1,370) or kara-age, and there are seasonal spicy-sour noodles (with a black-vinegar version) and a chilled ramen. Help yourself to garlic chives and chili.

The broth has a rich chicken-paitan base that diners find surprisingly refreshing. The favourite is miso ramen, bold and salty, with onion, garlic chives and chili, thin straight noodles, chashu and bean sprouts. Shoyu ramen and kara-age sets are on offer too. At ¥1,200 for ramen with fried rice it's cheaper than most of its neighbours. Buy a ticket at the machine. Mostly overseas customers, plus some Japanese regulars; reviewers say it's open 24 hours.

places.notes: [Ramen · Kamukura on the Sennichimae side] A 40-seat, counter-only Kamukura across from Ichiran on Dotonbori's Sennichimae end, open 9:00 to 7:00 the next morning. The narrow room has a one-way flow, so it's not for lingering. Fans call it Osaka soul food from before the chain went national: a light, slightly sweet, almost Western-style broth loaded with napa cabbage, the kind people want after drinking instead of heavy tonkotsu. One diner insists it tastes different from other branches. Try the vegetable ramen (¥1,110) or the ramen, kara-age and rice set (about ¥1,350); summer brought a cold pork-shabu ramen with ume, shiso and grated daikon (¥1,250). Buy a ticket at the machine out front. Service can be flat late at night, and one summer visitor found the cabbage bitter.

places.notes: [Chinese · build-your-own malatang in Shinsaibashi] A busy branch of the Yang Guo Fu malatang chain, open since 2022, with 31 seats and queues even mid-afternoon. With tongs you fill a bowl from a spread of vegetables, mushrooms, mountain jellyfish, wood ear, meat, squid, quail eggs, fish cakes and noodles (including vermicelli). The cashier weighs it to set the price, and you pick the spice level and broth. One diner prefers the tomato broth, which tastes almost like tomato ramen; another tamed the heat with sesame sauce. Even spice level one is quite spicy. Choose and pay before you join the seating line. Staff are largely from overseas, so Japanese may be limited.

places.notes: [Gyoza izakaya · late-night gyoza and a Jirō-style bowl in Minami-Senba] A casual 34-seat gyoza izakaya, since 2021, with tables and three private rooms, open late and busy with overseas visitors. Order Osaka-style gyoza, dressed in sauce, mayonnaise, green onion and bonito flakes, or shiso, garlic or plain gyoza, with dashimaki and shrimp chilli-mayo. There's also a Jirō-style ramen (¥1,100): a rich pork-bone miso broth with thick, flat, high-hydration noodles under pork belly, cabbage and bean sprouts. Set meals are cheap (ginger pork ¥900), and dishes come fast. One diner found the food more "not bad" than delicious. Smoking is allowed inside. Tabelog's listed hours (18:00–11:00) don't match the lunch visits reviewers describe, so check.

places.notes: [Ramen · beef-bone white soup, all night] An 18-seat counter, since 2011, three doors east of Mitsudera, serving Makotoya's beef-bone "gyū-paitan" around the clock. Regulars go when they want something that isn't miso, shoyu or shio. The beef broth is rich and smooth but not heavy, with a beefy aroma and sweetness that clings to thin noodles (choose your firmness). The favourite is the spicy red version with soft-boiled egg, chashu, wood ear, bean sprouts and green onion in a red bowl. Doctor it at the table with fresh garlic, garlic chips, pickled ginger and white sesame. Morioka cold noodles were ¥1,010 in August 2026. Buy a ticket at the machine by the door; one visitor found the street queue was for the malatang shop nearby.

places.notes: [Yakiniku · gluten-free Matsusaka beef by Hōzenji] The "hanare" annex of Yakiniku M's Hōzenji branch: a second-floor room off Hōzenji Yokochō where you take your shoes off at the door, with seven tables, six of them semi-private and one a private room. Matsusaka beef is grilled at the table. It is a celiac favourite: the restaurant says any dish can be made gluten-free with notice, and it makes its own gluten-free soy sauce, ponzu and dipping sauces, so the marinated beef and garlic rice can be done too. Celiac reviewers rave about the staff ("Best GF meal we've had in Japan"). It is pricey: one diner put it at ¥8,800–12,000 a head, another had the ¥12,000 premium course. When it was full, staff walked guests to another branch nearby. Book and mention gluten-free when you do.
places.chef: branch of Matsusakagyu Yakiniku M (matsusaka-projects.com) · Hōzenji branch annex ("hanare"), Namba 1-chōme · Part of the Matsusakagyu Yakiniku M group of Osaka yakiniku restaurants (official site); one FMGF reviewer counted four locations. · Matsusaka beef; house gluten-free sauces.
places.gfd: The restaurant tells FindMeGlutenFree that every food item can be made gluten-free on request, but asks for notice when you book: "Advance reservation required for gluten-free dining." It makes its own gluten-free sauces, including soy sauce and ponzu. Celiac reviewers on FMGF (14 recent ratings) describe staff who confirm gluten-free at the table, swap single items in a set and change the grill between gluten-free and regular dishes. One 2025 diner was brought regular sauces by a different ser…

places.n: 源氏蕎麦 法善寺参道店 (Genji Soba)
places.hood: Namba 1-2-19 on the Hōzenji Sandō approach, a stone-paved lane off Dotonbori — 7 min from…
places.cu: 100% buckwheat soba, hand-cut in the window · cold zaru and hot soba · prawn and vegetable tempura from a dedicated GF fryer · beef and duck soba · lunch and dinner set courses (¥3,300 / ¥4,800) · since 1929
places.notes: [Soba · 100% buckwheat and gluten-free tempura on Hōzenji Sandō] A soba house founded in 1929 that moved in March 2026 into a new shop on the stone-paved Hōzenji approach; the old shop is closed for now. The noodles are hand-made from 100% buckwheat (you can watch them being cut in the front window), which makes it a celiac favourite. The menu marks gluten-free and celiac-safe dishes, and the prawn and vegetable tempura is made with buckwheat and rice flour in a dedicated gluten-free fryer. The classic order is cold zaru soba with a big wild prawn and vegetable tempura (¥2,950). There are also grated-daikon, yam and Tamba black-bean natto soba, beef and duck soba, a two-soba lunch (¥1,850), and set courses upstairs by reservation. Some find the broth fishy. You order by QR code at the table, and dinner waits can stretch at busy times.
places.chef: 鳥倉 荘一 · Founded 1929 (official site) · Genji Soba ran at Namba 4-5-8; in March 2026 it opened on Hōzenji Sandō, and the new-shop letter is signed 「源氏蕎麦法善寺参道本店 鳥倉 荘一」. The site describes soba-making demonstrations in Melbourne (2023) and Canberra (2024–2026) and soba sold through Takashimaya and other department stores. · 「変わらぬ手打ちと、蕎麦本来の味を大切に、日本の文化を食べるお店として」 (new-shop letter, March 2026). · Hand-made 100% buckwheat soba; gluten-free tempura.
places.gfd: The soba is hand-made from 100% buckwheat (juwari). The menu marks gluten-free dishes, and celiac reviewers on FindMeGlutenFree (101 recent ratings) describe a separate, celiac-labelled section. On the official menu, the tempura is made with buckwheat and rice flour and "Fried in a Dedicated Gluten-Free Fryer". Gluten-free dipping sauce and soy sauce are made for gluten-free orders, while the regular sauces are also in use, so ask. FMGF flags that it is NOT a dedicated gluten-free facility. Sev…
places.vgd: The set courses note: "Gluten-Free & Vegan options are available upon advance request." There is a vegan soba on the à la carte menu, but in September 2026 a reviewer was asked whether egg was OK after ordering it, so it may only be vegetarian. Ask about the dashi and egg.
places.hours: 11:30–21:30 (L.O. 21:30), break 14:30–17:00; closed some Wednesdays (水曜不定休) (official site). Lunch and dinner set courses by reservation, upstairs. Reviewers say the celiac-safe tempura is dinner only. The original shop at Namba 4-5-8 is closed for now; this Hōzenji Sandō shop opened in March 2026.

places.n: Naki vegan sweets

places.notes: [Sweets · vegan and gluten-free tarts off Dotonbori] A tiny, quiet cake shop on a Namba side street with about four seats. Everything is vegan and gluten-free, and it is a celiac favourite (FMGF marks it reported dedicated gluten-free). Expect small tarts and cakes, around ¥1,000 each: mango, mixed berry cheesecake, chocolate pistachio, matcha and white chocolate, strawberry chocolate. Reviewers single out the cashew cream on a coarse almond crust, and the rice-flour and coconut-oil cookies, which one family bought to take home after being given some free. There is Italian espresso and peach cream soda. Service is gentle, once by a host in a kimono, though one 2026 diner found it unfriendly. Takeaway, and an online shop.
places.chef: Namba 1-chōme · A vegan, gluten-free sweets specialist with an online shop (naki-vegansweets.com); no source names the owner or pastry chef. · 「誰でも食べられる優しいお菓子」 — gentle sweets anyone can eat (official site). · Vegan, gluten-free tarts and cookies.
places.gfd: The shop calls itself a specialist in vegan, gluten-free sweets: 「ヴィーガングルテンフリースイーツの専門店」. FindMeGlutenFree marks it "Reported to be dedicated gluten-free", and celiac reviewers (30 recent ratings) report no symptoms. Reviewers mention rice flour, coconut oil and almond crusts. One caveat: in January 2026 a reviewer found the oat milk for drinks labelled "may contain gluten" and switched to soy milk. Ask about the milk in drinks.
places.vgd: Fully vegan. The shop says it uses no eggs, dairy or other animal ingredients, only selected plant ingredients (「卵・乳製品など動物性の食材を使用せずに厳選した植物性食材で作る」).
places.hours: Not listed on the official site. An FMGF reviewer (August 2026) found it open 13:00–20:00. Check before going. About four seats; takeaway available; also sells online.

places.n: Gluten-Free Vegan OKONOMIYAKI Vim
places.hood: Namba 1-3-13, up a tiny alley just off Dotonbori
places.cu: Gluten-free okonomiyaki (pork belly and vegan) · stir-fried noodles and pasta · oyster mushrooms · battered tofu · grilled scallops · fried chicken · Kirin gluten-free beer · six seats
places.notes: [Okonomiyaki · gluten-free okonomiyaki off Dotonbori] A tiny gluten-free okonomiyaki spot up a narrow alley off Dotonbori, with a counter downstairs and one table upstairs (about six seats). For celiac travellers it is a rare safe way to eat Osaka's signature dish. Reviewers order pork-belly okonomiyaki, stir-fried noodles and pasta, oyster mushrooms, tempura, battered tofu with rice balls, grilled scallops and fried chicken, with a Kirin gluten-free beer. The name says vegan, but meat and seafood are on the menu, so ask. Book ahead (online booking needs a Japanese phone number) or queue before the 5 pm opening. Several were turned away. Portions are small and prices high, one meal and one drink per person is expected, under-18s are not admitted, and it is reported closed on Thursdays. One reviewer mentions a sister restaurant around the corner.
places.chef: Namba 1-chōme · A gluten-free okonomiyaki restaurant; the official page (nanbavim.biz-option.com) gives only its name, phone and links. One reviewer names the host-chef as Miyo. · Gluten-free okonomiyaki.
places.gfd: A gluten-free okonomiyaki restaurant. FindMeGlutenFree marks it "Reported to be dedicated gluten-free", and celiac reviewers (through October 2026) call it entirely gluten-free and safe for coeliacs, with Kirin gluten-free and organic gluten-free beer. Reported features include a dedicated gluten-free fryer and kitchen. The restaurant itself publishes nothing beyond its name, so this rests on community reports. Confirm when you book.
places.vgd: Despite "Vegan" in its name, the menu also has meat and seafood: reviewers ate pork-belly okonomiyaki, grilled scallops, fried chicken and pork noodles. The vegan options include battered tofu and rice balls ("some vegan options"). Ask whether the batter, sauce and dashi for the vegan dishes are plant-based.
places.hours: No hours published. Reviewers: opens at 17:00 (June 2026); closed Thursdays (April 2026); once closed an hour early (October 2026). About six seats. Reservation strongly advised (booking online needs a Japanese phone number); queue before opening otherwise. No children under 18 (FMGF tip, June 2026…

places.notes: [Ramen · Ichiran's big Dotonbori annex, open all night] Ichiran's 82-seat annex at the Sennichimae end of Dotonbori, since 2015. The 30-seat booth counter runs 24 hours, and the table floors run 8:00–23:00. It is the familiar ritual: buy a ticket while you queue, then tick richness, fat, garlic, green or white onion, the red secret sauce and noodle firmness on the order sheet. The bowl is Hakata-style tonkotsu with firm, very thin noodles. One diner found it light and not greasy, another rich with no off-odour. The natural tonkotsu ramen was ¥1,180 and extra noodles ¥210 (August 2026), with a soft salted egg at ¥160. Queues can reach an hour (October 2026), even 10 minutes at 2 am. The table floors suit groups and families: one August visitor noted an adult can bring up to five children free. Souvenirs are sold on the way out.

places.notes: [Ramen · late-night abura-soba on Sennichimae] A two-floor, 26-seat Kirinji shop on the Sennichimae shopping street, since 2023, serving soupless abura-soba. Thick, chewy noodles come coated in an oil-and-sauce base under chashu, menma, plenty of shredded nori and sesame. Add a soft-boiled egg, kimchi or extra meat, then mix well and doctor it with the vinegar and chili oil on the table, as the wall instructions suggest. One fan says it becomes addictive by the third visit. It's cheap: a regular with soft egg came in under ¥1,000 in March 2026. A chashu rice bowl and a kara-age and rice set round it out. Regulars come after drinks or a live show, and lines of overseas visitors are common. Cash only.

places.notes: [Ramen · the old-school Naniwa tonkotsu counter on Sennichimae] A long-running 11-seat L-shaped counter on the Sennichimae shopping street under a "Ganso Naniwa Tonkotsu" sign, open from 5 am to late, and round the clock at weekends. Its Osaka-style tonkotsu is light and slightly sweet, with thin straight noodles, chashu, naruto, menma and green onion (¥1,080; ¥1,250 with a scalp-tingling spicy miso), and the first kaedama is free. Season it with the pickled ginger, sesame and garlic on the counter. The mountainous chashu ramen is ¥2,200. Several diners say the ¥100 gyoza with a ramen beat the ramen itself. Summer brings a chilled yuzu-lemon shio ramen with ginger (¥1,380), and there's a shrimp-miso abura-soba and tantan tsukemen. Some find it pricey for what it is. Buy a ticket out front. Smoking is allowed.

places.notes: [Ramen · frothy chicken paitan between Namba and Shinsaibashi] A 9-seat shop with five counter seats and a table, since 2022, on the first floor of a mixed-use building with no street sign. Follow the map, or the queue. The chicken paitan is whipped espuma-style into a fluffy, mousse-like broth, creamy and rich yet clean on the finish, over flat, chewy noodles. The special toripaitan (¥1,705, August 2026) adds a seasoned egg, chicken and pork chashu, purple onion and wood ear. The mentaiko version stirs spicy cod roe through the cream. Seasoned-egg rice goes well alongside. Expect waits even off-peak, as turnover is slow. One June diner waited over two hours on a Saturday, and another found it competent but characterless.

places.notes: [Ramen · the Shōwa-style chuka soba with the long queue] The Namba shop of Fujii, a small chain selling "nostalgic Shōwa flavour" chuka soba from Tokyo to Osaka. A sharp, easy-drinking shoyu broth comes with back fat you can scale down, and one diner was reminded of Onomichi ramen. Watch the fried rice being made at the counter: fluffy, and one regular's favourite anywhere. The ramen, kara-age and fried rice set is a generous ¥1,100 (October 2026). Nira soba piled with garlic chives arrived on 1 July 2026, served with a perforated ladle to catch them. Add garlic powder or vinegar halfway. Queues are the catch: 40 minutes to an hour and a half in October 2026, once 45 groups ahead on a Saturday. Take a number at the shop and wander until your phone pings. Closed Tuesdays; open to 3 am on Fridays and Saturdays.

places.notes: [Ramen · a basement counter by Nankai Namba] A small counter along a basement corridor of the Namba Hips building, next to a pachinko parlour, since December 2024. It is usually run by one person, so expect to wait while earlier orders go out. Two lines: a tonkotsu with one big slab of tender chashu, looking thick but drinking easily, and a back-fat shoyu with black pepper that is lighter than it looks. The umami miso tonkotsu (¥1,550 in May 2026) gets an accent from marinated onions, and the back-fat shoyu was ¥1,350. Add a tsukimi chashu rice bowl (¥500). The thin noodles run soft, which may divide people, and one diner tasted oden in the broth. It's cashless (card or PayPay), the only drinks are alcohol, and there's no restroom nearby. Often quiet, with no queue (September 2026).

places.notes: [Ramen · Minami's 24-hour pork-bone shoyu with free kimchi] A 17-seat, mostly counter shop on the shopping street by Hōzenji, open 24 hours and run by Arakawa Food Service. For years it was a late-night ritual for locals (one did "the sauna at Amza, then Hanamaruken"). The base is a pork-bone soy broth, rich but not heavy, with medium-thin noodles. The signature torokotsu ramen comes with two big pieces of tender pork, nori, menma, naruto and green onion. Free kimchi on the counter cuts the richness. Newer additions include garlic tonkotsu ramen (April 2026) and champon, and the fried rice has a following. Regulars say the old queues have eased, the crowd is now largely overseas visitors, and the regular bowl tastes lighter than before. The restroom is up narrow stairs.

places.notes: [Ramen · beef-bone white soup on Sennichimae] A ramen shop since 2023 on the Sennichimae side of Hōzenji, full of overseas visitors even on weekdays. The draw is a frothy beef-bone and chicken white soup: rich and creamy but easy to finish, built on chicken carcass and beef knuckle with a soy kaeshi and back-fat finish over thin straight noodles. It comes with two chashu, one charred and one tender, plus a runny seasoned egg, menma and green onion. There's also a lighter tonkotsu and a mala-style chili condiment on the table. Prices are high: a limited bowl topped ¥2,000 in September 2026, and the strip-loin rice bowl in the set ran salty. One diner flagged cleanliness. Cards and electronic payment accepted.

Matsusaka-beef courses are grilled at the table. For celiac diners the draw is the sauces, which the general manager says are all gluten-free. Staff even bring out the labelled soy sauce bottle, and one server who is celiac comes up again and again in reviews. Reviewers had non-GF set-course items swapped, though one notes the soup is the exception. Dinner daily, plus weekend lunch.

places.notes: [Okonomiyaki · gluten-free rice-flour okonomiyaki near the Glico sign] A casual bar-restaurant about five minutes from the Glico running man, with what it calls British roots: organic wine, European-style chūhai and British organic tea alongside beer and whisky. Celiac reviewers love it ("the best okonomiyaki I've ever had – really good ginger flavour and only 1100 yen", October 2026), along with a GF potato salad and pudding. The gyoza are wheat and share the griddle, so skip them. Usually there's no queue when nearby okonomiyaki places have long lines. The chef-owner speaks good English, and ordering is by app. Smoking only on the outside terrace.

places.notes: [Okonomiyaki · a one-person gluten-free okonomiyaki bar on Dotonbori] A small, wildly decorated okonomiyaki bar at the western end of Dotonbori, run single-handed by its owner-chef, Shiho, and one of the most-collected gluten-free spots in Osaka on FMGF (59 public collections). Order at the counter from a clearly marked menu, find a table upstairs (some have a view), clear it yourself, and listen for your number. Drinks are self-service for ¥100 a go. There are about five gluten-free okonomiyaki (beef and onion, triple meat, mushroom and sausage), or build your own with vegetables and beans. Portions are huge, so a medium is plenty. The GF gyoza and fries are favourites. Queue before the roughly 6 pm opening. One woman does everything, so waits of 40 minutes or more are normal. One symptomatic celiac reacted in 2026, so it is not risk-free.

places.notes: [Sweets · gluten-free steamed matcha cake south of Namba] A small matcha-sweets shop from the ROMAN TALE restaurant group, using organic matcha (rare in Japan) from the group's own Kagoshima farm. The signature is the 抹茶ふかしパウン, a lightly sweet, chewy yet fluffy steamed matcha cake served hot from the bamboo steamer and made without wheat flour, so it is gluten-free. Celiac visitors keep coming back for it: one ate it every day of a stay, another three times on one trip. There are also gluten-free ice cream cones, soft serve and an excellent matcha latte, with soy milk and no oat milk. Takeaway too. Hours aren't published in the sources we found, so check.

places.notes: [Tsukemen · clam tsukemen after midnight in Higashi-Shinsaibashi] A 12-seat, second-floor tsukemen shop that opens at midnight (8 pm on Fridays and Saturdays) and runs to 5 am. A rich shijimi-clam broth, lighter than the usual thick tsukemen, feeds a smooth dip for silky noodles. There's a clam cream version and a shijimi paste, the noodles can be warmed, and a broth is poured in to finish. The other signature is rice topped with egg and freshly shaved truffle. One diner credits the concept to a charismatic figure from the Shinshu (Nagano) ramen scene. Regulars come after drinking, and queues form late. Expect ¥2,000–3,000 a head. Cash only. It changed its name before March 2025.

The base is a standard Kyushu tonkotsu with very thin Hakata-style noodles. Alongside it are red miso chashu, a salt tonkotsu, and the house favourite, tomato ramen or tomato tsukemen: bright acidity, gentle sweetness and umami, closer to soup pasta than ramen, as one diner put it. There's also a Kyushu-style abura-soba and hot, juicy gyoza. Smoking is allowed, and cards are not.

The bowl arrives bubbling in a clay pot that keeps it hot to the end, loaded with tender, fluffy horumon in a hearty broth with no off-odour. Choose red (spicy, the popular one) or white. One diner liked it topped with corn. The shop nudges you to finish with rice in the broth, risotto- or porridge-style. A salt-seasoned kalbi rice bowl is the alternative. It's like a one-person hot pot, good after drinks or, as one inspector found, for an early breakfast. Rarely crowded. Cash only.

places.notes: [Ramen · Miyazaki karamen round the clock in Sōemonchō] A 24-hour, two-floor, 23-seat karamen shop in the Sōemonchō nightlife streets, since 2011. The signature karakara noodles arrive bright red under fluffy scrambled egg, garlic chives and minced meat, with real umami behind the heat and the egg adding creaminess. Pick your spice level, up to 100 (regulars brag about levels 30, 50 and 100), and your noodles, including konjac. Add tender pork if you like. For milder tastes there's a Hokkaido "100-year" miso ramen, and a cult omurice that one 2 am regular orders instead of noodles. It is kept cool inside, anticipating the heat. A post-drinks staple. The street outside can feel rough late at night.

places.notes: [Ramen · shellfish shoyu all night in Higashi-Shinsaibashi] A 10-seat, white-and-grey counter tucked into a building beside one of Minami's liveliest clubs, open from 8 pm to 8 am, since 2023. The star is a golden shellfish broth: oyster, asari and shijimi over chicken bones, with a mild soy sauce and chicken oil. It's gentle and gradually deepening, with a pleasant shellfish bitterness, over house-made medium-thin noodles of whole-wheat flour. The special (¥1,300, September 2026) adds rare pork-shoulder and belly chashu, a soft egg, mizuna, menma and red and white onion. There's also a rich shoyu on chicken and bonito with thin noodles, and a chilled shellfish ramen in summer. Pair it with the seared rare-chashu mayo rice bowl (¥400). One colleague group said to skip the sudachi rice. Buy a ticket at the machine inside.

places.notes: [Ramen · hangover-cure shijimi ramen after midnight] A 22-seat, second-floor late-nighter, since 2013, serving "recovery ramen" made with plenty of Yamato shijimi clams from Lake Shinji in Shimane. The broth is light yet deep (one diner compared its depth to tonkotsu), with a touch of butter for richness, in shio, shoyu or miso. The signature rich shijimi shio is ¥1,200, and the shop puts it at 496 kcal. Chashu is ¥200 extra and the salt gyoza ¥400. In summer, a clear chilled shijimi ramen with Morioka-style noodles, rare chashu, half an egg and rice crackers. The walls are covered in autographs: kabuki actors, Yoshimoto comedians, baseball players and Brian May of Queen. One diner found ¥1,200 for a plain bowl steep. Open 8 pm to 5 am, cash only.

places.notes: [Chinese · build-your-own malatang in Higashi-Shinsaibashi] A bright, recently renovated 38-seat branch of a malatang chain from China, popular with Chinese visitors and recognisable by its big red sign. It's weighed at ¥380 per 100 g (October 2026). The signature broth is beef bones simmered for 8 hours and finished with a fragrant sesame-and-peanut sauce, creamy enough that one diner had it with no spice at all. Others found level 2 plenty hot, with real numbing mala. Stir in sesame sauce or cilantro black vinegar at the table, and add fried bread for dunking, sesame balls or chicken wings.

places.notes: [Ramen · Fukuoka's fish-bone ramen, no membership needed] The third shop of Gyokotsuya, famous in Fukuoka as a members-only ramen bar. Here, as in Ginza, anyone can walk in. Upstairs in a Sōemonchō building, a chic black room with vermilion lattice feels more kaiseki than ramen shop. The broth is a creamy white soup from sea-bream bones, under chewy noodles and crunchy fried sakura shrimp, part of the shop's pitch for a "sixth flavour". Fish-bone ramen and tsukemen are ¥1,450, and the spicy versions ¥1,550. Tsukemen comes with a mini rice and a flask of broth to turn the leftovers into risotto. At night there are a medicinal hot pot and grilled eel-liver skewers. Not everyone is sold: one diner found the broth watery and sparse for ¥1,450. Closed Tuesdays.

places.notes: [Ramen · Osaka's old-school Kotan under Namba] A bright, 33-seat Kotan in the Namba Walk underground mall, steps from the Midōsuji Line, and for many Osakans the taste of childhood. The Kotan ramen comes in shoyu (soy-forward but not heavy) or shio (a light yet rich white broth), with thin noodles, chashu, bean sprouts, carrot and green onion. Regulars shower it in sesame from the table. The pork-belly Kotan is ¥950, a seasoned egg adds ¥120, and the spicy cold noodles with kimchi are ¥980 (September 2026). There are wonton noodles, and lunch sets with fried rice, gyoza or a croquette. Food comes fast, often in two minutes. A brisk hall manager in thick Osaka dialect keeps it moving.

The pork-bone broth comes two ways: koi-me, sweet with back fat, or assari, lifted with a seafood oil. House-made thin straight noodles have seven firmness levels. September 2026 brought a limited, squid-ink-black tsukimi ramen (¥1,100). Order on the touch-panel machines inside the hard-to-spot entrance. One regular found the koi-me too strong at this branch.

places.notes: [Ramen · Jirō-style mazesoba in Amerikamura] The 15-seat head shop of Menya Gaten, since 2013, built on a Jirō-style "MAZE soba": thick, chewy, firm noodles (150 g up to 300 g) under vegetables, thick-cut chashu, fat and garlic, all scaled when you hand over your ticket. Mix it hard (one diner flipped it, "tenchi gaeshi"), and add mayo halfway. There's a curry mazesoba with a decent kick, and a DX chicken paitan ramen (¥1,400, August 2026) with tender thick chashu that won over a paitan fan. Kimchi and egg soup are free and self-serve, when they haven't run out. Some find the mazesoba merely salty without Jirō-style depth. Cash only, smoking allowed.

places.notes: [Ramen · the original Kinryu at the east end of Dotonbori] The main shop of the Kinryu dragon-sign chain, a 38-place counter with standing space at the Sakaisuji end of Dotonbori, open 24 hours. The bowl is Osaka's light tonkotsu, much lighter than Kyushu-style and easy to finish, with generous chashu. Even the plain ramen carries several slices and trimmings, and the chashu ramen piles it on. The ritual is unchanged for half a century, as one diner put it: free kimchi, garlic and garlic chives to load in as you like, plus free rice in place of extra noodles. Waits run 10–30 minutes at busy times. Buy a ticket first. Cash only, smoking allowed.

Recent reviews date from 2025, so check it is still open.

The standard is a straightforward tonkotsu ("moto-aji"). The ajitama ramen adds a slick of dark black garlic oil that gives the broth depth. For something lighter, the meat soba (¥880, July 2026) has a clear, refreshing broth with thin straight noodles, pork bits, onion and grated daikon. places.notes: [Udon · late-night kasu udon in Amerikamura] An 8-seat counter up a graffiti-covered corridor in Mitsudera Kaikan, the pink-lit building that is one of Amemura's deep-drinking landmarks. It serves Osaka's kasu udon: a clear, refreshing dashi enriched by crispy, fragrant abura-kasu (fried beef offal) and green onion, with firm udon. A spicy seasoning deepens as it melts in. Try the plum and tororo-kombu version. A regular of more than ten years says prices have risen to around ¥1,000, but the taste hasn't changed. It's a classic finish to a night out. The owner plays 80s and 90s hard rock (Guns N' Roses, Van Halen), and young crowds fill it by 10 pm. Closed Wednesdays. It plans to move by June 2027.

places.notes: [Indian · a 1999 Indian restaurant above Dotonbori] A long-running, 45-seat Indian restaurant up a flight of stairs on Dotonbori, its sign hidden among the neon near the Glico man. The staff are Indian and English works better than Japanese. Beyond the usual curries (butter chicken, keema, lentil, spinach) and crisp naan, there is South Indian cooking: a dosa wrapped round potato masala and a tangy tomato rasam. The chicken biryani is big enough for two, and the kitchen will pack leftovers. The Mithila set (two curries, naan, salad) was ¥1,650 in August 2025, up from ¥880. Choose spice 1–5, since the standard level is very mild. Tabelog flags vegetarian options. Smoking allowed.

places.notes: [Café · a vegan, organic retreat on a Shinsaibashi rooftop] A calm 10th-floor café overseen by the Shinsaibashi beauty clinic W CLINIC and built around gut health. Celiac travellers praise the gluten-free pizza, bolognese pasta, bread, açaí bowls and desserts. Expect a dose of wellness messaging (hot water, brown-rice enzyme samples). Open days follow a calendar, so book through LINE, and one diner wrestled with the online ordering.

places.notes: [Jamaican · gluten-free Jamaican cooking in Kitahorie] A tiny, cheerful Jamaican kitchen in Kitahorie. Celiac reviewers say it is 100% gluten-free, with a dedicated fryer, and it is also dairy-free with lots of vegan dishes. The owner cooks everything in view and is careful about gluten, even flagging that the beer isn't safe. Order the jerk chicken plate with crisp potato wedges (smoky, slightly spicy, well cooked), a jerk chicken bean wrap, tapas, or the popular nachos, which sell out after lunch. Save room for the cakes. Portions are big. Hours are unpredictable: 12–6 pm is typical, but several have arrived to find it shut, so check Facebook or Instagram first.

places.notes: [Café · gluten-free brunch in Kitahorie] A small, quiet brunch café with a menu that marks its many gluten-free options: pancakes, banana bread, avocado toast and salmon-and-cream-cheese toast on good GF bread, açaí bowls, salads and smoothies, alongside vegan, vegetarian and meat dishes. Western breakfasts like these are rare in Japan, and gluten-free travellers love it ("the best pancakes, banana bread and coffee", October 2026). Portions are modest. Gyoza come two to a plate (¥350) and are big and juicy. Service can feel rushed. Closed Tuesdays.

Novelties include a chicken-katsu curry paitan and ramen with shrimp tempura or crispy chicken. Add a mini chashu bowl, and pepper or vinegar from the table. Order at the multilingual tablet by the door.

places.notes: [Ramen · Minami's 1971 shio ramen and gyoza counter] An 11-seat counter in a back-alley building in Ura-Namba, serving ramen and gyoza since 1971 and still a classic end to a night of drinking. The ramen is a clear, gentle chicken-bone shio, made by pouring a yellow tare into the bowl, then the sparkling broth, with sesame, bean sprouts, green onion and thin straight noodles. The chashu ramen was ¥1,200 in September 2026, and the wonton noodles ¥1,100. The hand-made gyoza (8 for ¥400) are light and chewy, and media favourites. Wontons are made fresh and can sell out. One regular has visited more than 140 times. It was long run by a married couple; the owner now trains a younger team. Evenings only, closed Sundays, cash only.

places.notes: [Gyoza · bite-sized Osaka gyoza across from Amza] The main shop of Yasudaya, an 18-seat gyoza izakaya across from Amza in Sennichimae, open late and lively, with multilingual menus. The gyoza are small enough to eat in one bite, so order several kinds. The original garlic gyoza (¥450–500 in October 2026) has a crisp, thin skin and a strong garlic punch. The juicy shrimp gyoza (¥550) is best with salt, as staff suggest. There are also squid, potato-cheese and vegetable versions. One diner found the potato-cheese and vegetable ones not to their taste. Wash them down with ¥600 draft beer and finish with salted tamago rice (¥990). Tables are cramped and service can be distracted. Smoking allowed, closed Tuesdays.

places.notes: [Ramen · a new 24-hour tonkotsu in Sōemonchō] Opened in December 2025 in the old Daikichi Ramen spot in Sōemonchō, with a bright sign that is welcome at 4:30 am. The tonkotsu ramen (¥980, April 2026) comes with three slices of chashu and half an egg over thin noodles, rich but not heavy. The special ramen adds wood ear and bean sprouts, and a spicy Sichuan version builds slowly. There's also a miso version that tastes like miso tonkotsu, and a glossy, medium-thin tsukemen whose dip one diner wanted richer. Free kimchi arrives as soon as you order, and stirring it into the bowl is the move. Sides are cheap and good: fluffy chashu fried rice (¥600), gyoza (¥450), kara-age sets. Buy a ticket at the machine.

Buy a ticket, swap it for a number tag, and help yourself at the self-service counter: unlimited white rice, kimchi, spicy garlic chives and chopped garlic. The broth is a gentle, cloudy pork bone that goes down easily after drinking, over straight medium-thin noodles with three thin slices of chashu. It becomes "your style" once loaded with garlic. The tatami-covered chairs are a Kinryu signature. Some find the rice soft. Cash only.

The order is the shio ramen: a light, clear chicken-bone broth with a gentle salt tare, slightly curly medium-thick noodles, mizuna and green onion. Melted butter or a seasoned egg rounds it out. The chashu don is sweet like eel sauce, a nice contrast, and the gyoza are sweet with cabbage. Opinions vary: some find it plain, and one reviewer thought the shoyu lacked character despite the media stickers. There is also a Daichan in Namba. Smoking allowed. Cash may be needed.

The fried rice and kara-age set is a guilty pleasure, and beer comes big. Points on the app earn free toppings. One summer visitor found the first-floor counter a little smelly.

It now also serves a gluten-free breakfast-and-lunch menu that celiac visitors rave about: French toast ("absolutely incredible"), waffles, a BLAT with egg, bacon and sausage plates, chicken sandwiches to take away. It is run by one person, so food can take a while, and it is pricey (about ¥5,000 for two plates and two coffees, October 2026). Only a few tables.

Reviewers love the zesty #1 ramen, the black garlic ramen and a rich miso, all with very tender pork, plus GF gyoza, GF beer and desserts, and a sake tasting. A vegan zesty ramen is also available. Sit at the counter for the show, or book the private room for a group. It is not a dedicated GF kitchen, but the staff are exceptionally knowledgeable.

places.cu: Signature mazesoba ¥1,200 (shrimp-and-scallop chicken-oil salt sauce, egg yolk, cubed chashu, fish powder, nori) · Taiwan mazesoba, curry Taiwan, salt Taiwan ¥1,200 · thick wavy whole-wheat noodles from 100 g to 400 g · kombu vinegar and shichimi · 2 floors
places.notes: [Ramen · Nagoya-style mazesoba in Higashi-Shinsaibashi] Arashi's mazesoba shop reopened on 1 October 2026 about 200 m west of its old spot, now on two floors. Reviewers who knew it in Nagoya were glad to find it. The signature mazesoba (¥1,200 for 200 g, a 100 g small for ¥1,000) dresses thick, wavy, house-made whole-wheat noodles in a light salt sauce of chicken oil infused with dried shrimp and scallop. On top go an egg yolk, cubed roast chashu, mizuna, green onion, fish powder and nori, with a punch of garlic and chili. Taiwan mazesoba comes in curry and salt versions too. Mix from the bottom, then add kombu vinegar or shichimi. Ordering is by QR code. In the first weeks, staff were still finding their feet and payment was cash only.

places.notes: [Ramen · a 50-seat Kamukura in Shinsaibashi] A long counter-only Kamukura on the Shinsaibashi side of Minami, open from 10 am to 6:30 am the next morning. It serves the chain's gentle, napa-cabbage-sweet broth that "felt like a warm hug" to one first-timer. The ajitama ramen was ¥980 in August 2026. Summer brings a cold version, slightly salty to stand up to the ice and served with yuzu juice to change the flavour, which regulars recommend on the hottest days. A dependable post-drinks stop, busy late at night.

places.notes: [Ramen · Jinrui Mina Menrui's water-and-soy-sauce shoyu, under Namba] A 14-seat counter in the Namba Walk underground mall, the first shop of a newer brand from Osaka's famous queue magnet Jinrui Mina Menrui, since April 2023. Expect chewy whole-wheat noodles, beautifully rare pork and carefully cooked chicken chashu. Summer brings the ice-cold "kin-kin" noodles in a bonito broth drizzled with chili oil (¥970). Rice refills are free, and the special toppings add a free half serving of noodles. Pay at the entrance. One diner felt the bowl looked half-empty.

places.notes: [Tsukemen · a noodle-maker's kombu-water tsukemen, all night] A late-night branch of Fuki Seimen Kenkyusho, a noodle maker with roots in Kumamoto and shops in Tokyo and Osaka, open in Shinsaibashi since June 2025. After the Fukai branch closed in May 2026, it became the only Osaka shop. The draw is the noodles: flat, chewy whole-wheat noodles served soaking in kombu water, so taste a couple plain first. The bonito-kombu tsukemen (¥1,100, July 2026) comes with a sweetish, katsuo-forward soy dip that the kombu water doesn't dilute. Squeeze in sudachi as you go. There's also a chuka soba whose broth one diner finished, and a popular "Guilty Jirō". Order on your phone at the seat. Open 9 pm to 6 am; smoking allowed.

places.notes: [Ramen · Sichuan tantanmen on the Nippombashi side] A 13-seat tantanmen shop with a few outdoor seats, dinner only, with queues that move fast. Ask the owner, who will steer you: in October 2026 the advice was to skip the Taiwan, Shanghai and Hong Kong options and order the Sichuan street-style dan dan, with a sharp chili-and-Sichuan-pepper heat over deep umami, under minced meat, garlic chives and bean sprouts. It cost ¥1,150 with cheese. Tame it with a raw egg or cheese, or go all in with extra cilantro. The yatai-style shoyu ramen also carries Sichuan pepper, over thin noodles. Portions are big, so come before you are too full. Cash only, smoking allowed.

places.cu: Sapporo miso ramen ¥1,170 · pork-bone and chicken-wing broth thickened with grated potato · lard cap keeps it piping hot · medium-thick curly yellow noodles · grilled chashu, menma, corn, green onion · ajitama +¥160 · spicy miso · 14-seat counter, open through the night
places.notes: [Ramen · Sapporo miso through the night in Higashi-Shinsaibashi] A 14-seat counter serving Sapporo-style miso ramen from 6 pm until morning, and on Friday and Saturday nights until 2 pm the next day. The broth is pork bone and chicken wings simmered long, with miso and a twist: grated potato thickens it to a velvety, potage-like body. A cap of lard keeps it scalding. Medium-thick, curly yellow noodles hold it well, topped with grilled chashu, menma, corn and green onion. The miso ramen was ¥1,170 and an ajitama ¥160 in October 2026. The spicy version isn't very spicy. Buy a ticket at the door. It gets crowded late, but turnover is quick.

places.notes: [Café · a gluten-free rice-flour café in Tenmabashi] A small café and baking school near Tenmabashi built entirely around domestic rice flour: gluten-free sweets, bread and a brunch-and-lunch menu that celiac visitors rave about. One called the sandwiches "the best I've ever eaten". Try the croque monsieur lunch set, which a mixed GF and non-GF table loved equally, or the French toast plate with bacon and greens, with a matcha espresso latte. The case holds scones, cakes, carrot cake, cream puffs and tarts to take away, and there is afternoon tea. Small, but turnover is quick. Open Wednesday to Saturday, 11 to 5.

Order the classic modern-yaki with pork, shrimp and squid (¥1,850, August 2026) or the cheese-tama with potato and mentaiko (¥1,350). Portions are big, so start with one each. places.notes: [Ramen · Zundoya's 24-hour Shinsaibashi branch] A 32-seat, round-the-clock Zundoya at the northern end of Shinsaibashi, with a few terrace seats. The chain began in Himeji. Lunch, 11 to 4, is set meals only, for example vegetable ramen with a small fried rice for ¥1,400 in October 2026. Buy a ticket at the entrance. Friendly, energetic staff.

places.notes: [Ramen · soy-tonkotsu chuka soba on EDION Namba's ramen floor] One of the shops on "Namba Ramen Ichiza", the 9th-floor ramen street in EDION Namba, and a regular's favourite there. The broth is a soy-sauce tonkotsu, comforting and fragrant, light yet deep for some and surprisingly rich and fatty for others. The shoyu ramen (¥980, June 2026) comes with thin curly noodles, and a fried-rice set adds ¥400. A spicy ramen with ajitama (¥1,150) has a real kick with garlic chives. There's also a curry ramen with big pieces of meat, and a minced-meat ramen with a small rice to mop up. The walls are signed by Yoshimoto comedians. Families come after toy shopping on 7F, and there are high chairs. Cash only.

A black shoyu ramen and a strong soy-sauce shoyu are the alternatives, and the fried rice (kimchi, or garlic and pepper) is good. Hours can slip: one October visitor arrived to find it opening late and out of Sichuan ramen. The stiff door is a known quirk. Cash only.

The takoyaki is made with rice flour and konjac in place of octopus, which the menu doesn't spell out, and comes as a set with salad and soup. Summer 2025 brought a chilled shio ramen made without animal products, topped with fried eggplant, okra and pumpkin, tomato and pickled ginger (¥1,780). A friend with a dairy allergy was delighted with the vegan chocolate ice cream (¥650). Prices are steep and it is often quiet. Multilingual, cashless, QR ordering.

The batter is famously fluffy ("the fluffiest okonomiyaki I've ever had"). The signature combination is beef tendon, green onion and konnyaku, rich and generous, while the mixed pork, squid and shrimp is lighter. Start with teppan plates like grilled squid with salt and lemon or chicken thigh with ponzu. Negi-tonpei, modern-yaki and a butter-mentaiko yakisoba round it out. Ingredients are big, and service is skilled and quick. Closed Tuesdays; lunch at weekends only.

It sits on EDION Namba's 9th-floor ramen street. The broth is rich tonkotsu shoyu made, the shop says, with an extraordinary amount of domestic pork bones and chicken carcasses. It comes over thick, firm noodles with spinach in place of green onion, plus nori, and garlic and ginger on the table. Rice is free, in a large size if you like. An ajitama ramen with nori and small rice was ¥1,250 in October 2026. A limited "Musajirō" Jirō-style bowl (¥1,300) piles on vegetables, back fat and garlic. Reviewers call it consistent, classic iekei, if not remarkable.

The shellfish-broth ramen hits with salt and umami at once, over smooth, medium-thick curly whole-wheat noodles; add black pepper halfway. At weekday lunch, large noodles and rice are free. Prices run high, and two reviewers found the service brusque.

places.notes: [Tsukemen · Kyoto-born rich tsukemen on EDION's ramen floor] A branch of Menya Takei, a tsukemen shop with its main branch in Kyoto, on EDION Namba's 9th-floor ramen street, and one regular's favourite there. Rich tsukemen runs about ¥1,200–1,280, and the special with ajitama was ¥1,540 in October 2026. There's also a rich chuka soba (¥1,150) and a spicy topping (¥150). One diner likened it to a Kansai take on Noroshi. Another found it just normally good for the price, and a regular felt the noodles had softened lately. Open all afternoon.

places.cu: Yakuzen (medicinal-herb) spice curry, gluten-free · three-curry "san-mi ittai" set: soy-milk tomato chicken, black-sesame red-miso pork-hijiki keema, mackerel and lotus-root green curry ¥1,600–3,880 · vegan curry line ¥1,700–1,900 · basmati and 15-grain rice · roast chicken leg ¥1,280 · GF bar drinks and natural wine · 14 seats
places.notes: [Curry · gluten-free yakuzen spice curry by Dotonbori] A 14-seat curry café and evening bar run on a "food as medicine" concept by a yakuzen (medicinal-cooking) specialist. Everything is gluten-free by the shop's own account. The signature is three curries to mix: a soy-milk, onion, tomato and ginger chicken-breast curry; a black-sesame and red-miso pork-and-hijiki keema; and a mackerel and lotus-root "green Popeye" curry. Each is tangy and spiced, and they come together into one flavour when mixed. They sit over basmati and 15-grain rice (Simple ¥1,600; Standard ¥2,000 with soup, salad and toppings). A separate vegan line covers root-vegetable, soy-mince salsa and tropical chickpea curries. At night it becomes a bar with GF drinks, natural wine and tapas. English menu; book online.

places.cu: Egyptian café and shisha bar · koshari · ta'ameya (falafel) · hummus with pita · garlicky molokhia soup · shish tawook chicken plate ~¥1,600–1,800 · kahk and baklava · hibiscus juice, mint tea · shisha ¥2,200 · halal options · dance-show events
places.notes: [Middle Eastern · an Egyptian café and shisha bar in Amemura] A moody, Egyptian-styled café on the 3rd floor of a building in Amerikamura that serves lunch and runs as a shisha bar at night, with occasional dance shows. Staff explain the dishes and share stories about Egypt. Order koshari, the national dish of rice, macaroni and lentils in tomato sauce under crisp fried onions, with garlic vinegar and chili oil to season. There's also ta'ameya (Egyptian falafel), hummus with pita, a rich, garlicky molokhia soup, and shish tawook chicken plates (about ¥1,600–1,800). Finish with baklava or kahk and hibiscus juice or mint tea. Tabelog lists vegan, vegetarian and halal options. Opening days vary, so check Instagram or book. On event nights, food can take an hour.
places.chef: Opened 23 August 2020 (Tabelog) · An Egyptian restaurant and shisha café; operating days announced on Instagram (Tabelog remarks). No source names the operator. · Koshari; Egyptian home cooking.
places.gfd: Ask. Koshari contains macaroni and hummus comes with pita, but rice plates and grilled skewers may suit; nothing is described as gluten-free.
places.vgd: Tabelog lists vegan, vegetarian and halal options. The Egyptian menu includes koshari (rice, macaroni and lentils with tomato sauce and fried onion), ta'ameya falafel, hummus with pita and molokhia soup. None is described as vegan in reviews, so ask about ghee, stock and dairy.

places.notes: [Sweets · Namba's famous crêpes and galettes] A 50-seat French crêperie up steep stairs just south of Dotonbori, named to Tabelog's Sweets WEST "100" in 2023 and 2026, with a takeout line downstairs. The crêpes, made with French flour, Échiré butter and salt, are crisp at the edge and chewy inside. The plain Échiré butter and sugar is the one regulars call the best they've had. At lunch, try a daily galette from the blackboard, say beef stew over mashed potato and cheese, or tandoori chicken, in the crêperie lunch (¥2,200, October 2026). There's also a milk-jam crêpe set with vanilla gelato (¥1,480), quiche and Mont Blanc. The takeout queue is about 10 minutes. Cash only.

Smoothies are made to order from fresh vegetables and fruit, like the smooth green komatsuna, apple and banana, or a seasonal peach. There are also matcha crêpes with shiratama (¥700), lattes and bagels for a light bite. Service at the kiosk can be brisk when it's busy with overseas visitors.

À la carte, fried rice is ¥770 and stir-fried squid with garlic chives ¥820 (September 2026). Prices hold to the menu, with no extras. Service is quiet to curt, and you order on your phone. Cash only.

Autumn 2026 brought a limited hot-and-sour ramen, lighter than the usual thick suan-la, just right for some and refreshing for others. A ramen, gyoza, fried rice and beer set makes a hearty lunch.

Charcoal-grilled Kyushu-style yakitori comes as shareable pieces rather than skewers: an assorted three kinds is ¥1,320 (April 2026), alongside grilled vegetables (¥1,078) and fried mehikari (¥858). Finish with kamameshi, rice cooked to order in an iron pot, like the chicken soboro and burdock, so order it early. Ordering is by LINE. The upstairs can get smoky from the grill, and there's a pleasant terrace. Note the name: Tabelog lists it as Nakamoto, while several 2026 reviews call it "Yakitori to Kamameshi Gotchin".

places.notes: [Chinese · malatang with a beef-bone white broth in Nippombashi] A clean, 20-seat malatang shop a few minutes from Nippombashi, relaxed enough when reviewers came that you can take your time at the ingredient case. The difference is the broth: beef bone, and the original white version is rich enough at zero spice to taste like ramen soup. Vegetables soaked in it, broccoli especially, are the reviewers' pick. Spice runs from 0 up to a numbing level 3 at least, and chili oil comes on the side. One mala fan ranks it third of 19 places tried. Spend over ¥1,000, as most do, and a can from the fridge is free. The aroma inside takes a minute to get used to.

places.notes: [Ramen · late-night abura-soba in Amemura] A new Roman shop, opened on 20 September 2026 among the Amerika-mura live houses and open until 5 am. Roman is an Osaka brand that began in Morinomiya in 2022. The abura-soba (¥850) is the plain, steady kind, on thick, curly house-made noodles cut short enough to slurp. Reviewers douse it in vinegar and chili oil, add garlic or kimchi, and find it not greasy at all. The mazesoba (¥1,000) comes with more sauce than expected and a strong soy edge, and there is a Taiwanese mazesoba. After 10 pm the shop adds something the name doesn't promise: a smooth, milky tonkotsu ramen on thin straight noodles (¥900; ¥1,100 piled with chashu), creamy but light enough for that hour. You buy a ticket at the machine; about three tables and eight counter seats.

places.notes: [Korean · Japanese-Korean sundubu in Namba Walk] A calm, 17-seat sundubu shop in the Namba Walk underground mall, by Nippombashi Station, here for about a year by autumn 2026. The soft-tofu stew is rich and sweet beneath the heat. Spice runs from 1 to 4, with 2 as standard. Several reviewers found 3 easy going, and 1 not spicy at all. Sets come with rice and three small sides, and a scoop of lychee sorbet arrives at the end. The Namba-only sundubu ramen puts noodles in the stew (one visitor added rice for ¥100), though one reviewer compared the noodles to boiled dried noodles rather than real ramen. Other picks are the grilled-pork sundubu with clams and minced meat, grilled-cheese sundubu ramen, and Wakan herb cold noodles. The manager runs the floor attentively; you buy a ticket at the entrance. Tabelog spells the name "Juraku"; the kana じゅろく reads Juroku.

places.notes: [Ramen · Wakayama-style ramen until dawn on Dotonbori] A Wakayama-style ramen shop by the Sōemonchō end of Dotonbori, open from 9 am until 5 am (6 am on Fridays, Saturdays and the night before a holiday), full of tourists from home and abroad. The Kishu Wakayama ramen (¥950 before tax, September 2026) is a soy-tonkotsu bowl on thin noodles. There's a light option, a rich one, and an "aged" ramen, which one July 2026 reviewer found just right in flavor and fat as an after-drinks bowl. Also on the menu: a shrimp-heavy tsukemen, and in September a limited Japanese-style tororo cold ramen (¥1,210) with chicken chashu and a tempura egg on chilled thin noodles. Opinions split in autumn 2026. One returning visitor found the broth weak and lukewarm, while another drank every drop. Watch the menu: the big number is before tax. You pay on the way out.

places.notes: [Ramen · mapo tofu ramen under Higashi-Shinsaibashi] The Shinsaibashi branch of a mapo-tofu-ramen specialist from Naramachi, Nara, in a calm, chic basement with a long counter, tables and a projector. The Nara shop describes made-to-order mapo on smooth, chewy medium-thick noodles, and one reviewer ended up sweating and ordering rice for the leftover sauce. A limited bowl changes through the year. October 2026 brought a seafood and meat-miso mazesoba (¥1,300) with egg yolk, fish powder, chives and bean sprouts on thick, chewy noodles. Summer had a chilled basil mapo ramen. Finish with saba-dashi rice (¥300). The shop says it offers vegetarian and halal options; ask the staff. One October 2026 visitor found it empty at Friday lunch and had to call for service.

The menu is Middle Eastern and Mediterranean, and the shop says it covers vegetarian, vegan and gluten-free diners; tell them when you book. The reviewed vegan plate is the domestic-corn tartine on rye bread, with sweet charred corn, hummus, avocado, tomato and marinated onions. One September 2026 diner found that nothing felt missing. Falafel pita sandwiches and grilled-chicken shawarma lead at lunch. Breakfast runs to English breakfast, Turkish eggs and a smoked-salmon bagel. The coffee is roasted in-house. English menu and English-speaking staff.

places.notes: [Curry · halal Pakistani biryani under Shinsaibashi-suji] A basement Pakistani and Arab kitchen by Shinsaibashi Station that calls itself a halal restaurant, with halal wagyu on its own site. Tabelog has listed it among its 100 best for curry (2019–2020) and Asian/ethnic food (2022–2024). Biryani is what it's known for: ¥1,600 à la carte, or a huge ¥1,000 lunch plate with a drink (October 2026). Vegetarians have real choices: an eggplant-and-potato baingan aloo (¥1,200), the potato samosa (¥800), and a falafel set with hummus and Arabic pickles (¥2,000). The spinach-heavy palak paneer has cheese, and nobody says whether ghee is used, so vegans should ask. Tables fill with visitors from around the world. Closed Thursdays.

Every house dressing is vegan and additive-free, made without white sugar, eggs, dairy or honey (shop text), and the coconut-lemon oil dressing is refreshing in summer. Sweets include a gluten-free lemon cake with pistachio and vegan chocolate-chip cookies, and lattes come with soy, oat or almond milk. places.notes: [Ramen · Yukuhashi kurobuta tonkotsu on the EDION 9F ramen floor] The Namba Ramen Ichiza branch of Kanadaya, a tonkotsu shop from Yukuhashi in Fukuoka. Its Kurobuta ramen (¥980, October 2026) comes in a thick, creamy broth whipped to a fine foam that reviewers compare to a cappuccino. One reviewer credits that to kurobuta bones simmered for over 20 hours. It's rich but not funky, on thin straight noodles you can order firm. Toppings are three large charred slices of chashu, kikurage, green onion and a big sheet of nori, and pickled mustard greens and red ginger sit on the table. Add the B set (rice and three kara-age, ¥460) or grilled gyoza. One reviewer rates it thicker than Ichiran or Ippudo. It's often quiet before noon, a rare hearty tonkotsu in Namba with no line.

places.notes: [Ramen · Sendai abura-soba on the EDION 9F ramen floor] An abura-soba shop from Sendai that opened on the Namba Ramen Ichiza floor in December 2025. The original Sendai abura-soba (¥1,150) is mild on its own: chewy medium-thick noodles in a light sauce, under grilled "toro" meat soft enough to melt, half an egg, green onion and nori. You build it yourself with the vinegar and chili oil the sign tells you to add (twice), plus pepper or Sichuan pepper. Beyond it are a punchy G-style bowl with pork fat and garlic, a Taiwanese mazesoba (¥1,150), a rich two-cheese mazesoba with egg yolk (¥1,200) and a tsukimi abura-soba with tororo (¥950). Summer brought a chilled soy-milk tantan mazesoba. There's also a clear Date's salt ramen. Mix the leftover sauce with rice (¥100), or add beef-tongue curry (¥400). Spacious, clean, counter and tables.

places.notes: [Ramen · Amemura's original niboshi tsukemen] Suzume's 12-seat counter in Amerika-mura has been pouring tsukemen since 2010, and people still queue outside. The dipping broth is niboshi-based but smooth and deep. One reviewer, back after 15 years in Tokyo, still calls it the original taste of tsukemen. It's rich with seafood umami, for thick, chewy noodles you can have at 200 g or 300 g for the same price. The cult order is the spicy tsukemen (¥1,000), with heat levels; level 2 is rich rather than fierce. Swap in the red, chili-infused noodles for ¥30. The special (¥1,300) adds thick, tender chashu. Mix, taste, then add vinegar and chili oil. Some long-time regulars feel it isn't quite what it was. Cash only.

places.cu: Wagyu ramen served course-style · Osaka wagyu ramen 100 g ¥3,900, 250 g ¥6,900, 450 g ¥10,900 · chicken-bone and flying-fish (ago) shoyu broth · medium-thin wavy noodles from Taiyo Seimenjo · an ago-dashi starter with gold leaf · grilled flying fish ground to powder at the table · wagyu finished on a small teppan
places.notes: [Ramen · course-style wagyu ramen in Nippombashi] A new evening ramen counter that opened on 29 June 2026 in the former Men no Hiromiya space by Nippombashi. It is a new concept from the Dotonbori tonkatsu shop "Ganso 5cm Katsu Don" (review), and the price matches the show: ¥3,900 for 100 g of wagyu, up to ¥10,900 for 450 g. It runs like a little course. A flying-fish dashi with gold leaf comes first. Then a grilled flying fish is cut with scissors and ground into powder in a mortar, and the chef adds it to your bowl. The ramen is a low-viscosity chicken-bone and flying-fish shoyu, light and smooth with a mild seafood sweetness, on chewy medium-thin wavy noodles from Taiyo Seimenjo. The seasoned wagyu flank arrives on a small teppan over a burner so you can cook it to your liking. Only one review so far (July 2026).

Lunch sets come with egg-drop soup, side dishes good enough to be mains, almond jelly and free rice refills. Go after 2 pm to skip the queue. Dinner adds xiao long bao, spicy chicken and water spinach (draft beer is ¥950), and booking is wise.

places.notes: [Café · high-protein bowls in Kitahorie] A small healthy-bowl café in Kitahorie, three minutes from Nishi-Ohashi, popular with gym-goers and dog owners (it even sells jerky for dogs). The house PROTEIN LAB bowl (¥1,600) comes with very tender chicken breast, and there's a Mexican bowl (¥1,480). The fun is at the counter: free, unlimited kimchi, spicy garlic chives, garlic and rice, which turn the mild soup into a stamina bowl. You sit on low tatami platforms without backrests, and you might wonder about shoes. It's built for after drinking, or a ten-minute breakfast.

places.notes: [Chinese · shark fin in the Daimaru food hall] A stall of Nihombashi Kojuken, a well-known shark-fin restaurant, in the B2F food hall of Daimaru Shinsaibashi, often featured on Kansai TV. The No. 2 seller is the mapo tofu set, hot from the start and finishing on Sichuan pepper. Seating is self-service and crowded with tourists at weekends. One long-time visitor finds nearly ¥3,000 too much for lunch now.

places.notes: [Kushikatsu · rice-flour kushikatsu on Nankai-dori] A 50-seat kushikatsu house a minute from Nankai Namba, open since 2012 and often with a line. The difference is the batter: rice flour instead of wheat, fried in plant-based oils, so the skewers come out ultra-thin and crisp. October 2026 reviewers found it light on the stomach. That's not a gluten-free claim, though; breadcrumbs, sauces and the shared fryer aren't described, so coeliacs should ask. The skewers are big: plump shrimp, excellent pork, a soft quail egg (best with the white soy sauce), plus tulip wings and asparagus. Dip in the special sauce, grilled salt or white soy, and start with doteyaki. Frying happens downstairs, so the second floor stays free of oil smells. places.notes: [Ramen · Yokohama iekei at the east end of Dotonbori] A Yokohama iekei shop that opened in April 2026 near Nippombashi. Reviewers call it a direct branch of Daikiya, a well-known Tokyo iekei shop, and there's already a queue of 7–20 at peak times. The broth is very thick pork bone with a sharp soy edge, served with spinach, nori and a seasoned egg; set firmness, richness and oil to taste. Several people warn it's very salty, so start mild if you're not used to iekei. The smoked chashu is the star. Rice is ¥100 for all you can eat, from a self-serve bar of garlic, mayonnaise and a spicy sauce; wrap it in nori dipped in the broth. Tsukemen (large ¥1,150) has a slightly spicy pork-and-chicken dip, with hot or cold noodles. Buy a ticket at the machine; open 10 am to midnight.

places.notes: [Thai · Shinsaibashi's long-running Thai house, open to 2 am] A 100-seat Thai restaurant in Higashi-Shinsaibashi, open since 2000 and often full. The reliable orders are koh muu yang, grilled pork neck charred outside with a spicy sauce, and gai yang chicken thigh with a nam pla dip. The yam woon sen glass-noodle salad is packed with shrimp, clams and minced seafood, and the pad thai is a regular's craving. Expect real heat even in dishes you thought were mild. For a late finish there's pho in a hot pot, with mango pudding or coconut ice cream. Portions suit two or three people sharing. A long-time regular thinks prices have crept up.

places.notes: [Ramen · Onomichi-style back-fat soy ramen off Shinsaibashi-suji] An eight-seat counter a block from the Shinsaibashi shopping street, open since 2011, with the nostalgic feel of an old Chinese eatery and the TV on. The Onomichi ramen is a light soy-and-niboshi broth with flecks of back fat and a touch of heat, with sweet chashu. The shoyu mixes soy and tonkotsu, gentle enough to drink to the last drop, and there are also shio and tonkotsu bowls. The owner asks whether you want the noodles firm. Gyoza and a fragrant, moist fried rice round it out. It fills up with overseas visitors at lunch. Buy a ticket; cash only. Smoking is allowed.

places.notes: [Café · gluten-free, additive-free café by Nagahoribashi] A calm, natural-materials café three minutes from Nagahoribashi, open from 7:30 am. Its own billing is gluten-free, additive-free and free of white sugar. Lunch runs to rice-flour craft burgers and a gluten-free curry whose spices win over doubters, plus a Buddha bowl of rice and fermented vegetables and quinoa-mixed rice. One reviewer credits the recipes to a physical therapist. The sweets are the draw: a light, moist brown-rice-flour chiffon (¥700), a kinako chocolate cake, lemon cake and cheesecake to take away, with oat-milk coffee (¥650). Evenings switch to a casual French-style dinner. Portions are modest. Closed Tuesdays; check Instagram, as event days change the hours.

There are owner-chosen wines and seasonal sake. All seats were smoking-friendly in late 2025.

Many local workers know it. The striking bowl is the black tonkotsu shoyu (¥1,000; ¥1,590 with everything) in black-garlic oil. It's rich in pork bone without any funk and not heavy, though one reviewer found it mild until two spoons of garlic went in. A back-fat ramen rides on thin, straight, firm noodles. For a junky finish after drinking, regulars order the abura-soba with garlic, minced meat and green onion. Extra noodles are ¥220, which adds up. Pay as you leave; cash.

Of note for gluten-avoiders, the chain's menu includes an allergen-free curry made without wheat, egg, milk, buckwheat, peanut, shrimp or crab. The sauce is served in its sealed package for safety, at ¥464 with 200 g of rice. Not every branch carries it, so ask first. A May 2026 visitor ordered the low-carb curry on cauliflower rice. Regulars also come for spinach curry with crispy chicken, a summer eggplant-okra-tomato chicken curry, or hayashi rice. Mostly overseas staff; one diner found them unsure about coupons. Rarely crowded.

places.notes: [Ramen · Kyushu tonkotsu and tomato ramen opposite NGK] A branch of the Kyushu Ramen Kio chain facing Namba Grand Kagetsu, with tablet ordering, open until midnight. The signature Kio ramen is a creamy, rich tonkotsu mellowed for Kansai palates, with no gaminess, on ultra-thin straight noodles. One reviewer ordered the extra noodles extra-firm and got them almost raw. A long-standing favourite is the tomato ramen (¥890), spicy at three levels and milder than Shin Ramyun; there's a tomato tsukemen too. For something heavier, the burnt-back-fat tonkotsu shoyu with thick noodles and lots of garlic works as a gentle Jiro-style. Summer brings a chilled abura-soba (¥890), and the half fried rice is ¥490. A lunch mix of tourists and local office workers.

places.notes: [Ramen · Kamukura in PARCO's basement dining street] A 24-seat Kamukura on the B2F dining street of Shinsaibashi PARCO, a minute from Shinsaibashi Station. The basic bowl stays under ¥1,000, and the braised-egg ramen has a runny yolk. Build it up from the table: garlic, doubanjiang and chives turn it into a hearty, spicy bowl. A winter special ran in early 2026. A line forms at the ticket machine when tourists arrive, but turnover is quick.

places.notes: [Ramen · Lake Shinji shijimi-clam ramen near Nippombashi] The Namba branch of Shi43ya, a shijimi-clam ramen shop, hidden at the very back of a mixed-use building three minutes from Nippombashi. The No. 1 order is the rich shijimi shio (¥1,100, September 2026), made with plenty of Yamato shijimi from Lake Shinji in Shimane: light, low in fat and packed with clam umami. There are miso and shoyu versions too, and the clam rice with egg is popular. One reviewer counts it among Namba's best clam-broth bowls. In summer the cold ramen with shijimi turns rich once you stir in the oyster paste. Spring 2026 brought a dashi-keema mazesoba with the curry shop Niji no Hotoke. It's light enough to finish a night out; open until 12:30 am. Cash only.

Service is by verbal order; one August 2026 visitor had a rough exchange with the kitchen staff. Cash only.

places.notes: [Ramen · Ippudo in Minami-Horie, with a branch-only shoyu tonkotsu] Hakata Ippudo's Horie branch, three minutes from Yotsubashi. The classic Akamaru Shinaji (¥980) adds spicy miso and fragrant oil to the rich tonkotsu; the Shiromaru is the plain version. Exclusive to this branch is a shoyu tonkotsu (¥950) with soy, back fat and garlic chives on slightly thicker noodles; pair it with a small Hakata fried rice (¥430). Tsukemen fans get thick noodles in a red-oil meat-miso dip, or a limited tantan version (¥1,090). Extra noodles are ¥150, with bean sprouts, takana and pickled ginger now ordered on the touch panel. Staff service is well drilled.

places.cu: Yokohama iekei, direct line of Oudouya · ramen ¥1,000 with two big slices of chashu, spinach and three nori · smoked chashu ramen and chashu rice · Oudou ramen with rice · famous horumon fry · kara-age · firmness, richness and oil to order · unlimited garlic, chopped ginger and mayonnaise at the table · open from 7 am
places.notes: [Ramen · Oudouya-line iekei by JR Namba, open from 7 am] A Yokohama iekei shop in the basement of Minatomachi River Place, a minute from JR Namba, in the direct line of the famous Oudouya. Open December 2024, it runs from 7 am to 3 am and still has a 15-person queue after midnight. The ramen (¥1,000) is a pork-bone soy broth with the sharp soy edge of the style and pork-and-chicken umami, on chewy medium-thick noodles, with two big slices of chashu, spinach and three nori sheets. The smoked chashu is the star of the chashu ramen and chashu rice. Order firmness, richness and oil to taste, then load up on the table garlic, chopped ginger and mayonnaise. The fried horumon is a known side. One devotee calls it Osaka's No. 1 iekei; the saltiness varies visit to visit. Cash only.

It's usually run by one person, so service can be slow or brisk; one 2026 visitor found it unfriendly, another the staff kind.

places.notes: [Izakaya · creative oden and regional sake upstairs on Shinsaibashi-suji] A 14-seat second-floor oden bar off Shinsaibashi-suji with a strong local feel and a crowded counter that makes room for you. The oden is the creative kind: tomato, soy-milk sake-kasu, and an Italian-style pot finished with risotto. Avocado with wasabi is a repeat visitor's favourite. The sake list is the other draw, with bottles from all over Japan, some rare in Osaka, split on a blackboard into chilled and warm. Some find the seasoning light or the prices high for what you get. The owner and staff are friendly, and the room went non-smoking in 2026. Phone to check for seats.

places.cu: Tabelog 100 yakiniku and meat kaiseki (Yakiniku/Grill WEST 2023–2026) · omakase ¥19,800, one seating · aged Matsusaka and aged Miyazaki wagyu · wagyu-bone broth with clam · yukhoe · aged tuna and seasonal à la carte · finish with as much yakiniku as you want · wine pairing · 10 counter seats
places.notes: [Yakiniku · a 10-seat aged-wagyu omakase in Hozenji Yokocho] A reservation-only counter of ten seats in Hozenji Yokocho, on Tabelog's yakiniku and grill 100 lists every year from 2023 to 2026. The operator, Plan Do Action Co., is led by Hiroyuki Takeshita, born in Miyazaki Prefecture in 1976, who grew up around pigs and cattle and became a chef to bring cooking into the livestock business. There's one seating at 7 pm and one menu, the ¥19,800 omakase, and bookings run months out. It plays like meat kaiseki more than a grill: a broth of wagyu bones and water with a touch of clam, a yukhoe, aged tuna and seasonal plates, all built on aged Matsusaka and aged Miyazaki wagyu bought straight from producers. At the end you can have as much yakiniku as you like, though one diner was already full by then; the chefs grill it in front of you. Wine pairings are good. A 10% service charge applies. A September 2026 review says a restaurant group runs it.
