places.cu: Oden and seasonal Japanese dishes · omakase 10-dish course ¥6,000 · clam oden and Tajima-chicken oden in a deep dashi · whale, sardines and seasonal fish · a wide Japanese-sake list (sake omakase) · 10 counter seats, run by one owner
places.notes: [Oden · a one-owner oden counter in Hozenji Yokocho] A ten-seat counter in Hozenji Yokocho, run single-handed by a friendly owner who keeps drinks and dishes moving. The draw is oden in a carefully built dashi, gentle but deep, especially the clam and Tajima-chicken oden. Around it come seasonal plates: whale, sardines, meat and fish. The omakase of ten dishes (¥6,000) is the way in, and there's a broad Japanese-sake list with an omakase pour. It's quiet and calm, good for a slow drink. Book online, as it's often full by 7 pm. With one person running everything, dishes can take a moment. No children under elementary-school age.

places.notes: [Ramen · a kissa that's really a handmade-noodle ramen counter, Amemura] It looks like a coffee shop, but Kissa Shiroinu is a serious ten-seat ramen and curry counter near Amerika-mura, run quietly by an owner who once ran a rock bar. Self-taught, the owner makes the noodles in-house; a sign talks up the flour. The shoyu ramen (¥770, September 2026) is a bargain for the area, strong on niboshi with fish powder, gentle and rich without being heavy. The shoyu-and-mini-curry set (¥1,100) shows the curry could be a main in its own right. Late at night there's a back-fat shoyu, a curry tsukemen and an iron-pan tamago kake gohan. Open until 1:30 am most nights; closed Mondays.

places.notes: [Ramen · Kotan's classic soy-tonkotsu in the Namba CITY basement] A branch of Kotan, a long-running Osaka ramen chain, in the B2F food floor of Namba CITY by Nankai Namba. It's open straight through, handy when you miss lunch. Kotan's signature is a soy-and-tonkotsu broth with shredded carrot and crunchy bean sprouts, on straight noodles a little thicker than medium; add the sesame on the table. Fans return for the nostalgic taste, and one came back after 15 years. A shio version exists, though the shoyu is the comfort order, and there's a vegetable-heavy nananmen. Fried-rice sets are popular but uneven. Summer brings cold noodles and a chilled tantanmen. The counters are well spaced, service is quick, and Namba CITY cardholders get 10% off. Closed the third Thursday.

places.notes: [Thai · a Thai-run kitchen by the Kuromon Market entrance] A 24-seat Thai restaurant on the corner by the Kuromon Market entrance, a minute from Nippombashi; don't mix it up with the similar Thai place two doors down. It's run by Thai staff, Thai is the language in the room, and plenty of Thai customers eat here, a good sign. The spice isn't softened for Japanese palates. The yum woon sen is a standout, balancing lime, fish sauce and cilantro. The gapao is authentic, and the tom yum goong and coconut-rich green curry draw praise. The lunch sets (¥1,100 in 2025) are the value play; à la carte prices have climbed, and one diner found the portions small for Kuromon-area prices. Service can slow when busy. Closed Tuesdays.

places.notes: [Ramen · an eight-seat machi-chuka by Yotsubashi] A long-standing, old-fashioned local Chinese counter of eight seats on the south side of Yotsubashi Station, cheap and fast, mostly men at lunch. You squeeze past each other to reach the back. The shoyu ramen has a nostalgic, slightly sweet broth, thin wavy noodles with a good bite, bean sprouts, nori and thick marinated chashu. Order it as a half to pair with something: half tantanmen and half shoyu is ¥800. There's also a shio butter-corn ramen and gyoza. The five-dish set meal (¥1,000) piles a Chinese omelette, happosai, kara-age and chashu over cabbage with rice, and a Chinese rice bowl is just ¥650. Cash only; closed Saturdays.

places.notes: [Ramen · Tabelog 100 oyster ramen on Doguyasuji] A 15-seat oyster-ramen shop on the Doguyasuji kitchenware street, two minutes from Namba, named to Tabelog's Ramen OSAKA 100 for 2025. The house bowl is "Koeru", a triple-soup oyster paitan whose rich oyster umami and slight bitterness come through in every sip, with a citrus lift. There's also "Ikasu", an oyster dashi, plus oyster shoyu and a white version. Soft noodles and juicy, not-greasy chashu carry it; add the table spices for a change. Fried oysters come with salt and lemon, and the shirasu rice bowl with sesame is the side. The room is unusual too, with projection mapping. Buy your ticket outside and wait to be called; queues are mostly overseas visitors.

places.notes: [Ramen · a Chiikawa-character Jiro-style ramen shop in PARCO] A character collaboration in PARCO's B2F, decorated top to bottom in Chiikawa style down to the bowls, ladles, aprons, cups and chopstick wrappers. Fans book ahead and still wait up to an hour; the lift opens at 11 am. The ramen is Jiro-style, but gentler than the real thing: a garlicky soy broth that's lighter, with softer fat, on chewy thick noodles. You call your garlic, vegetables, fat and seasoning. Even "mini" is a full meal, and most people order it; a large with extra vegetables and fat runs ¥1,950. Reviewers split between delicious and "mainly for the merchandise", but the cuteness is the point.

places.notes: [Gyoza · Osaka Ohsho in Amerika-mura, open past midnight] The Amerika-mura branch of the Osaka Ohsho gyoza-and-Chinese chain, in a bright, glass-fronted room three minutes from Yotsubashi. It opens at 9 am and stays open past midnight, to 1:30 am on Fridays and Saturdays, busy with tourists late at night. Gyoza are the obvious order; one diner regretted picking the sweet-and-sour pork set over gyoza. The menu is long: strong-flavored ramen, cold noodles in summer, fried rice and a sauce-covered chahan, "TOKYO niku-si" fried rice with gyoza, and an authentic-tasting shrimp chili with a beer set. Portions are big. PayPay or cash.

places.notes: [Ramen · a seven-seat creamy chicken paitan in Kitahorie] A seven-seat counter near Yotsubashi, often with a line, serving a chicken paitan covered in fine foam: smooth and rich, the chicken clear without heaviness. The bowl carries three chashu, including low-temperature pork loin and chicken breast, plus shredded leek, mizuna and onion. One menma lover calls the thick, tender, well-soaked bamboo shoots the best ever. Noodles are medium-thick and straight; one August diner got them undercooked. A yodare-chicken rice bowl is the side. In 2026 a touch panel replaced the ticket machine, beef options joined the menu, and a younger crew took over; one long-time fan misses the old feel. It gets warm inside. Cash only.

places.notes: [Udon · late-night udon and soba in the Soemoncho bar district] A ten-seat udon and soba stand next to a club in Soemoncho, open at lunch and again from 6 pm until 3 am, or 6 am on Fridays and Saturdays. It's busy late with people from nearby bars and quiet earlier. Expect a gentle Kansai dashi, chewy udon and decent soba. A January 2026 diner also liked the katsudon, neither too sweet nor too salty. The menu is long, from kakiage udon to oden and a sea-urchin cream udon you can finish as risotto. Critics call it station-stand quality at nightlife prices, but it's quick, served in about a minute. Buy a ticket; some items are ordered verbally. Prices quoted here are from 2024–2025 reviews.

places.notes: [Yakitori · a one-owner charcoal yakitori hideaway north of Dotonbori] A 14-seat yakitori counter tucked into the ground floor of a mixed-use building north of Dotonbori, run by an owner who manages the room alone and still serves quickly. It grills Yamato chicken and Kawachi duck over charcoal. The duck sashimi in several cuts is the signature, and the chicken sashimi is limited, so order it ahead. Raw duck liver, negima and skin skewers, potato salad and an excellent tamagoyaki fill out the evening. Courses run from ¥3,300 (five duck sashimi and five skewers, October 2025) to ¥5,500 (January 2026). There's a good Japanese-whisky list and wine to pair. It closes when sold out, so book. places.notes: [Sushi · a young Edomae counter in Hozenji Yokocho] A ten-seat sushi counter behind a soft green noren in Hozenji Yokocho, open since October 2025 and already packed with Japanese diners as well as visitors. The head chef was just 25 when reviewed, working alongside a more experienced chef, aged 40-something, who had recently returned from Australia. A very young team runs it. Nothing is bought in ready-made: kanpyo, dashi and desserts are all house-made. The dinner omakase (¥14,300, August 2026) moves through aged sea bream, Aomori flounder, bonito marinated with katsuobushi, kasugo, and sweet squid sent unfrozen from Kushimoto, with anago brushed with a sauce from its own bones. The rice is large-grained, lightly pressed and punchy with vinegar, salt kept low. A white-miso pudding closes. There's a lunch course too. Book, and note the shop doesn't take guests who can't eat raw food.

places.notes: [Kappo · a monthly-changing omakase counter at the Hozenji Yokocho entrance] A small kappo counter at the mouth of Hozenji Yokocho, where an owner-chef does nearly all the cooking and the omakase changes every month, so regulars come back each season. An older review notes the chef's wife helping in the room, and that the chef had recently become a father. A June 2026 meal opened with an assorted platter featuring a rarely seen fish and tiny junsai, then sashimi on a block of ice, sweet swordfish and grilled conger eel with plum. The chef quietly adjusted one dish for a diner's bonito allergy. Earlier courses brought a Yanagawa-style hot pot; there are about eight courses with dessert. There's no drink list as such: the chef picks the sake, and the homemade fruit sour is good. Some guests leave with onigiri. Expect roughly ¥10,000–30,000 a head. Closed Wednesdays.

places.notes: [Ramen · shellfish shio in a kaiseki-style room by Nankai Namba] The sister shop of Men ni Hikari o, two minutes from Nankai Namba, in a modern-Japanese room that feels more kaiseki than ramen bar, with a queue of 20 at opening. The signature is "Kai no Hikari" (¥1,290), a shio of Hiroshima oysters, clams and dried seafood. It's light yet packed with flavor, served piping hot with a breath of yuzu, on smooth medium-straight noodles from Hinomoto Seimen, topped with chashu, menma and ikura. A sansho version (special ¥1,670) adds a gentle numbing note to the shellfish. The special shoyu (¥1,570) is a clear, deep-amber bowl with assorted chashu and mitsuba. Every bowl is plated like a work of art. Cash only; closed Wednesdays and Thursdays.

places.notes: [Ramen · a late-night iekei counter by Nippombashi] A clean, counter-only Yokohama iekei shop two minutes from Nippombashi, open until 3 am; one reviewer heads to the sauna afterward. The chashu ramen with quail eggs and nori is a classic combination, and the tsukemen has firm, springy noodles in a rich dip. Two staff keep it moving quickly. It's a balanced, crowd-pleasing take on the style, which one reviewer believes is independently franchised.

places.notes: [Ramen · medicinal-herb tantanmen by Yotsubashi] A tantanmen specialist a minute from Yotsubashi, open since March 2026, built on more than 20 medicinal herbs, per the staff. There are two styles: the signature Kyoto-style white tantanmen, sesame-rich with a herbal edge, and a Sichuan-style red one (¥1,200; large ¥1,400). A September 2026 diner found the Sichuan soy-milk version thin, so start with the Kyoto. Summer brought a chilled Kyoto-style bowl (¥1,300) that a reviewer likened to a famous Shijo-Omiya shop in Kyoto. Add the staff's recommended herbal vinegar or the homemade doubanjiang (sold at ¥300 to take home). The fluffy lettuce fried rice is a sleeper hit. Staff explain everything to first-timers. Reviews range from a favourite to just average.

At night the ramen is ¥1,290, with a salted egg and extra garlic at ¥180 each. Tourist queues can mean a 40-minute wait, though the line is well managed. One 2:30 am visit was walk-in.

Booking is hard; one diner got in by phoning at 5:30 pm. The mapo tofu is the must-order: properly spicy, fragrant and numbing with Sichuan pepper, and one course made it with fugu milt. A Chaozhou-style kanpachi sashimi shows the range, alongside soft-shell crab in chili sauce, mayonnaise shrimp, fluffy egg with shrimp, and squid one diner couldn't imagine bettering. The popular laziji is properly hot, softened by peanuts and cilantro. The Hakata-style chive omelet, fluffy and a little runny with pickled mustard greens, cools things down, and one fan orders a chive-and-egg rice bowl for everyone, every time. Steak is the main event: A5 wagyu chuck tender or filet, with salt, wasabi, garlic, soy and truffle on the side. Lines run 30 minutes to an hour; you wait at the door and order from the menu while you queue. The draw is the special rich seafood tsukemen (¥1,200, October 2025): a pork-bone and seafood dip with chewy, almost soba-like whole-grain thick noodles, a large sheet of nori and thick-cut tender pork. A large portion costs the same; say so when you hand over your ticket. The dip can cool fast against the cold noodles. There's also a tonkotsu ramen with thin, firm noodles, milder than its pork flavor suggests, a black tonkotsu and a chashu-mayo rice bowl. Buy a ticket from the machine outside, and bring cash.

The signature is the Rosanjin tsukemen (¥1,350, October 2026; large 300 g for ¥150 more). The noodles arrive in frothy whipped kombu water made with Rausu kombu, so you taste them on their own first. Then dip them in a piping-hot shijimi-clam sauce with a faintly Western edge. A QR code at the table shows how to work through it: tororo kombu, then prosciutto with sudachi or lemon, and finally the leftover kombu water poured into the dip. There's also a light, well-balanced shio ramen. The tempura rice bowls are a hidden hit; one diner thought the egg-tempura bowl could stand as a dish on its own. Buy a ticket at the machine and bring cash. Closed Tuesdays.

places.notes: [Ramen · niboshi-tonkotsu ramen in Kuromon Market] A 12-seat counter in Kuromon Market from GENKIFACTORY, a group based in Tenma known for blending niboshi with tonkotsu. One loyal diner has been coming for about 20 years, through a relocation. The niboshi ramen pairs a pork-bone broth with domestic dried sardines and soy: easy-going, with a gentle niboshi flavor, a good balance of oil and salt, and fish powder waiting at the bottom. Medium-thick curly noodles are springy, and the chashu is thick and tender. At lunch until 3 pm, the set adds tamago kake gohan with niboshi furikake for ¥1,100 (May 2026). Two regulars usually order the tsukemen. In September 2026 a chilled shoyu ramen with frozen-broth ice was ¥1,200, and limited back-fat, shio and spicy versions ran April–June 2026. A couple of reviewers found it merely average. Buy a ticket at the machine. Closed Sundays.

The bowl is a rich, sharp soy broth with more acidity than one visitor expected, thick straight noodles with low moisture, and chashu, best with an extra heap of chopped green onion. One reviewer who knows the original Takaida shop found the same chashu and noodles here, with a slightly milder broth. Chuka soba is ¥800 and a large chashu ramen ¥1,100 (September–October 2026). There's a garlic spice on the counter. People drop in after a night out, or for a morning bowl at 8 am. One person works the shop at a time, and a service charge may be added.

places.notes: [Ramen · light tonkotsu shoyu beside Nankai Namba] A 16-seat counter right beside Nankai Namba Station, open since 2019 and good value. Every ramen here is pork-bone based, and though it looks rich and fatty it eats surprisingly light, with a depth of dashi and medium-thick noodles that soak it up. Generous crunchy green onions add to that. Say how firm you want the noodles when you hand over your ticket. Pickled ginger from the counter works well with the tonkotsu. The ramen-and-pork-bowl set is ¥1,280 (September 2026), and the pork is stir-fried after you order. There's also abura soba (¥1,000) with three slices of chashu, spicy meat mazesoba that can sell out, and tsukemen with a free large size. One diner found it a bit salty. Tabelog only says it opens at 11:00, so check closing times.

places.notes: [Standing bar · a Tabelog 100 tachinomi with no sign, behind Namba] A small standing bar just off Midosuji near Namba Hips, named to Tabelog's 2025 standing-bar 100 and a sister of Oishi Stand. There's no sign, so it's easy to walk past; the shop's Instagram says to look for it. It gets packed; one evening a regular shuffled over to make room. Reviewers note many women among the crowd, unusual for a tachinomi. Small plates make it easy to try a lot. The cream cheese with crackers, slightly sweet, won over one reviewer who doesn't usually like cream cheese, and the blue cheese has fans too. There's Shine Muscat with prosciutto as shira-ae, an Ezo venison steak served rare, and house satsuma-age with cheese, corn and edamame, fried after you order. A hamburger is limited to three servings. Expect ¥2,000–4,000. Cash only. Closed Wednesdays.

places.notes: [Burgers · American burgers and world beer by Hozenji] A stylish American-style burger bar a few steps from the Hozenji entrance, open since 2011 and drawing overseas guests too. The toasted buns get singled out; one burger hunter ranked it in a personal top three, buns especially. The cheeseburger is ¥1,480, plus ¥350 for a drink (July 2026). The bacon cheeseburger layers thick bacon over a juicy patty, and the avocado burger is creamy and rich. The tender pulled pork with an addictive barbecue sauce looks as good as it does on Instagram. A macaroni-topped burger has been on TV. The grilled-cheese sandwich comes on toasted whole-wheat bread with thick bacon and avocado, and the chef adjusted the cheese on request. The fries are crisp without being greasy. There's a long list of bottled beers from around the world. Lunch is burgers only. Closed Mondays.

places.notes: [Japanese · a hidden creative kappo by Hozenji Yokocho] A creative kappo counter with private rooms, tucked deep inside a nondescript building by Hozenji Yokocho, open since 2021. Finding the door takes some effort. The kitchen builds colorful courses on Japanese seasonal tradition. Lunch is the easy way in: a weekday mini course with seasonal clay-pot rice for ¥3,000, or ¥5,000 for more. Recent courses ran from a lotus-root dumpling in vivid broccoli sauce to fried sanma served as a salad, with crispy okra among the starters. The clay-pot rice, chestnut in autumn or corn, scallop and shiso in summer, leaves enough for seconds, and what's left is made into rice balls to take home. Several diners praise the tableware and care. One critic found the dishes pre-plated and the egg rice hard and clumped. Dinner runs about ¥8,000–15,000. Closed most Tuesdays.

places.notes: [Teppanyaki · Kobe-beef teppanyaki with a Dotonbori night view] A 14-seat teppanyaki counter on the eighth floor above Yoshinoya, looking out over the lights of Dotonbori. The head chef came up through luxury hotels (reviewers name the St. Regis Osaka and the Ritz), and the cooking shows it. You choose black wagyu, Matsusaka or Kobe beef for the omakase. A 14-course black-wagyu strip loin course was ¥12,000 (April 2026), and an anniversary course with tenderloin ¥16,000. Beyond the steak, diners rave about the seafood: crisp-skinned sea bass with shiso genovese, and teppan-fried Nagasaki horse mackerel with a pickle tartar, one diner's best ever. Wagyu dumplings in consommé and seared wagyu sushi round it out, and rice cooked in a kamado from Kyoto's Gihei closes the meal. One diner found the seasoning a little salty. Many guests are from abroad; the menu is in English and staff speak English.

places.notes: [Ramen · a six-seat morning-ramen counter in Shimanouchi] A six-seat counter in Shimanouchi, rated 3.64 on Tabelog, open since 2022 and run by the owner with one helper. The owner previously worked at Menya Joroku and runs the six-seat counter with one female staff member. It opens at 7 am on weekends, and lines can form outside by 8. The regular menu is shoyu: a chicken and seafood broth that's easy to drink to the last drop, chewy flat whole-wheat noodles from Menya Teikaku, and in the Shoyu Special (¥1,600) four kinds of chashu, from low-temperature chicken breast to hanging-roasted pork belly. The fun is the rotating bowls announced on social media. Recent ones included a cement-gray niboshi soba from Himi sardines that is clean, with no bitterness, a clear niboshi-and-scallop shio, a thick crab-and-scallop shio, and a tachiuo tsukemen with a raw-egg kamatama dip. Finish with a ¥100 bowl of rice in the leftover soup. There are no table condiments. Cash only, and bring small notes for the machine. One first-timer singled out the owner's service. Check X or Instagram for closures.

places.notes: [Ramen · a new iekei shop by Kuromon] An iekei ramen counter in a quieter part of Kuromon Market, opened in summer 2026 by an owner who trained in the Kanto region; one reviewer says at Men Master Takenaka in Tokyo. The broth is made in-house and the noodles come from Suzuki Seimen. Reviewers split on the broth: one found it bold, salty and deeply colored, others say the salt is toned down so it's easier to drink than most iekei. Either way, set firmness, richness and chicken oil to taste. The noodles are firmer and more wheaty than usual, so one diner suggests ordering them softer. Prices are fair for the market: regular ¥900, large ¥1,100, with ajitama ¥150, extra chashu ¥400 and spinach ¥200 (September–October 2026). The moist, lightly roasted chashu stands out. Get rice and wrap it in nori. The owner works fast and keeps the energy up. Cash only.

places.notes: [Ramen · Jiro-style staff-meal ramen near NGK] A Jiro-style shop a short walk from NGK, open since 2011, with 18 counter seats and a line of about ten at busy times. The menu is built on the "staff meal": a rich pork-bone broth in shoyu, shio or miso, 400 g of thick, chewy noodles even in a regular, a heap of bean sprouts, generous back fat and two thick slices of chashu. Garlic is your call; the vegetables and fat are fixed. The shoyu staff meal is ¥950 and the shio ¥980 (October 2026). There's a ladies' size, the oil can be halved, and there's a ponzu ramen made with Asahi Ponzu, and a daily-limited rich tsukemen with a ponzu tang. Fans add Tabasco or vinegar near the end to cut the richness. One longtime visitor was underwhelmed. Buy a ticket at the machine.

places.notes: [Ramen · clear tonkotsu chuka soba by Nankai Namba] A ramen shop under a bright yellow sign beside Nankai Namba Station, open since June 2025 and run, per one reviewer, by Yoshinoya Holdings. The specialty surprises people: tonkotsu that's transparent rather than cloudy, in the style of Tokyo's "chan-kei" chuka soba. It's light, with the pork's richness coming through without the heaviness, and plenty of thinly sliced chashu over smooth thin noodles. One diner found it strongly salty, another wanted more punch. Try it plain, then work through the condiments as the shop's guide suggests. The pork-bone clear soup noodles are ¥1,000 (September 2026). A menu revamp on 17 September 2026 added a back-fat chuka soba with rice for ¥880, and there's a spicy umami soba (¥1,000) with optional extra heat. Bottled beer and a ¥500 snack plate of toppings make it a quick drinking stop.

places.notes: [Abura-soba · the Ura-Namba branch of the Kirinji oil-noodle chain] A Kirinji abura-soba shop in Ura-Namba, a few minutes from Nippombashi, open since 2021. When the Sennichimae branch had a long line, one diner walked over and got straight in. Buy a ticket, and the bowl comes with medium-thick curly noodles, chashu, menma, nori and white sesame. Mix it with the vinegar and chili oil on the table; it's lighter than it looks. The soft-boiled-egg version was ¥950 in January 2026. One diner reported that saying "Kirinji" when handing over the ticket got a free egg. The chain's slogan is that three visits will get you hooked, and one fifth-time visitor agrees. Kara-age and a kara-age and TKG set round things out. Cash only.

places.notes: [Chinese · Sichuan beef noodles in Shimanouchi] A small beef-noodle shop in Shimanouchi run by a chef from Sichuan, where most customers and staff are Chinese and the ticket machine is labeled in Chinese. There's always a line, and each bowl is made with care, so allow time; one diner spent an hour from the door to the bowl. The draw is hong shao beef noodles, rich and aromatic with real Sichuan-pepper numbing. There are also premium beef noodles, a spicy beef noodle soup with tender marinated beef and chewy noodles, and a fat-intestine version. Add honeycomb tripe. You pick the numbing and the heat, and even "mild" makes people sweat. One diner found medium numbing and medium spice perfectly balanced. There's no rice to finish. Closed Sundays. Cash only.

places.notes: [Tsukemen · Shiraishi-group tsukemen in Namba, 7 am to 1 am] A 14-seat tsukemen counter in Sennichimae, opened in November 2025 by the Shiraishi group and open from 7 am to 1 am, so it covers both morning and late-night ramen. Flat, chewy whole-wheat noodles are good enough to eat plain, and a large portion is free. The dip sits over a small flame and stays boiling hot to the last bite, so mind the bowl. Choose the house kombu-water tsukemen or the rich chicken-and-seafood one (¥1,200 with an ajitama, October 2026). There's also a special rich shrimp version with sakura shrimp and a spicy tamago tsukemen. Squeeze sudachi or lime over the noodles near the end. One diner missed a soup-wari to thin the rich dip, which isn't offered. Expect a 20–30 minute line at weekend lunch. The crowd skews to visitors from abroad.

places.notes: [Yakitori · a 1958 yakitori counter by Hozenji] A 12-seat L-shaped counter a few steps from Mizukake Fudo in Hozenji Yokocho, grilling yakitori since 1958. Chicken from Ise Akadori, shamo and Tajima birds goes over Kishu binchotan. The tare is just soy sauce and sake, rich and smooth with no extra sweetness, and diners say it lets the chicken speak. First-timers must take a course (Matsu, Take or Ume; one group paid ¥6,000 a head for a course in September 2026) and can order à la carte afterward. Expect negima, chicken breast with shiso and ume, the house Midori-yaki, chicken skin, "tulip" wings and stuffed shiitake, with onsen egg and yamakake on the side. Check sake prices, which add up fast. One September diner found the meat tough and the hygiene off-putting. Book ahead; closed Sundays.

places.cu: Zenzai (sweet red-bean soup) since 1883 · Meoto Zenzai ¥820: one serving split into two small bowls, Tanba Dainagon azuki with a few whole beans, a rice-cake dumpling, salt kombu and green tea · chilled zenzai in summer · matcha-azuki kakigori · Meoto Zenzai goods · 18 seats at 5 tables
places.notes: [Japanese sweets · the zenzai shop of Oda Sakunosuke's story, by Hozenji] The zenzai shop beside Mizukake Fudo in Hozenji Yokocho, dating to 1883 and made famous by Oda Sakunosuke's novel "Meoto Zenzai". The signature (¥820, September 2026) arrives as one serving split into two small bowls, a nod to a married couple, and ordering it as a couple is said to bring luck. Don't share: it's one order per guest. The zenzai is made with Tanba Dainagon azuki, gently sweet and a little thick, with a few whole beans and a soft rice-cake dumpling. Salt kombu and green tea cut the sweetness, and staff refill the tea. In summer there's a chilled zenzai, plus matcha-azuki kakigori. Today it's run by the Wasyoku Sato group and open 10 am to 10 pm, handy for dessert after takoyaki. There's a shelf of Meoto Zenzai souvenirs.

places.notes: [Tempura · an 8-seat tempura counter in Hozenji Yokocho] A bright, clean eight-seat tempura counter on the cobbled lanes of Hozenji Yokocho, open since July 2025. Each piece is fried in front of you and served at once: a crisp, light batter that isn't greasy, with the seafood and vegetables tasting of themselves. The ¥12,000 course (November 2025 and January 2026) runs from three appetizers and three sashimi through ten tempura, such as shrimp, crab, large scallop, milt, sweet potato and persimmon, then noodles, rice and dessert. There are surprises, like kiwi tempura. Dip in matcha salt, yuzu salt or tentsuyu with grated daikon, and the staff will suggest which. You can also order à la carte. The chef is cheerful and chatty. Upstairs, the shop's sake bar AWA pours a wide range of sake and whisky for after. Closed Wednesdays.

The all-you-can-drink courses are good value (¥2,750 with three dishes in April 2025, ¥4,950 with skewers and sashimi in March 2025). One January 2026 visitor found it average. The newest review is from January 2026, so check before going.

places.cu: Takaida-style chuka soba, Tabelog Ramen 100 every year 2017–2025 · near-black shoyu broth that is lighter than it looks, black pepper, medium-thick straight noodles, thin chashu, menma, green onion · small ¥900, regular ¥1,000 · hayazushi ¥200, wrapped in leaves from Wakayama · shrimp shio ramen with sakura shrimp and niboshi · first-Sunday morning ramen · 7 counter seats
places.notes: [Ramen · Takaida-style black chuka soba, a Tabelog 100 regular] A seven-seat counter down a narrow alley near NGK, named to Tabelog's ramen 100 every year from 2017 to 2025, with lines and a waiting area at lunch. It opened in 2008 at Tempozan Marketplace and moved to Namba in 2010. The chuka soba is Takaida-style: a broth that looks nearly black and smells strongly of soy, yet drinks lighter and less salty than you'd expect, with black pepper on top. Medium-thick straight noodles soak it up, with thin chashu, menma and green onion. A small is ¥900 and a regular ¥1,000 (October 2026). Add the ¥200 hayazushi, vinegared rice wrapped in leaves from Wakayama. There's also a shrimp shio with sakura shrimp and niboshi, limited bowls such as a garlic ramen on special days, and on the first Sunday of the month it opens at 7 am for morning ramen. A Hokkaido visitor found the soy too assertive. Cash only; closed Wednesdays.

The pork rice bowl is a favorite but isn't served late at night. Sides are just ramen toppings (¥150), and drinks just canned beer (¥400). places.notes: [Noodles · an 8 am–3 am tsukemen and udon shop by Nagahoribashi] A self-service noodle counter a short walk from Nagahoribashi, open from 8 in the morning until 3 at night, so it works for breakfast, lunch or the last stop of the evening. The motsu tsukemen comes with plenty of offal in a seafood-tinged dip, and the duck tsukemen has duck slices, grilled leek and lemon. There's also katsu udon with mizuna, and ramen. Opinions vary: one diner found the duck dip very sweet and watched staff mix it from cartons. Another noted prices have gone up. Closed Sundays.

It comes loaded with four chashu, from low-temperature Daisendori chicken to juicy pork belly, plus a chicken-cartilage tsukune scented with ginger or yuzu, kaiware and menma. One diner wanted more salt; another found the salt pronounced. On weekends there's a special ura shoyu soba at the same price. The set adds a chashu rice bowl heaped with meat. It's cramped when full, and one diner found service slow. Cash only.

places.notes: [Ramen · rich late-night ramen near Otaro Road, open to 5 am] An old-school eight-seat counter near Otaro Road, open since 2009 and serving until 5 am, a favorite after a night out or a missed last train. The ramen is thick and rich, with noodles that soak it up and good chashu. It's ¥800 (April 2026), ¥100 less for a small, and ¥180 for a full extra serving of noodles. The tsukemen pairs thick noodles with a rich dip of chicken bones, pork bones and vegetables, plus chashu, menma, a seasoned egg and plenty of shredded green onion, good with a cold beer. The spicy green-onion ramen has a moderate kick. Vinegar, pepper and chili oil sit on the counter. Expect overseas visitors and a short queue late on weekdays. Buy a ticket at the machine; cash only. Closed Tuesdays.

places.notes: [Ramen · clam and shijimi ramen south of Nankai Namba] A roomy shellfish-ramen shop three minutes from Nankai Namba's south exit, open since 2022, with tables that work for families. The clam ramen packs plenty of clams into a shoyu broth with deep shellfish umami, and big slices of rare chashu drape the rim, softening when dipped. Thick crunchy menma and shredded white negi keep it lively. The shijimi ramen is lighter, a good post-drinks bowl, and one regular always orders it. In summer there's a cold clam ramen with myoga (staff check you're fine with it). The "golden" TKM is egg-yolk-coated noodles scented with scallop broth, with rice to mop up the sauce. The noodles seem to be whole-grain, with a strong wheat flavor. One diner wanted a bigger portion, so consider a large. Cash only.

places.notes: [Teppanyaki · casual wagyu teppanyaki in Souemoncho, open to 3 am] A 19-seat teppanyaki counter opposite Queens Court in Souemoncho, open since 2020 and serving until 3 am. The star is a limited domestic black-wagyu filet; in July 2026 it was an A5 chateaubriand, seared on the teppan and rested to medium-rare with rosemary; an August diner had it with mashed potatoes. Beyond steak there's wagyu ichibo roast beef, Hokkaido scallop and asparagus in butter soy, a seafood yakisoba, Camembert fondue and white fish with Genoa sauce. Courses add a truffle-scented salad and a pairing of sirloin cap and filet, with wasabi, salt, soy, garlic chips and truffle oil to dip. Reviewers spent ¥5,000–15,000. places.notes: [Chinese · build-your-own malatang by Nagahoribashi] A two-floor malatang and hot-pot shop two minutes from Nagahoribashi, part of the Tonsha group, with a calm counter downstairs and private rooms upstairs. You order on your phone: pick from more than 40 ingredients and one of five spice levels, and the price isn't by weight, so a loaded bowl comes to about ¥1,300–1,500. The broth leans more numbing than hot, with real umami, and level 1 already has a kick. Fans recommend winter melon, white fungus, shrimp balls and knife-cut or sweet-potato noodles (two noodle types at most), with the sesame sauce and free green onion, coriander and garlic piled on. There's also a tomato mala soup with sweetness and acidity. Hot-pot courses run in the evening.

places.notes: [Okonomiyaki · a negiyaki counter off Shinsaibashi-suji since 2004] A long counter under a red lantern, tucked into a building of snack bars off Shinsaibashi-suji, cooking okonomiyaki right in front of you since 2004. The draw is the negiyaki "Fujiyama", heaped with green onion over tender beef tendon; one visitor came back a year later just for it. The batter is made with soy milk and nagaimo for a smooth texture, and the sauce is a house blend of Osaka sauces. There's also a seafood negiyaki packed with shrimp and octopus, a well-balanced mixed okonomiyaki, a modan-yaki with chewy noodles and the popular tonpeiyaki, with around 30 shochu to drink. Sets for two let you try a mini negiyaki and two okonomiyaki. Prices are low for the area, and there's an English menu. No reservations; closed Mondays.

The specialty is live lobster, steamed in front of you and served with three sauces; order it by the day before. Ask the friendly master what's best today, and plates arrive in a well-paced order. Cuts run about ¥1,500–2,000 each (January 2026): thick salted tongue to finish with lemon, kuri, hanging tender, nakaochi, thin top blade and tripe. Regulars praise the quality for the price, though one August diner found the meat average. Finish with the strip-loin dashi chazuke or yuzu-tea rice. Courses can be built to a budget. It fills up on Fridays, but same-day online booking sometimes works. There's a ¥500 cover charge. Closed Sundays.

Thirty to forty creative skewers use seasonal ingredients in a light, crisp batter, each with its own sauce. The fun is the omakase: skewers keep coming one by one until you say stop. There are set courses too, such as a ¥5,720 seasonal course of ten skewers with fresh vegetables, a drink and ochazuke or rice with red miso soup (January 2025). One diner who has been coming for more than 50 years says it never sits heavy. Expect ¥8,000–15,000. Closed Thursdays.

places.notes: [Ramen · light shrimp ramen by Kuromon Market] A nine-seat counter on the Nippombashi 2-chōme street by Kuromon Market, marked by stall-style plastic curtains, run by the owner with one helper and open since 2022. The owner and one female staff member run the nine-seat counter. Unlike the thick shrimp-miso style, the ebi shio here is light and gentle: a clear chicken-bone broth with a sauce from sweet shrimp, and the shrimp flavor hits from the first sip. It's ¥950, or ¥1,350 as the special (May and October 2026) with two wontons, bean sprouts and a hint of yuzu. You pick your chashu from thick pork belly, pork shoulder or fatty beef. The Kiwami Kuromon shoyu layers several soy sauces over chicken, pork, shrimp and scallop, with medium-thin noodles from Mie's Ayahikari flour; one diner found the soy drowned the shrimp. Most customers are visitors, and there's a short line at weekend lunch. Pay after eating, in cash.

The noodles are chewy and medium-thick in a slightly sweet, not-too-oily sauce; the "A" version with egg yolk and parmesan tastes almost like carbonara, and there's a spicy miso too. Large and extra-large are free, so many go big; a paid jumbo comes in a basin-sized bowl, though one diner found its toppings sparse. Grab free onion, pickled ginger and garlic, play with chili oil and vinegar, then add rice to the leftover sauce or ask for soup to finish it as ramen. Free drinks (jasmine and oolong tea, fruit water) and paper aprons make it good value. A cheese set is ¥1,000 (October 2026). Open daily until 11 pm.

Downstairs you stand around the kitchen; upstairs is seated (¥330) with mobile ordering and its own menu. Big platters of daily obanzai line the counter. Small plates are cheap and inventive, mostly ¥380–600 (October 2026): assorted sashimi, spicy coriander pork shumai, fig and prosciutto with ricotta, smoked mayonnaise with chikuwa, and a squid liver in an Okinawan-style marinade that one regular orders every time. Drinks run to mega highballs, fruit sours and a grated-peach bellini, and you can grab bottled beer from the self-service fridge.

Each order is ten bite-size gyoza for ¥550 (September 2026): thin, crisp-bottomed wrappers with a little chew around a punchy pork filling heavy on pepper and garlic. Eat them with just vinegar, or vinegar and soy. Two servings per person is the suggestion, and some order four or five between two. The popular mentaiko cream udon is a recipe handed down from a former Italian-restaurant chef. The base is a Kansai-style dashi of kombu and sea bream with chewy Sanuki udon. The most popular bowl is the creamy mentaiko cream udon (¥1,380, April 2026); a chilled pork shabu-shabu udon (¥1,180) is lighter, and one repeat visitor raves about the ume udon with wakame and that dashi. A newer herbal hot-pot course piles leafy greens into a gentle Chinese-style broth, then chicken, pork and beef with an egg dip, and udon to finish. There are kara-age and drinking snacks, free karaoke and TV for sports. Smoking is allowed throughout. ¥300 charge; cash only; closed Mondays.

Expect tuna aged 13 days, aged sea bream, four-day striped horse mackerel and dry-aged chutoro from the Oki Islands, alongside a rare-fried pike conger or a rare-fried eel sandwich and French-inspired sides that impressed diners. Choose black, a clear 100% jidori chicken broth with dark soy, or white, a shio with a light yuzu lift. The draw is the wontons: springy shrimp ones and juicy pork ones in big, slippery wrappers; the pork and shrimp wonton noodles are ¥1,200 (September–October 2026). places.notes: [Ramen · late-night tonkotsu with a marked order sheet, near Nippombashi] An 11-seat tonkotsu counter two minutes from Nippombashi exit 7, open since 2013 and now serving until 1 am. The broth simmers pork bones and vegetables until they dissolve, then adds seafood and kombu, for a dark, thick, additive-free dip with a gentle flavor. Tsukemen is ¥1,050, or ¥1,150 with a seasoned egg (June 2026), and one repeat visitor loves the chashu and noodles in the large chashu tsukemen. The onsen-tamago special ramen has a niboshi-forward fish tonkotsu, easy to drink, on medium-thin firm noodles. Limited bowls rotate: rich niboshi or spicy tsukemen, a standout chilled curry ramen, a mackerel ramen. One diner wanted the dip hotter and the noodles chewier. The listed hours aren't always kept, so check first. Cash only.

Both use chewy medium-thick champon noodles. For ¥50 more it becomes a set with rice, which you can drop into the leftover soup like porridge; a set with fried rice is ¥1,200. The young owner is attentive, and the sake list is good. Book ahead; it fills up. Courses run 5, 7 or 9 skewers, and nine skewers with chawanmushi was just ¥3,500 in August 2026, big skewers, perfectly seasoned. Favorites include seseri, chochin, negima, cartilage and the rare "sori" cut. Start with the very fresh liver sashimi or tataki, and don't skip the soy-marinated kumquat. The liver kamameshi, cooked to finish, is a highlight. The sake list is strong (a limited Toyo Bijin junmai daiginjo stood out), and draft beer comes from a swing tap. One October diner noticed fewer items than in August for the same price. The owner accommodated one guest's special requests. ¥500 service charge.

places.notes: [Tempura · casual counter tempura with local sake near Shinsaibashi] A narrow tempura izakaya on the ground floor of a Shinsaibashi-suji building, open since 2020, with eight counter seats and a table at the back. The owner, who cooks the menu, has 30 years in the trade. It's tempura without the stiffness: pieces from ¥275, fried to order and sent out at a steady pace, light and not greasy, so diners feel fine the next day. The head-on shrimp is the star, crisp head and juicy body, and sweetfish, conger eel and maitake are favorites; finish with a tempura-egg rice bowl. Meals start with a ¥550 sashimi-platter otoshi, and the local sake list is long. The owner is friendly and the service attentive. Expect ¥5,000–8,000 with drinks. Closed Wednesdays.

Pick from five sauces: demi-glace, ponzu, onion, teriyaki or salt. The Western Mama 200 g is ¥1,100 and the 500 g "Wrestler" ¥2,700 (2025–2026). places.notes: [Abura-soba · back-fat abura-soba on the Otaroad side of Nippombashi] A 12-seat abura-soba specialist toward Otaroad, open since 2018, small inside but with repeat visitors. Mix the bowl from the bottom: medium-thick curly noodles in a shoyu sauce with back fat, crunchy cabbage and bean sprouts, and chashu that isn't greasy. A couple of newcomers expected heavy and found it surprisingly light. Then work through garlic, mayonnaise, chili oil and vinegar. The chicken-and-pork version adds seared meat, and spicy limited bowls run from "Shakunetsu no Rei" to the hotter "Yogan" cold tantan with diced meat, which left one diner's mouth sore. A small ginger soup comes first, and weekday lunch adds rice or ice cream. Cash only.

The cooking is by a Chinese chef. The tantanmen is creamy with sesame and milder than its level suggests; one regular finds it a touch sweet alone and pairs it with the numbing mapo rice bowl in a half set. Sets add half fried rice, mapo rice or Tianjin rice, and half sizes keep it manageable. There's a mapo ramen too, and in summer a chilled tantanmen over ice with watercress, cucumber and meat miso. Some found the thin noodles clumped and the fried rice light; the spicy tantanmen (¥1,200, September 2026) gets its heat from chili oil. A long menu of sides like gyoza and water spinach makes it a drinking stop too.

Wheaty, medium-thick noodles go with a reliable rich tsukemen, a spicy version, or a light chilled sea-bream shio tsukemen with yuzu peel; you can choose hot or cold noodles. On the 3rd of each month a coupon makes all toppings free. The kara-age is better than you'd expect. One diner found the toppings ice-cold with cold noodles, and another the chashu a little tough.

The regular favorite is the Kamatsu tsukemen, noodles soaked in kombu water seasoned well enough to eat on their own; upgrade to the smooth Mochihime noodles for ¥100. The shellfish-broth ramen is gentle and comforting, with a perfectly seasoned egg. Seasonal limited bowls are the draw: in October 2026 a creamy Tanohata duck paitan shio (¥1,300), and a chilled ramen of double Rausu kombu with mushroom oil that one diner rated above any kombu tsukemen. Finish with a dashi rice ball. Cash only; open Thursday and Friday evenings only.

A friendly owner and one female staff member run the room. The signature is the chicken-bonito extreme shio (¥1,000, October 2026): a deep, chicken-packed salt broth brightened with plenty of yuzu, two kinds of chashu and a soft-boiled egg on Teigaku noodles. The shoyu version is just as refined, and the chicken doro tsukemen (¥1,300) brings a bubbling-hot, thick chicken-soy dip for glossy flat noodles. Limited bowls appear on social media, like a salt chicken paitan or the hearty Youji ramen. Add a rare-chashu rice bowl (¥350) or the stone-grilled cheese omurice. Buy a ticket outside and wait for your number. Cash only.

The core is a soy-heavy chuka soba on thick, wheaty curly noodles: one diner called the regular the best shoyu ramen ever, strong yet gentle and not greasy, and there's an extra-rich back-fat version and mazesoba. The fun is the monthly special: October 2026's ankake spicy-numbing shoyu (¥1,350) is thick like mapo with an egg yolk and garlic chives, though several found it milder than its name; September brought a miso-butter corn bowl under back fat. Don't skip the rich fried rice (+¥280), and small rice is free at lunch until 2 pm. Cash only; closes by 5 pm.

The range is wide: a jet-black shoyu that isn't too salty, with soy richness and garlic umami; a shellfish-forward chuka soba; clam and oyster ramen; and a creamy chicken paitan that one diner rated highly. The standout for one tsukemen skeptic was the special tsukemen, a rich seafood dip with chewy thick noodles and plenty of moist rare chashu, which jumped to the top of a personal ranking. Rice bowls run from chashu to chicken tataki and seafood. Reviews are mixed on value, with one large clam ramen and mini bowl at ¥1,710, and one diner found the soup lukewarm. Cash only; closes when sold out.

Downstairs is a counter that suits solo diners, upstairs tables. Weekday lunches are the bargain: around ¥1,000–1,100 for a plate like the Familiar Lunch of bite-size cutlet, shrimp fry and omelet, with rice and a mini bowl of somen. À la carte, the pork cutlet (¥1,600) is fried hot for a light, crunchy coat, the hamburg (¥1,600) comes juicy with spaghetti, a fried egg and bacon, and the big crab cream croquettes are creamy inside. The demi-glace tastes properly old-school. Cash only; Sundays lunch only.

The ground-floor case is a pink wall of shortcakes, tarts, éclairs and daifuku, with crepes and soft serve to go. Upstairs, the 20-seat café, with dried flowers and strawberry-shaped lamps, serves cake plates with ice cream and a free drink (¥2,000, March 2026). Most sweets are made by in-house pastry chefs. The café opens at noon, takeaway at 11. Cash or PayPay only.

The draw is raw oysters from different regions, best as a tasting of five; in summer the rock oysters from Murotsu in Hyogo and Naruto in Tokushima were called rich, "the milk of the sea". Cooked, there are steamed and fried oysters (hot and much praised), gratin, ajillo, a spicy oyster jjigae and oyster pasta. Order the oyster clay-pot rice first, as it takes about 30 minutes. Prices are fair for the amount of oysters, with wines to match. One repeat visitor found a batch of raw oysters a bit fishy. Open until 1 am.

There's no menu: the meal opens with ten to twenty obanzai-style bites served in sake cups and little plates, such as braised butterbur, vegetables, fish, meat and chawanmushi, then moves to seasonal dishes cooked in front of you, like crab, oysters or milt. The master pairs wine or sake to your taste, and the list is deep. Flavors run a little bold; one regular calls it reassuring. It's built around drinking: one non-drinking couple found the welcome cool. Expect about ¥8,000–15,000. Reserve; closed a few irregular days a month. The newest review is from March 2026.

places.notes: [Ramen · a seven-seat chicken-and-seafood shoyu counter near JR Namba] A small seven-seat counter three minutes from JR Namba's south exit, open since 2011, with regulars who come for the limited bowls. Two ramen anchor the menu. The Kanade shoyu (¥1,050, September 2026) balances sweet chicken umami with a tightening seafood finish over thin noodles, and two chashu, moist pork and chicken. The most popular Chicken Kanade ramen (¥1,000) layers chicken paitan, seafood and shoyu into a thick but drinkable broth that one diner found a touch sweet. Add garlic to punch it up, or a seared-chashu rice bowl (¥450). There's mazesoba too. One diner found the seafood fishy. Waits are short; buy a ticket at the machine. Closed Sundays, and Tuesday and Saturday are lunch only.

places.notes: [Ramen · a shio-ramen specialist south of Nankai Namba] A shio-ramen specialist two minutes from Nankai Namba, open since 2019, in a clean room of white wood and stainless steel. The clear broth of chicken and seafood is accented with chicken katsuobushi: light, but full of umami, and good enough that one diner drank every drop. A hint of black pepper gives it punch. Teigaku noodles, chewy, flat and wavy (one reviewer likened them to Kitakata), soak it up, with chashu, ajitama, green onion and kaiware. The fluffy fried rice, whole or half, is a classic partner. In summer there was a chilled ramen with lemon vinegar to finish. It's rarely crowded late in the afternoon. Cash only.

places.notes: [Ramen · a lunch-only niboshi shop in Kozu, opened 2025] A lunch-only ramen counter in Kozu, opened in April 2025 and run by the owner with one helper, already drawing regulars who have been more than twenty times. A cheerful owner and one female staff member run the seven-seat counter. The heart of it is niboshi: a clear sardine shoyu (¥950) with a whole niboshi on top, or the shio niboshi clear soup (¥950), sardine-forward on the first sip, then clean, with a little ume, though one fan found the niboshi subdued. There's also a special, shoyu, shio and an old-style bowl, all on chewy medium-thin noodles. Limited bowls keep coming: back-fat shoyu mazesoba until the end of November, and in summer chilled chuka soba and chilled niboshi. Pair it with tamago kake gohan (¥300) or a seared-chashu bowl (¥350). Pay after eating, in cash. Closed Mondays.

places.notes: [Ramen · Jiro-style ramen on the Otaroad side of Nippombashi] A small Jiro-style counter toward Otaroad, open since 2017 and part of the same group as Fukuchan Ramen and Tenchijin. The Juku-cho ramen has a punchy broth and noodles fans like; customize with free extra vegetables, chashu fat and garlic, or swap garlic for ginger if you're working tomorrow. The garlic is fierce, so go easy. The soupless miso Juku-cho (¥1,060) and the dry ramen with grated cheese are hits, and the spicy Juku-cho is ¥1,100 (August 2026). The house kombu salt for the bean sprouts gets special praise, and the chashu is thick. A smaller noodle portion with extra vegetables suits lighter eaters. One person runs everything, so expect a wait at weekends and brisk seating directions. Cash only.

places.notes: [Ramen · a Ramen 100 chicken-soba shop north of Shinsaibashi] A Tori Soba Zagin branch open since 2015, picked for Tabelog's Ramen 100 every year from 2019 to 2024, with a quietly upscale feel for a ramen shop. The tori soba is a creamy chicken broth that one diner likened to a rich potage, intense yet smooth. Thin curly noodles, two chashu (moist chicken and chewy pork) and crunchy fried burdock root complete it. Choose shoyu (¥1,000) or shio, or the spicy version (¥1,100), which ran hotter than one fan of spice expected. Summer brought a chilled jidori soba with flat noodles and plenty of chicken chashu, and there has been a limited Jiro-style bowl. Expect a line: 20 to 40 minutes at peak times. Open 10:00 to 22:00 daily. Cash only.

places.notes: [Ramen · Tokyo's Tsujita tsukemen on Senba Shinsaibashi street] The Shinsaibashi branch of Kanda's Tsujita, the Tokyo tsukemen chain, opened in October 2024 on the Senba Shinsaibashi shopping street. The rich tsukemen pairs noodles with a great texture with a thick dipping sauce of seafood and pork. Squeeze the sudachi over the noodles to freshen it and add black shichimi, then finish with soup to thin what's left. The rich flavored-egg tsukemen was ¥1,210 in September 2026. One diner called it a reliable classic rather than anything new. Lines were long after opening and mostly overseas visitors on one Sunday; now there are days with no wait. Buy a ticket at the machine. Open until midnight on weekdays.

places.notes: [Ramen · Mugen's beef-bone white soup north of Shinsaibashi] The Shinsaibashi branch of Mugen Ramen, open since September 2024, five minutes from the station. The beef-bone white soup ramen (¥1,050, October 2026) is creamy and bubbly, with a rich, slightly sweet broth that drinks easier than it looks, and a rich option. Thin, firm noodles reminded one diner of Hakata ramen. Add a seasoned egg (¥130) or pair it with a small melt-in-your-mouth chashu rice bowl. One of the two chashu was a little gamey for one diner, and another got only one slice. The priciest bowl carries marbled strip loin like roast beef, and there's even a kiwi ramen. Toppings may differ from other branches. Lines can be long. No cards. See also Mugen Ramen Sennichimae.

places.notes: [Ramen · a late-night abura soba counter near Nagahoribashi] A 15-seat counter two minutes from Nagahoribashi, open since 2011 and serving until midnight, which makes it a stop after a night out. The draw is abura soba (mazesoba), with ramen and niboshi dishes too. The spicy oil noodles impressed one diner with heat balanced by umami and a sauce that clings to the noodles. The chashu has fans, best with a green onion chashu rice bowl. Water comes with lemon slices. The staff changed about a year before April 2026, and a long-time customer found the flavor milder since and the new staff attentive. Not everyone is won over: one September visitor found the oil soba mediocre. Buy a ticket at the machine. Closed Sundays and holidays. Cash only.

places.notes: [Japanese · a seafood-and-seasonal izakaya off Shinsaibashi-suji] A 19-seat izakaya open since 2019, which calls itself a hideout for adults built on hot pot, seafood, seasonal vegetables and drink. One diner says the food comes first. Fresh assorted sashimi is the constant. The signature giant shrimp tempura is plump and crisp; one diner had shrimp tempura wrapped in sakura shrimp. Karasumi goes with drinks, and the karasumi soba finish eats almost like pasta. Others order grilled grouper in Saikyo miso, horse sashimi with tategami fat, a rich potato salad, oysters, and seasonal crab. A ¥6,000 Japanese course is an option. The appetizer rarely changes. Smoking is allowed, which one non-smoker minded. Reserve; it gets busy. Closed Sundays.

places.notes: [Japanese · an Aomori izakaya with live Tsugaru shamisen in Sennichimae] A rare Aomori izakaya in Osaka, open since 2011 on the third floor of a Sennichimae building, a little hard to find. Live Tsugaru shamisen plays twice a night, around 19:00 and 21:00, and one diner was captivated by its power. Start with the Horoyoi Set of sake, sashimi and appetizers, then move to northern dishes: Nebuta-zuke, koji-marinated herring and red salmon, Appa-yaki (scallops simmered in egg), komai, and iburigakko with cream cheese. The taro croquettes, tempura, chicken nanban and beef tendon round it out, with Aomori sake. The owner is bright and attentive, and the regulars make newcomers feel at home. Book early. Cash only.

places.notes: [Japanese · counter shabu-shabu and sukiyaki in Souemoncho until 4 am] A 16-seat counter in late-night Souemoncho where each diner gets a personal pot, so solo diners are at ease. Choose shabu-shabu or sukiyaki: kuroge wagyu and Kurobuta pork that melt in the mouth, with a homemade sesame sauce. The top beef can even be eaten raw with wasabi and soy over rice. One regular's after-drinks order is a rice bowl of seared rare beef with a sweet-spicy sauce. The menu has run to stew, hamburg steak and chicken sashimi too. Staff walk first-timers through it. It isn't cheap: reviewers spent ¥6,000–15,000 on hot pot. Open until 4 am most nights; closed Sundays. Smoking allowed.

places.notes: [Yakitori · a creative skewer counter on quiet Dotonbori 2-chome] A yakitori izakaya open since 2014 on the quieter stretch of Dotonbori west of Midosuji, three minutes from Namba. Chicken leads: hearts, seseri, tamahimo and chochin (one diner reserved just for it), plus charcoal-grilled thigh and cheek. The tsukune is grilled just right. Pork, beef and seafood skewers keep it varied; the meat-wrapped cherry tomatoes burn the unwary. There's chicken sashimi, salmon tartare and a filling katsu udon, and the daily specials are worth asking about. The master is fun to talk to from the counter, and there are semi-private rooms in back. One May evening the room was half overseas visitors. Otoshi ¥200. Smoking allowed.

places.notes: [Japanese · a kinki shabu-shabu specialist in Higashi-Shinsaibashi] A seasonal seafood restaurant tucked at the back of the ground floor of a nightlife building, behind a cabaret-style entrance that can make a first visit feel like a wrong turn. Inside is a calm Japanese room with private rooms, used for business dinners and special occasions. The specialty is kinki shabu-shabu: the Hokkaido fish, rare in Osaka, has a refined fat that melts into the broth, and the course ends with a rich rice porridge. Sashimi and the simmered, grilled and fried courses also draw praise, as does a deep sake list. It's a splurge: reviewers spent ¥8,000–30,000. The shop has moved from its old building. Menu in English and Chinese. The newest review is from March 2026.

places.notes: [Ramen · a new Tenka Ippin branch in the Shinsaibashi shopping district] A clean, new Tenka Ippin that opened in August 2026 three minutes from Shinsaibashi Station, with counter and table seats and ordering by tablet. The kotteri (¥920) is the classic thick broth of chicken bones and vegetables seasoned with soy, deep in chicken and a little salty, over thin straight noodles you can order extra firm. Stir in the spicy miso from the table. One diner found the extra-rich MAX just gooey and wished for the regular. There's also assari, yatai no aji, miso and shio, plus a kimchi and fried rice set (¥460). About twenty diners were already in at 2:15 pm on one visit. Open until 23:30 daily.

places.notes: [Ramen · Kurume and Hakata tonkotsu in Kozu] A 13-seat tonkotsu counter near Nipponbashi, open since 2010; the owner changed in August 2025 and lunch was added. The rich broth comes white, red or black. Hakuryu, the basic rich tonkotsu (¥900), is soy-seasoned, a little oily and properly salty over very thin, firm straight noodles. The White Dragon is a Kurume tonkotsu with a red chili paste in the center, the White Tiger is Hakata-style, and the Kuro Ryu is the garlic version; one diner had black garlic oil. Toppings are chashu (thin and fatty), crunchy kikurage and green onion; pickled ginger, spicy takana and sesame sit on the counter. Add rice (¥150 at lunch), extra noodles, or garlicky gyoza. Service is quick, and it's often quiet. Closed Wednesdays; Sunday is lunch only.

places.notes: [Ramen · an overnight tantanmen counter off Matsuyamachi-suji] An eight-seat tantanmen shop and izakaya that opens in the evening and runs into the next morning, so it feeds night-shift workers and late drinkers. The soup tantanmen comes white or black (¥1,000; ¥1,100 for the black in August 2026). The white is sesame-rich but surprisingly light; the black is thick and jet-black. Both numb with Sichuan pepper and homemade chili oil, over thin straight noodles topped with meat miso, dried shrimp, mizuna and takuan, which one diner likened to a laksa note. There's a brothless version on thick wavy noodles, spice up to level 5, extra noodles, and a garlicky kara-age. Water comes scented with orange peel. Hours shift, so check first.

places.notes: [Chinese · hand-pulled Lanzhou beef noodles with free refills near Nagahoribashi] A spacious 79-seat Lanzhou beef-noodle shop open since 2024, where a noodle maker stretches and twists the dough after you order, a show in itself. The beef noodle soup (¥950) is a light, clear broth of beef bones and meat with beef, daikon, garlic shoots and cilantro. Pick the noodle width, from 1 mm threads to extra-wide flat ribbons like lasagna sheets, and refills are free and unlimited. Spice comes to order; add chili oil and the black vinegar the wall recommends. Lunch set B (¥1,000) adds three gyoza and a small vegetable dish. There are also shrimp dumplings in sour soup, a cumin beef burger and beef skewers. It's busy at lunch, and the room has an overseas feel.

places.notes: [Chinese · build-your-own mala tang in Namba Parks] A small, cramped mala-tang counter on the sixth floor of Namba Parks, around since before the mala-tang boom, and packed with young women on one visit. Mark your noodles, broth, ingredients, sides and spice level on a sheet at the table; it's slower than the usual line-and-grab, which suits first-timers, though the small print makes the total hard to add up. One regular builds a bowl of mulukhiyah, white fungus, king oyster mushroom, tomato and cilantro with thick sweet-potato noodles (seven items ran ¥1,500 in August 2026). The broth tastes strongly herbal, with an addictive numbing heat, and garlic, black vinegar and Sichuan pepper oil wait on the table. Portions can feel small; add a pork shabu-shabu rice bowl if hungry.

places.notes: [Ramen · espuma chicken paitan in Minamisenba] A 16-seat chicken paitan shop open since 2019 as Mugi x Tori and renamed Kinmugi in September 2026, the name the group's other shops use. Domestic chicken is simmered for hours and foamed just before serving, and you can hear the frothing while you wait. The result is a creamy, bubbly broth over chewy medium-thick straight noodles from Kyoto's Menya Teigaku. The most popular special topping ramen (¥1,450) adds rare, tender pork-loin and chicken-breast chashu, egg and menma. Limited bowls rotate, such as an uni ramen with a delicate sea-urchin aroma, though one diner couldn't find the uni in the tsukemen. Summer brings chilled corn soup noodles (¥1,400); add rice to finish as risotto. There can be a line at noon. Cash-only ticket machine.

places.notes: [Ramen · rich chicken paitan near Nagahoribashi] A 12-seat chicken paitan shop near Nagahoribashi, open since 2020, with lines even after lunch and a ten-minute wait at Saturday noon. Buy a ticket at the cash-only machine outside, then wait to be seated. The chicken paitan is rich, bold and piping hot, clinging to the noodles, and two diners drank nearly every drop. The special ramen with extra-fat rice came to ¥1,800. The mazesoba is the other draw: homemade flat medium-thick noodles tossed with the sauce and an egg, with coarse black pepper, and free rice to finish. Tabelog lists kara-age too. A sister shop runs elsewhere.

places.notes: [Ramen · late-night Iekei with free noodles and rice near Matsuyamachi] A 17-seat Iekei shop near Matsuyamachi, open since 2016, serving lunch and again from 21:00 to 3:00 am. The tonkotsu shoyu is creamy with a punch that still lets the pork through, topped with nori, spinach and quail egg; shio is an option. Medium noodles are the house choice. Large noodles, rice and extra noodles come free, as do kimchi and pickles, so a full meal ran in the ¥900s. One diner found it closer to Hakata tonkotsu. Ordering extra-rich made it far too salty for a newcomer. Sides include a negi chashu bowl, mini kara-age bowl and gyoza. The owner has been seen running it alone and comes across as friendly. Hours can slip, so check first.

places.notes: [Chinese · a neighborhood Chinese diner near Nagahoribashi] A long-running neighborhood Chinese restaurant near Nagahoribashi, strong on takeout and delivery, with counter and tables in a dining room one diner found very clean. The pick is the Kansai-style champon (¥858): a scalding, thick ankake soup over thin noodles, piled with stir-fried vegetables, pork and seafood. Pair it with moist fried rice in a ¥980 set. The yakisoba (¥770) is simple and huge, the gyoza come seven to a plate, and the kara-age (¥880) is crisp and soy-seasoned. Set meals run in the ¥900s, served through the afternoon. Groups order widely: century egg, shrimp chili, twice-cooked pork, sesame balls. The shoyu ramen and Tianjin rice were plain to one diner. No children, per one diner. Smoking allowed.

places.notes: [Sushi · a six-seat alley counter off Shinsaibashi-suji] A six-seat sushi counter at the end of a narrow alley, where only the sign shows from the street. It's been open since 2015, and the owner has thirty years of experience. The meal is an omakase of seasonal fish, sushi and small dishes, and you can add favorites. Diners remember the kohada (one called it the best ever), sweet red sea urchin, nodoguro, katsuo tataki, crab, and winter fugu milt. It finishes with ushiojiru. The chef pairs sake to the food. The owner is gentle and the room calm, and regulars keep it full; reservations are hard to get. Courses are good value, drinks less so. Reviewers spent about ¥10,000–30,000.

places.notes: [Japanese · a chicken specialist beside Hōzenji] A chicken restaurant in the building next to Mizukake Fudō, cooking domestically raised young chickens from sashimi to rice. The chef is quiet but kind, and the chef's wife is warm and welcoming. The assorted chicken sashimi is fresh and bouncy, the thigh tataki hits hard with garlic, and the kara-age, especially the crisp wings, is a favorite; one diner ordered four plates of grilled cartilage. Look also for fried chicken skin rolled with green onion, liver, gizzards and a spicy simmered chicken skin to eat over rice. Courses run to mizutaki, refined in chicken flavor, with rice porridge, and there is a dry curry omurice. Service is quiet but kind, with plates split for groups. Seats fill within minutes, so reserve. Sake is limited; beer and shochu are there.

places.notes: [Yakitori · a six-seat back-alley counter in Souemoncho] A tiny yakitori counter so deep in a Souemoncho back alley that one diner would never have found it unaided. The current owner took over in January 2014 and kept the name. Skewers are generous and thick: bonjiri, skin, negima, tsukune and yagen nankotsu are favorites. The house draw for some is the chicken liver sashimi, cooked at low temperature. Also on the board: thigh tataki, gizzard, red sausage, a spicy yam kimchi, smashed cucumber, and a chazuke in chicken broth to finish. It's a proper old-school local joint. One diner waited a while for orders. Only six seats, so call ahead. Open until 3 am; closed Sundays. Cash only.

A young third-generation chef chooses the ingredients personally. The head chef is particular about fish, and once turned away a red clam that wasn't fresh enough. Blue crab is a long-running highlight. A July 2026 dinner ran from sashimi and rock oysters to uzaku, an abalone gunkan and tekka maki, with Kamo Tsuru Gold sake, which carries petal-shaped gold leaf. Stories of the shop's history come with the meal. It is pricey: reviewers spent ¥15,000–30,000, and one walk-in felt the bill outran the value. Closed Mondays.

places.notes: [Yakiniku · a six-seat alley counter where the master grills] A hidden yakiniku counter in a narrow Souemoncho alley, next door to Hiromiya. The owner is young and easy to talk to, so it suits solo diners. There are no grills at the seats: the master grills each cut and serves it at its best, so up to about seven diners squeeze in close. Portions are about half the usual size, so you can try many cuts. Start with white senmai, when there is any, with sesame oil, salt and a moreish miso. Then go to aburi yukke, wagyu tataki, salted tongue, outside skirt and kalbi. A Korean-style cold tofu with kimchi and seaweed is a side. It's easy to drop by alone, and the owner suits the room. Open late, to 2 am. Cash only; smoking allowed.

The dipping sauce is thick pork bone and seafood, bonito-forward, and it clings to homemade thick, flat noodles chilled in water for a chewy, wheaty bite. Add diced onion and aji daikon as you go, then finish with soup or Dive Rice, a small bowl of rice with green onion to drop into the sauce. The TOKYO-X premium tsukemen (¥1,500) carries juicy rare chashu. There's also a seafood tonkotsu ramen (¥1,000) with a free large size. On Saturdays there is a 7 am morning ramen, such as a charcoal-grilled chashu miso. Noodles were too soft for one pair. Expect a short line at lunch. House rules: one bowl each, no phones while eating.

places.notes: [Ramen · a two-person tsukemen shop at the south end of Otaroad] A 13-seat noodle shop at the southern tip of Nipponbashi's Otaroad, open since 2013 and run by two: a chef in the kitchen and one person serving, both notably polite. A young owner-chef creates the specials; one review describes the shop as run by a husband-and-wife team. The draw is chicken-shoyu tsukemen (¥1,330 for medium): smooth, glossy noodles and a gentle soy dipping sauce full of chicken, with tenkasu and black shichimi, mild enough to drink on its own. There's also chicken paitan on medium-thick curly noodles; this autumn it carried a curry ball you break into the broth. In summer the chilled niboshi soba (¥1,250) comes with a rice to drown in the cold broth. One bowl took about 15 minutes. Lunch only; closed Tuesdays.

places.notes: [Ramen · clam-broth chuka soba for lunch near Nagahoribashi] An eight-seat lunch counter near Nagahoribashi, open since 2021, built on a clear shellfish broth. The kaidashi shio ramen tastes most clearly of clam, light yet deep. The asari shoyu is lighter still, too subtle for some, and the shichimi from Sakai's Yamatsu Tsujita lifts it. Smooth, chewy noodles are the constant praise; one diner ordered extra noodles. Thin chashu, seasoned egg and menma complete the bowl, and the shio set adds rice with clam tsukudani; sansho on the counter suits it. There's also a meat soba, and it once served cold pasta. A calm room with many women dining. Lunch only, Monday to Saturday. Cash only.

places.notes: [Ramen · Jiro-style mazesoba on Otaroad] A Jiro-style mazesoba counter on Otaroad, open since 2017; one regular also goes to the Namba branch. The MAZE soba comes with 300 g of thick, smooth noodles and tender chashu, and noodles, vegetables, garlic and fat can be adjusted for free. Garlic hits hard, so go light before a meeting. The Taiwanese version (¥1,150) adds ground meat, chives, nori, fish powder and egg yolk; there's a mildly hot curry mazesoba and a brothless shio ramen with yuzu that one fan rates the best of its kind. The counter is stocked with black pepper, shichimi, Sichuan pepper, chili oil and vinegar, kimchi is free, and a ¥100 gacha picks a surprise topping like mentaiko. Allow ten minutes. places.notes: [Ramen · Mugen's beef-bone shop in Nambanaka 3-chome] A Mugen Ramen shop open since 2020 near Daikokucho, whose beef-bone aroma greets you at the door. One diner found nearly all the staff and customers to be Chinese. The beef-bone white soup ramen is rich and creamy, topped with tender roast beef and fatty brisket. The spicy chashu noodles (¥1,350) add Sichuan pepper, garlic chives and heat a little milder than Shin Ramyun. Opinions split: one diner found it phenomenal, one found the chashu tough and over-seasoned, another didn't think it worth the price, and the mini chashu rice bowl was mushy and salty for one diner. Staff and customers are mostly from overseas, and service was slow for one diner. Open until 23:00. See also Mugen Ramen Sennichimae and Shinsaibashi.

places.notes: [Sushi · a sushi kaiseki counter in Higashi-Shinsaibashi] A modern sushi counter at the back of a building's ground floor, open since 2021 behind a noren, with amber light on the counter and private tables with sliding doors. The young chef has a calm, gentlemanly manner that never feels stiff. The ¥22,000 omakase runs 15 to 18 items, mixing Edomae sushi with kaiseki dishes. It opens with fig tempura and ginger. Then come kombu-cured flounder and botan shrimp, shima-aji, a fragrant seared scallop roll with sudachi, and Hokkaido uni served in a glass. places.notes: [Ramen · Kappa's Namba Parks South branch, with an ULTRA-rich bowl] The Namba Parks South branch of Kappa Ramen Honpo, open since 2023 in a bright, roomy space. The exclusive here is the ULTRA rich: a thick, fatty tonkotsu that clings to medium-thick curly noodles. The regular Kappa ramen comes light or rich, the Aka Kappa adds a gentle chili kick to the tonkotsu shoyu, and the vegetable ramen comes white and sweet or spicy red with chili oil. Every bowl earns a free extra-noodles coupon, thin and firm, with firmness to order. Kimchi, fresh garlic and fried garlic are free. Pair it with a half fried-rice or kara-age set. Order on your phone; lines can form at peak times. Open 10:00 to midnight. See also Kappa Sennichimae and Amemura.

Thin straight noodles carry a fragrant wheat flavor. On top: thick chashu torched for smokiness, a half egg, green onion, shredded chili and nori heaped with bonito flakes, which scatter if you blow on the noodles. The tori-ton tsukemen comes on thick, wheaty noodles, and there's mazesoba. Buy a ticket outside. It fills fast around noon. Closed Wednesdays.

places.notes: [Japanese · lunch-to-late Japanese courses off Shinsaibashi-suji] A calm second-floor Japanese restaurant just inside Mitsudera-suji, unusual for serving from lunch until 1 am. Finish with shaved ice in homemade syrup. Friendly staff, and international guests too. Closed Sundays.

Closed Wednesdays.

places.notes: [Sushi · a red-lit late-night sushi counter in Higashi-Shinsaibashi] A casual sushi counter opened in December 2025 among the flashy signs of Higashi-Shinsaibashi, serving until 3 am. The shop is run by Issei, a former charismatic host, and the listing credits the sushi to a master with 30 years of experience. Inside, a red-themed counter keeps it relaxed rather than stiff. Order omakase nigiri or graze: eel that one diner loved, jumbo shrimp, a special tuna salad, wagyu tataki, sake-steamed clams, a salmon tasting plate, and a fluffy dashimaki full of dashi. The head chef and staff are friendly, and it has worked for both dates and business meals. No table charge. Closed Wednesdays.

places.notes: [Yakiniku · a smoky alley yakiniku off Sennichimae] A small yakiniku restaurant down a narrow alley off the Sennichimae shopping street, open since 2020, whose red lanterns make it look like an izakaya. rm.bowl: Ramen, ¥1,200, call vegetables, garlic and fat (October 2026).

places.notes: [Ramen · a big Jiro-style shop open all night near Ebisucho] A large, clean Jiro-inspired ramen shop between Ebisucho and Namba, open since 2022, with 27 seats including tables. Noodles and broth are made in-house: flat, wavy noodles of Maturité flour that one diner found dense and packed with wheat. A bowl (¥1,200 in October 2026) comes with 100 g to 300 g of noodles for the same price; call your vegetables and fat, and add garlic yourself. Expect a fatty, heavy broth and thick chashu; one diner found the soup too sour, another the pork underheated. There is also R's set meal (¥1,000), which one diner had on a weekend morning: bean sprouts, thick chashu and a fried egg with rice, tonkotsu soup and kimchi. Open 24 hours Saturday to Monday and until 04:00 most other nights. Cash only.

places.cu: Sichuan Chinese, also called 本格四川料理 功夫 · daily lunch set ¥780–790 with soup and dessert, e.g. pork with green peppers (chinjao rosu) or mapo eggplant · liver and garlic-chive stir-fry set · knife-cut noodles with cilantro and garlic to taste · Sichuan dan dan noodles, mapo noodles, mapo tofu · fried rice +¥400 · yakisoba · all-you-can-eat-and-drink courses from ¥3,980 (about 50 dishes) · gyoza, o…
places.notes: [Chinese · Sichuan cooking and knife-cut noodles in the Shinsaibashi arcade] A large Sichuan restaurant in the covered shopping arcade near Honmachi, with many Chinese customers. The shop bills its cooking as authentic Chinese by a Sichuan chef, and says its two chefs each have more than 30 years of experience. The listing credits the cooking to a veteran chef with 30 years of experience. Lunch is a bargain: a daily set for about ¥780, such as a generous chinjao rosu (pork with green peppers) or mapo eggplant, with soup and dessert, served fast; one repeat visitor returns for the liver and garlic-chive stir-fry. Noodles include knife-cut noodles you can customize with cilantro and garlic, Sichuan dan dan noodles and mapo noodles; add fried rice for ¥400. At night groups can book the all-you-can-eat-and-drink courses (¥3,980 for about 50 dishes in September 2026), with gyoza and oyster with stir-fried lettuce among the hits and seasonings that taste less Japanized. Private rooms with a big round table seat up to 20. Order by ticket or QR code. Cards accepted.

places.cu: Jiro-style mazesoba ¥1,050 with thick noodles, bean sprouts, crispy garlic chips and onion · spicy mazesoba ¥1,150, large 300 g · chilled soupless Jiro-style ramen ¥1,200 in summer · seasoned egg +¥150 · chicken paitan ¥950, light, with scallop broth and scallop pieces, curly egg noodles, large menma · rare chashu · extra rice ¥50 · chopped garlic and vinegar on the counter · 7 counter seats
places.notes: [Ramen · Jiro-style mazesoba and a light scallop paitan by Honmachi] A tiny seven-seat counter near Honmachi, open since March 2025 and named as the brand's head shop. The mazesoba (¥1,050) is the draw: thick, chewy, wheaty noodles in a rich sauce with crunchy bean sprouts, onion and crispy garlic chips. Add chopped garlic from the counter, as it can taste flat without, and vinegar near the end; the spicy version (¥1,150, large 300 g) adds plenty of back fat, rare chashu and fried onion. In summer there is a chilled soupless Jiro-style ramen. The chicken paitan (¥950) is the opposite: light and smooth, with scallop broth, chunks of scallop, curly egg noodles and big menma; one diner found it only average. Extra rice is ¥50. Some nights there is a 10-minute wait.
