places.n: 酒菜舎虎純 (Sakanaya Kojun)
places.hood: Shinsaibashisuji 2-7-11, back of the 1F arcade — 4 min from Namba Stn exit 14, 5 min from…
places.cu: Fish-led Japanese izakaya · sashimi of fish bought each morning · keema curry dashimaki with Ryu no Tamago eggs · fried dishes with tartar, e.g. chicken tempura · Kojun potato salad · Beniharuka sweet-potato tempura with salt · lotus-root dumplings with duck · fried ginkgo · sansho rice balls and red miso soup · house-smoked dishes · sake from around Japan, rotated, plus bone sake · wines chosen …
places.notes: [Japanese · a fish-led izakaya and sake bar run by a couple off Shinsaibashi-suji] A hidden counter izakaya at the back of a building's ground-floor arcade, open since 2019 and run by a husband and wife, per a review. Chef Nakagawa, a veteran of more than 20 years in Japanese cuisine, previously worked at Koudai Z in Fukushima Ward. The owner is a cook of Japanese cuisine and a sommelier, so it suits both sake and wine drinkers: sake from around Japan rotates, and wine is chosen to match what you eat. Fish comes first, with sashimi from the morning's buying, but the menu wanders: the signature, per the shop and one weekly regular, is the keema curry dashimaki (house keema rolled into egg), alongside chicken tempura with tartar, potato salad, salted sweet-potato tempura and sansho rice balls with red miso soup to finish. Seasonal set courses are available by advance booking; one December 2025 course included abalone chawanmushi and an assorted sashimi platter. One regular praises the pacing and attentive but unintrusive service. Book counter seats online; closed Tuesdays.

places.cu: Kushikatsu fried to order and served one skewer at a time · thin batter · dip in sauce, shrimp salt or lemon soy · kelp with roe · shrimp bread (ebi pan) · shrimp-salt rice ball to finish · drinks from the fridge, self-service; write your own order · 8 counter seats
places.notes: [Japanese · a one-person basement kushikatsu counter on Shinsaibashi-suji] An eight-seat counter down a flight of stairs off the Shinsaibashi-suji arcade, run single-handedly by a woman; one diner felt most customers were regulars. Kushikatsu are fried to order and handed over one at a time, so each is crisp; the batter is thin enough that the ingredient shows through, and one diner found not a single miss. Beyond the usual sauce you can dip in shrimp salt or lemon soy. One diner recommends the kelp with roe and the shrimp bread (ebi pan), and another ended with a shrimp-salt rice ball. Portions are small, so you can try many. It's homey: take drinks from the fridge yourself and write down your order. With one person cooking it can feel busy. Book ahead; it fills up. Smoking allowed.

places.cu: Classic bar · fresh-fruit cocktails, e.g. grapefruit, vodka and cranberry · gin and tonic, short cocktails left to the bartender · Bowmore and other whisky · straight rum · nuts and dried fruit, dried orange slices · records playing · counter and a table for four, 16 seats · non-smoking
places.notes: [Bar · a hidden wood-rich bar up a staircase by Hozenji] A classic bar you would walk past: in a narrow alley near Hozenji, a barely-marked steep staircase leads to a second door and then a warm, wood-rich room with records playing, a counter and a table in back. One reviewer notes that charred marks from a 2002 fire still show on the counter. The drinks list is short but well made: fresh-fruit cocktails squeezed to order, gin and tonic, a short cocktail left to the bartender, whisky such as Bowmore. Snacks are nuts and dried fruit; one diner loved the dried orange slices. Diners describe the master as easygoing and easy to talk to, and it's calm despite Hozenji Yokocho next door, with overseas visitors among the customers. A seat charge applied (about ¥1,000 in 2024); six drinks for two came to ¥7,500 in February 2026. Non-smoking. Mind the stairs.

places.notes: [Teppanyaki · a casual creative griddle bar in Sennichimae] A small second-floor teppanyaki bar in Sennichimae with a counter and a few tables, casual enough to drop in for a drink. The young owner is friendly and chatty, which makes it easy to come alone. The griddle menu runs to sirloin steak shabu-shabu dipped in ponzu or a sweet yolk sauce, large shrimp grilled until the heads are crisp, horumon, and grilled vegetables that two diners singled out (the onions are sweet). Start with the potato salad topped with thick-cut bacon. Finish with soba-meshi, garlic rice or fried rice, or the honey toast for dessert. One diner found the staff friendly and accommodating. There's wine. Smoking allowed; closed Sundays.

places.notes: [Japanese · a fresh-fish izakaya bar over the Dotonbori canal] A fourth-floor izakaya bar right by Dotonbori Bridge, open since 2011, whose windows look out on the canal; the four-seat sofa by the window is the spot. The master is a former high-school baseball player and a keen fan. True to the name, fish leads, bought at the market daily: excellent sashimi, crisp katsuo tatsuta-age, marinated mackerel, and a shrimp mapo tofu more than one diner insists you try. The menu runs to 60-plus dishes with Okinawan touches, and an eel rice ball makes a filling finish. Drinks are the other draw, with 200-plus choices, including over 100 sakes a year, which the manager will suggest, plus a good shochu list. The master is friendly. Courses with all-you-can-drink suit groups, up to 30 for private hire. A ¥550 appetizer charge applies; one diner found the billing unclear. Cash only; smoking allowed.

places.hood: Awaza 1-12-21, 1F (Nishi-ku) — 1–2 min from Honmachi Stn exit 23
places.cu: Tabelog Ramen OSAKA 100 (2023, 2024, 2025) · dashi soba ¥690: frothy chicken paitan with katsuobushi, shoyu tare of Aichi soy sauces · premium toppings +¥150 for extra chashu and a seasoned egg · house-made medium straight noodles · moist, smoky chashu and egg · cold soba with roast-pork rice bowl set under ¥1,000 · pepper and yuzu kosho on the counter · 9 counter seats
places.notes: [Ramen · a Tabelog 100 frothy chicken dashi soba for under ¥700] A nine-seat counter a minute from Honmachi exit 23, open since 2015 and picked for Tabelog's Ramen OSAKA 100 in 2023, 2024 and 2025, famous for big quality at a small price. The owner spent 15 years as a French chef before turning to ramen. The dashi soba (¥690 in October 2026) is a foamy, espuma-style chicken paitan with katsuobushi; one diner found bonito flakes settled at the bottom and stirred them in. It's creamy yet not heavy, seasoned with Aichi soy sauces. House-made medium straight noodles are smooth and chewy, and the chashu and egg have a smoky edge. Premium toppings add extra chashu and a seasoned egg for ¥150; a cold soba with roast-pork rice bowl comes in under ¥1,000. Diners report lines of five to eight and 10- to 15-minute waits at lunch, with chairs outside; bowls arrive in about five minutes, and rice can sell out. Lunch only; closed Fridays.

places.notes: [Ramen · chicken-and-pork shoyu with house noodles by Sakaisuji-Honmachi] A lively little ramen stand a minute from Sakaisuji-Hommachi, open since 2019, busy with local workers, with hip-hop on the speakers and energetic, attentive staff. The chicken-and-pork shoyu (¥1,000) is the standard: house-made straight noodles, chewy and smooth, in a well-balanced soy broth, with thin chashu, menma, chopped white leek and mitsuba. Shio fans can have the chicken-and-pork shio (large ¥1,100), and there are chicken-only shio and shoyu bowls and a mazesoba. At lunch rice is ¥100 in any size; pair it with the table's "Devil's Garlic", or pickled garlic and mayonnaise, and there are spicy garlic chives too. One diner found it a bit salty. Cash only; closed Sundays.

places.notes: [Ramen · Osaka's famous Jiro-style line by Ebisucho] The Nipponbashi branch of a well-known Jiro-style name, open since January 2024, with long lines: 15 to 50 people, rain or shine, and 40 minutes to over an hour from joining to eating. Buy your ticket in line. Bowls are thick noodles (150 g to 400 g) under a mountain of crunchy bean sprouts in a rich soy-based pork broth sweet with back fat, piping hot to the end; call your garlic, vegetables and fat, or go "everything extra". There's also a dry ramen, plus toppings like double pork, cheese and egg. The staff are the other draw: energetic, patient with first-timers and cheering you on, but there's a strict no-leftovers policy, so order honestly. Closed Sundays.

places.cu: Tsukemen · signature spicy tsukemen ¥1,000, spice level 1–3: a thick red dip of pork bone and dried mackerel with miso, several chilies, chili oil and shrimp · ajitama tsukemen in pork-bone and seafood · hot (atsumori) noodles ¥950 · 200 g or 300 g · medium-thick chewy noodles · thick pork-belly chashu, seasoned egg, nori · yuzu soup to finish · black Chinese-style ramen · grilled gyoza · garlic …
places.notes: [Ramen · spicy shrimp-miso tsukemen in a chic room near Shitennoji] The Yuhigaoka branch of Suzume, whose main shop is in Amerikamura, open since 2013 a few minutes from Shitennoji-mae Yuhigaoka. The room is dark and stylish, with counter, tables and sofas, roomy for a tsukemen shop. The signature spicy tsukemen (¥1,000, level 1 to 3) has a thick red dip of pork bone and dried mackerel blended with miso, chilies, chili oil and shrimp, nicely balanced between seafood and heat, and it stays warm. Noodles are medium-thick and chewy, 200 g or 300 g, with thick pork-belly chashu and a seasoned egg; finish with the yuzu soup. The ajitama tsukemen is the classic, and one diner had the hot-noodle version for ¥950. Grilled gyoza on the side. Buy a ticket at the door. Cash only; open daily.

places.notes: [Ramen · clear iriko shio and charcoal chashu by Matsuyamachi] A small, wood-toned shop by the Yokobori River, open since March 2026 and already featured in Ramen Walker, with a posted note about its additive-free cooking. The shio ramen (¥950) is the lead: a clear dashi of Ibuki iriko, mackerel flakes, kombu and dried shiitake, finished with salt tare and a shellfish oil, light but full of seafood umami. House-made thin straight noodles of Hokkaido wheat are chewy; chashu is grilled over charcoal on a shichirin. The special shio (¥1,380) brings four chashu cuts, and the wontons (shio wonton ¥1,280) are plump and juicy; one diner ranks them among the best in Osaka. The shoyu blends two soy sauces; one diner found it less striking than the shio. Weekday waits were short; Sunday afternoon was packed.

places.notes: [Ramen · a light chicken shoyu with tuna bonito, open past midnight in Honmachi] A small counter shop near Honmachi, open since 2023, that serves lunch and then reopens at 19:00 until after midnight, handy after drinks. The default bowl is the white-shoyu maguro-bushi ramen (¥1,030): a light soy broth of chicken bones and niboshi lifted with tuna-bonito flakes, with medium-thin straight noodles, chashu and a generous heap of crunchy wood-ear mushroom, green onion and bean sprouts; add katsuobushi halfway to change the flavor. The yuzu ramen is lighter still. In summer there was a chilled salt-shoyu with lemon-pickled onion and prosciutto (¥800). Portions are modest, so pair it with the kara-age and half fried rice set (¥600). Buy a ticket at the machine. Closed Saturdays.

The draw is the Taiwan mazesoba (¥900, regular or small, garlic to taste): spicy Taiwan-style minced pork with green onion, garlic chives, garlic and chili, balanced by egg, on thick chewy noodles that hold the toppings. Mix hard, change it up with kombu vinegar, then follow the house routine for oi-meshi: leave the spoon in your empty bowl, set it on the counter, and ask for rice (¥50) to mop up the rest. There's also a spicy ramen with grilled chashu that one diner found lighter than it looks. The master is friendly. Open until 02:00 on weeknights; cash only.

places.notes: [Chinese · a spice izakaya with craft gin, open until 05:00 on weekends] An alley izakaya in Sennichimae, open since 2020, that layers aroma rather than raw heat onto familiar Chinese dishes. The house favorites are the yodare-dori, tender chicken in a nutty sesame-spice sauce, and the iron-pot mapo tofu; diners also praise the shrimp chili, the spicy lamb stir-fry and even the kimchi, and small plates let you try many. Spice curries close the night, rotating flavors such as chicken neck with tomato, Akashi octopus, or duck keema with shiso and umeboshi; on some days there's a curry lunch, which one eight-time regular calls the best in Osaka. More than 20 craft gins are matched to the food, and staff are generous with recommendations. Hot-pot courses come with two hours of drinks. Seating is a bit tight. Open until 24:00, Fridays and Saturdays until 05:00.

places.notes: [Japanese · low-temperature tonkatsu of Watanabe Berkshire pork in Sennichimae] A small counter-and-table tonkatsu shop in Sennichimae, open since 2024, built around Watanabe Berkshire pork from Kagoshima, with the lighter Imoko SPF pork as the alternative (a menu chart and the shop's own manga explain the difference). Cutlets are fried low then high, so allow about 20 minutes; the reward is tender, juicy meat, and one diner called the tenderloin the most tender tonkatsu ever. The Spencer roll (ribeye) is the rich choice. Taste it with rock salt, dashi soy, mustard or the house sauce, which has a slight curry note; one diner preferred salt. Cabbage with a carrot-and-perilla dressing can be refilled, and the pork miso soup is good. Many customers are from overseas; ordering is by QR code. Tables are cramped. Open daily.

places.notes: [Japanese · rare local fish, sashimi and tempura off Mitsudera-suji] A hidden fish izakaya at the back of a building on Mitsudera-suji, open since 2018: noisy street outside, calm room inside, with a handwritten menu. The draw is fish you rarely see, much of it from Owase in Mie; the sashimi platter is full of names one diner had never heard, all very fresh. Tempura is crisp and often unusual, and grilled fish comes crunchy outside and fluffy inside. Add oysters with ponzu, then finish with a grilled rice ball, a tempura rice bowl or Inaniwa udon. A wide sake list is fairly priced. A ¥5,500 course was offered in late 2024. Diners praise the well-timed service, and one regular says every friend introduced keeps coming back. Smoking allowed; closed Sundays.

places.notes: [Okonomiyaki · a one-person Hiroshima-style griddle on the edge of Amerikamura] A small, long-running okonomiyaki spot on the quiet side of Amerikamura, where the owner cooks, serves and takes payment alone. The specialty is Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki, layered and packed with cabbage; one regular calls it the best in Osaka, and the soba niku tama double comes with crispy fried noodles and a spicy sauce. Around it is a cheap, beer-friendly teppan menu: teppan kimchi with beef intestine, beef sinew with ponzu, fried squid legs, octopus and scallops, shio yakisoba. In summer the draft beer comes in a frozen mug. The owner can seem reserved at first; one diner found it cool, another found real warmth by the end. Prices are low; cash only; open until 01:00, closed Sundays.

places.notes: [Japanese · unsteamed Kansai-style charcoal eel and eel skewers by Shinsaibashi] An eel specialist on Mitsudera-suji, open since 2007 and featured on TV (Matsuko no Shiranai Sekai, 2022). Eel, mainly the Kiso Sansen brand, is killed to order and grilled over charcoal in the Kansai jiyaki style without steaming, so the skin is crisp and the flesh fluffy, with a tare that isn't too sweet and Wakayama sansho. The unaju comes on a round lidless plate so steam doesn't soften the skin. What sets it apart is the eel skewers, rare in Osaka: belly, neck, burdock roll and more, from ¥880 each or five for ¥4,180; smoked eel goes well with sake. Monthly omakase courses (¥8,800 and ¥11,000) run through liver sashimi, shirayaki, skewers, salad and an eel rice bowl. Diners praise attentive staff. Book dinner; it fills. Closes when the eel sells out.

The special adds plump shrimp and meat wontons, rare shoulder chashu and a soft egg. There's also a hand-kneaded abura soba. Buy a ticket outside. Weekdays only; cash only.

places.notes: [Ramen · Onomichi back-fat shoyu with free rice refills near Tanimachi 6-chome] A bright, clean 13-seat counter on a back street south of Tanimachi 6-chome, open since November 2025 and bringing the rarely seen Onomichi style to Osaka. The owner, a woman, previously worked at Chuka Soba Shintaku in Hiroshima, and runs the 13-seat counter with female staff. The chuka soba is a chicken-bone shoyu with a bold, slightly tart soy edge, scattered with pork back fat and served so hot that staff warn you; noodles are firm and medium-thin, with thin, tender chashu and menma. The deal is the ¥1,000 set, which adds free rice refills and a raw or seasoned egg: put the egg on rice, splash on some broth, or try the house tip of ao-gappa pickles with mayo. Gyoza are better than expected. Staff are cheerful, and you leave with a topping coupon. Lunch can stay nearly full until 13:30. Closed Thursdays; Wednesday lunch only.

The counter can be packed at noon, but staff greet you cheerfully and cook with care. Closed Sundays.

places.notes: [Ramen · Osaka's famously thick tonkotsu by Imamiya-Ebisu] A pilgrimage bowl for tonkotsu lovers near Imamiya-Ebisu, open since 2005 and on Tabelog's ramen 100 lists most years since 2019. The broth is extraordinarily thick, slightly gritty and concentrated, like a pork-bone stew, yet not overly salty; it clings to thin curly noodles. Buy a ticket, then tell staff your noodle firmness, broth richness and green-onion amount. One regular always orders the chashu ramen, loaded with tender chashu, and recommends the thick spare ribs; get rice too. Change it up with garlic soy, pickled ginger and spicy takana from the table. Opinions in October 2026 were mixed: most still rave, but one long-time fan found the soup lukewarm and changed, and another found the noodles soft. There can be a line at opening. Cash only; closed Mondays.

The special (¥1,680) carries chicken breast, chicken thigh and pork belly chashu and aosa seaweed; the seasoned-egg shio is ¥1,370. Save some broth for the yuzu ochazuke with shredded chashu. House rules: one bowl each, photos of food only, quiet please. Lunch only, until the soup runs out; check Instagram before going.

The chuka soba (¥1,050) is a clear shoyu with a citrus aroma and an elegant hint of Sichuan pepper, clean and deep, with no harsh heat; the Prime adds rare chashu and a seasoned egg. You choose flat or round house-made noodles, both chewy and wheaty. The dry chuka soba with egg and sudachi is the rich option, and in early October there was a chilled kiwi ramen (¥1,300). Self-serve rooibos tea. It often closes early when the noodles sell out, so go before late afternoon. Cash only; closed Sundays.

The chuka soba is a nostalgic clear shoyu of chicken bones with seafood and a hint of shiitake, deepened by back fat and paired with medium-thin straight noodles; set the firmness, richness and back fat, and extra green onion is free. The soy is on the strong side and the normal broth is rich, so one diner would go light next time. Sets are the draw: the ¥1,100 lunch set adds half fried rice and two crisp kara-age, and there's a nira soba buried in garlic chives with an egg yolk. Take a number from the machine inside and wait by phone; on a Sunday afternoon one diner was 20 groups back. Open until midnight, 01:30 on weekends; closed Thursdays.

places.notes: [Japanese · a one-person obanzai counter tucked above Dotonbori] A hideaway on the fourth floor of a building just west of Midosuji, run single-handedly by a chatty, warm owner. There are eight seats at a sunken kotatsu-style counter facing the kitchen and one table, so it suits solo diners and couples. The cooking is homey seasonal Japanese: an assortment of six obanzai with a drink, sashimi you can build from three of the day's fish, light, crisp tempura (young corn in its husk, sweet potato that tastes stone-baked), braised chicken wings, sweet simmered herring and bamboo shoots in dashi. One regular comes two or three times a month, and the owner will adjust dishes to requests. One diner found the prices very reasonable. Lunch and dinner; closed Thursdays.

Chicken here is served very fresh, with a sashimi platter (¥1,800), liver sashimi and tataki. There's a ¥500 seat charge, and dinner can be a timed seating when the next booking follows. Many guests are from overseas. Book on the official site; when the main shop is full, guests are sent here.

Start with the chicken heart (¥500), the house specialty, juicy with a 'magic' seasoning, then work through the vegetable list that regulars swear by: grilled lettuce, crisp Moroccan green beans, teppan konnyaku with ponzu. The tonpei-yaki, pork tamagoyaki and negi modan-yaki (¥1,400) are the heartier choices, and the yakisoba comes the classic way with aonori and pickled ginger. The cook is friendly. Sauce smoke clings to clothes, so dress casually. Cash only; generally no reservations, so call first.

Get the grilled mochi (¥200) hot from the grill: white or yomogi, charred, stretchy and filled with red-bean paste, best eaten on the spot (one diner's takeaway stuck to the bag). There's also warabi mochi (¥350), ohagi five for ¥900 in kinako and smooth or chunky anko, and shiso mochi. Mochi is made without additives, so it doesn't keep; vacuum packs are available for souvenirs. The owner is friendly. PayPay accepted; closed Sundays.

places.notes: [Ramen · niboshi and clam shio by two people at Uehommachi] A fresh, stylish little shop a minute from Osaka-Uehommachi, open since September 2025 and run by two, the owner and one staff member per a regular. The owner trained at Gokujyu Bimen umami, a very popular ramen shop in Higashi-Osaka. The broths are the point: niboshi shio or shoyu (¥1,200) with the sardine umami balanced, never overwhelming, and the shoyu showing a slight acidity; a sea bream and clam shio (¥1,450); and a limited shio tsukemen (¥1,350) whose dip blends clear chicken, seafood and domestic clam broth, with smooth house-made flat noodles of Haruyutaka wheat worth tasting with just salt first. Rare chashu turns tender in the hot broth. Add the sesame-scented sea bream rice. One regular reports a bronze at the Ramen Walker Grand Prix Kansai 2026. No table condiments; pay after. One October diner found service slow and the tsukemen noodles stuck together. Closed Tuesdays.

places.notes: [Ramen · a 2002 Uehommachi shop with house noodles and seasonal shio bowls] A neighborhood ramen shop a few minutes from Osaka-Uehommachi, open since 2002 and making its own noodles since 2006, with regulars logging dozens of visits. The everyday bowl is the original ramen (¥1,050), a light, refreshing shoyu with moist chashu and spinach, gentle on the body; the Manpuku set (+¥480) adds gyoza, kara-age and rice. The real draw is the rotating limited menu, with careful sourcing: chilled chicken shio topped with thick Hida tomato and Tokushima sudachi (¥1,500), a cold "adult" aemen with shiso, myoga and Senshu water eggplant, a Banshu Hyakujitsu chicken shio with chicken ham, curry tsukemen. Smooth, glossy house noodles; one seasonal bowl cost the same in any size. Add ginger or Sichuan-pepper oil. On one rainy Sunday, families lined up soon after opening. Closed Tuesdays.

The chicken soba is the other side, jidori chicken deepening with each sip under a sharp soy, on thin straight noodles with low-temperature chashu. places.notes: [Ramen · a long-running Onomichi ramen counter by Nishinagahori] A small, traditional ten-seat counter near Nishinagahori, described by diners as a pioneer of Onomichi ramen in Osaka, with regulars lingering over gyoza and beer at night and a quick-turning line at lunch. The Juuroku Ban ramen is a nostalgic shoyu of Rausu kombu dashi and seafood with a layer of back fat, slightly sweet and easy to drink, on thin flat noodles brought from the Sebe noodle shop in Onomichi. Unusually for the style, it's meaty: thin lean chashu plus a tender, sweet-fatted kakuni of Wamochi pork, which one diner liked best with rice. Rice-and-kimchi sets run about ¥1,280, and the slightly large gyoza carry a hint of garlic. One diner found the bowl just average. Closed Sundays.

places.notes: [Ramen · pork-head and seafood double-soup tsukemen by Honmachi] A spacious tsukemen shop a minute from Honmachi, open since 2014 in a district crowded with ramen shops, from a tsukemen brand with other branches. The dip is a "double soup" of pork head and seafood, rich with fish powder and onion yet not heavy on the finish, clinging to thick, chewy, wheaty noodles; a hot stone rewarms it at the end. Toppings range from seasoned egg and chashu to niboshi, sudachi and umeboshi, and in summer there was an umeboshi tsukemen (¥1,100) with lime that even skeptics liked. For a bowl, the seafood tonkotsu ramen (¥950) has a powerful fish aroma. Open late on weekdays and Saturdays, all year; delivery via Uber Eats. Cash only.

In summer there was a chilled soba of kombu and bonito dashi topped with kumquat and minced chicken. Opinions on other bowls vary: one diner found the shio too oily and salty, another found the broth lukewarm at opening. places.notes: [Japanese · a Tabelog 100 tempura counter frying in olive oil] A calm basement counter of hinoki wood just off the Soemoncho nightlife strip, open since 2021 and picked for Tabelog's Tempura 100 in 2025. The chef and the chef's wife are both very kind. The difference is the oil: extra-virgin olive oil at low temperature, which the shop says soaks in less and drains well, so even a long course stays light. The omakase opens with a surprise katsu sandwich, then runs through seasonal seafood and growers' vegetables: several kinds of shrimp including heads and roe, young ayu, sea urchin, sweet carrots and sweet potato, plus Kagawa Olive Beef, and finishes with tencha. Diners describe the chef as friendly and talkative about the ingredients. About ten seasonal sakes. One seating nightly at 18:00, plus Sunday lunch; book ahead.

places.notes: [Japanese · refined oden and sake hidden in Higashi-Shinsaibashi] A quiet, old-Shinsaibashi-style oden counter at the very back of a building's second floor, open since 2014, with classical music playing. The oden is the heart of it, delicately seasoned: daikon, konnyaku, big clams with kuzukiri, green onion with abura kasu, tuna negima, whale saezuri and yuba. Around it come seasonal plates: an oden-broth soup with wild mushrooms and free-range chicken, a shime-saba sandwich, hairy crab packed in its shell, umazurahagi with its liver, a fluffy sardine tsukune that converted a sardine skeptic, crisp grilled eel. Good sake to match. Dinner runs about ¥10,000–20,000 with a 10% service charge, and one table waited a long time for dishes. Book ahead, especially in winter; closed Mondays.

Founded more than 100 years ago, it is now run by the fourth-generation owner. Book the omakase of appetizers and 12 nigiri, or order à la carte; one diner found the prices reasonable. Highlights in reviews: crisp torigai, thick lightly grilled nodoguro, abalone with its liver sauce over rice, a refined anago, and sea urchin that melts away. Seasoning is balanced, neither too sweet nor too sour. Not every visit lands: one diner found some pieces fishy or too salty. Enter by 21:30; closed Sundays.

The chef seems reserved at first but warms up; the host is friendly. Three seatings a day; book well ahead.

places.notes: [Sushi · a busy, generous Minami sushi bar regulars rebook] A popular 19-seat sushi bar a block off Dotonbori, usually full, with regulars who book the same day and come back often. The shop describes itself as run by a husband-and-wife team. Portions are big: oversized toppings, huge rolls and sashimi platters piled with toro, kazunoko, scallops, flounder and geoduck. The favorite is the toro-taku roll (only one toro item per table, so choose between it and the toro tekka); aburi salmon, rare and juicy, comes close behind, with eel and anago. Start with the crab-claw sunomono in sweet vinegar or the kani miso, which pull you toward sake. There's no price list, but two diners paid about ¥17,000 with drinks. Popular items sell out; one diner found the rolls unevenly cut. Closed Mondays.

The shoyu chuka soba is a chicken-and-seafood broth with a strong, nostalgic soy edge, gentle rather than salty, on medium-thin low-hydration noodles with three slices of chashu, menma, sprouts and green onion; at lunch, extra sprouts and onion are free. For more richness there's a back-fat version. Sets add gyoza or a small soy-dark fried rice (¥1,200 with gyoza), and evenings bring a beer set with fatty chashu. Grated garlic is on the table. Service is attentive. Closed Sundays.

places.notes: [Ramen · a beginner-friendly Jiro-style bowl by Uehommachi] A Jiro-style shop two minutes from Osaka-Uehommachi, open since February 2025, with a relaxed atmosphere that diners call easy for first-timers. Garlic mayo (+¥100) and spicy fried garlic push it further into junk-food territory, and the back-fat rice bowl is a guilty side. One diner could not add garlic on a daytime visit. Busy at lunch; open daily.

places.notes: [Ramen · a Tabelog 100 Nagoya Cochin shoyu by Sakaisuji-Honmachi] A seven-seat counter a few minutes from Sakaisuji-Honmachi, open since 2013 and on Tabelog's ramen 100 lists in most years since 2017, yet on two October 2026 visits there was no wait. The chuka soba (¥1,000) is built on Nagoya Cochin chicken: a clear amber broth with a rich soy aroma and long finish, firm, slightly wavy medium-thin noodles with real wheat flavor, two slices of chashu, menma and a seasoned egg included. The chicken soba (¥1,100) is a robust chicken paitan glossed with chicken oil and sharpened with raw onion; one diner found the chicken edge too strong, another the finish a bit sweet. The shio soba sells out first. Add a chashu rice bowl. Lunch only on Wednesday and Saturday; closed Sundays; cash only.

The rich tsukemen (¥1,200) pairs house-made thick, chewy, slightly sweet wheat noodles with a dip so thick it clings, built on pork, chicken, sardine flakes and niboshi; order it soy or curry, the curry adding a gentle spice. Large noodles are free, but the dip is strong and a small rice comes at the end to mix with the leftover dip and yuzu kosho, so regular may be enough. Lemon halfway brightens it. The mazesoba (¥1,150) adds cheese, fried onion and garlic chives. One regular has eaten here twenty times. Buy a ticket outside; open daily; cash only.

places.notes: [Sushi · a showy tuna omakase counter just off Dotonbori] A six-seat counter on a third floor near Namba, calm despite the crowds below, built around tuna and theatre. The omakase (¥12,000 in October 2026) opens with a bowl heaped with uni, ikura and otoro that the chef sears in front of you, then the "Dragon Roll" of otoro, negitoro, uni and egg yolk, and a tuna flight of akami, chutoro and otoro. Shira-ko with ponzu, a gold-leaf uni tofu, nigiri of shrimp, sea bream, scallop and salmon, and an unagi dog handed straight across the counter round it out. Reviews call it visually spectacular and, past the show, well made. Open from noon, so it works for a splurge lunch too. Book ahead.

places.notes: [Sushi · a lively ¥4,400 omakase in two seatings on Soemoncho] A counter sushi bar from the 881 ("Yabai") Group, open since June 2025, whose idea is authentic counter sushi made approachable and fun. The head chef, Hibiki, is a former sumo wrestler, just 21 when reviewed, who trained at Sushi Yamato; the chanko on the course is the chef’s own. There's one omakase (¥4,400), or ¥6,600 with all-you-can-drink, served to eight guests at a time in two seatings at 17:30 and 20:00, opening with a group shout-out. The course runs about 15 items: Tosa katsuo, chawanmushi, seasonal fish sandwiches, kamasu, yuan-yaki, tuna, unadon, then chanko and a ramen made from the broth of the sushi fish. Diners love the warm, playful atmosphere and the head chef's friendliness; one found only six nigiri and no chutoro, and the shaved-ice dessert plain. The door shows only a QR sign. Reservation only.

places.notes: [Chinese · a late-night gyoza counter open until 3 am in Higashi-Shinsaibashi] A casual counter Chinese bar, open since 2022, made for a second or third stop: it runs until 03:00 most nights. The gyoza are the reason to come, crisp-edged and bursting with sweet, juicy filling, light enough that two people keep ordering; try one with truffle oil, as staff suggest, and compare pan-fried, boiled and fried. Around them come bold drinking food: yurinchi in a sweet-spicy sauce, shumai, shrimp mayo, fried rice, garlic-sprout namul, and in winter a shirako mapo tofu. Staff are friendly. Smoke from the kitchen can fill the small room when busy, and smoking is allowed. Closed Sundays.

places.notes: [Udon · thin-noodle curry udon, the Minami night-out finish] A small, glass-fronted counter just north of Aioibashi, run by a couple, where diners end a night of drinking with curry udon. The curry is light and rich in dashi, with noticeably good beef, and it comes over very thin noodles that slip down easily, unusual for curry udon (¥1,100; kizami with fried tofu ¥1,200; tempura too). Add kayaku gohan (¥350). For something gentler, there's a sudachi udon fragrant with citrus, a warm nyumen with fluffy egg, or plain kizami udon. On one weekday evening it was busy with families and regulars, and more overseas visitors have found it lately. Open 18:00 to 01:30; closed Sundays; cash only.

places.notes: [Japanese · a creative seafood-and-meat izakaya in Higashi-Shinsaibashi] A tucked-away izakaya in the middle of the Minami nightlife streets, open since 2015, with a counter downstairs and a second-floor room that groups of about ten can book. The menu runs from seafood to meat and seasonal plates: bluefin tuna and yellowtail-belly sashimi, shirako with ponzu, scallop butter that left one table speechless, fried oysters, sanma and matsutake in foil, a beef cutlet and uni cream pasta, but the dish people come back for is the shrimp mayo. The sake list is broad. There are no prices on the menu and portions scale to your group, so ask; dinners ran about ¥5,000–15,000. One diner found service slow and the room noisy, another found it calm and suited to business dinners. Book ahead; closed Sundays.

places.notes: [Ramen · the foam-whipped chicken paitan of Honmachi] The main shop of Wadachi, a minute or two from Honmachi's Yotsubashi-line exits, open since 2014 and a Tabelog ramen 100 regular from 2017 to 2023. Its signature Fuku Ryu ramen (¥930) is a chicken paitan shoyu whipped into a creamy, cappuccino-like foam, topped with rare chashu, green onion, mizuna and a slightly tangy foam that blends in as you go; thin straight noodles stay firm. Portions are modest, so add the kara-age and rice set. One regular prefers the niboshi shoyu with onions and thick chashu, lighter than it looks; others order the Mazenibou niboshi mazesoba, best with vinegar and a few pieces of meat saved for the rice. Fills by noon on weekdays. Open daily; bring cash.

places.notes: [Ramen · additive-free whole-chicken chuka soba near Sakaisuji-Honmachi] A clean shop five minutes from Sakaisuji-Honmachi, open since 2022 and committed to no additives or chemical seasonings. The marudori (whole-chicken) chuka soba looks dark but drinks light and refreshing, with medium-thin noodles, rare chashu and tender menma; the special (¥1,300) adds a well-seasoned egg. The shio comes with a dab of wasabi to stir in midway, and there's a niboshi mazesoba with a strong sardine note. In season, a chilled abura soba (¥1,050) with chashu, egg yolk and fish powder is good with plenty of vinegar. The rare chashu rice bowl is a strong lunch side, and lunch sets are ¥100 off. One diner found the soup lukewarm and wanted more depth. Pay on the way out; cash only.

places.notes: [Ramen · a ¥750 shoyu with mitsuba, and ¥500 morning ramen, by Ebisucho] A ten-seat counter a few minutes from Ebisucho, open since 2021 and loved for good ramen at a low price. The shoyu ramen (¥750) is a seafood dashi deepened with chicken bones and chicken fat, easy to drink, on thin but chewy noodles, with thin chashu and an unexpected sprig of mitsuba; there's a shio too. Early risers can get a plain morning ramen for ¥500, a clear, dashi-rich bowl that soothes a hangover. On rainy days extra noodles are free. Add a ¥300 chashu rice bowl or the limited meat-and-egg bowl. Staff service is warm. Hours seem to vary, so check before an evening visit; closed Mondays; cash only.

places.notes: [Ramen · seafood tonkotsu and rich tsukemen by Awaza] A lively counter shop a minute or two from Awaza, open since 2023 and packed even on a rainy weekday evening. The seafood tonkotsu ramen (¥970) is rich and creamy, with medium-thick straight noodles, chashu, a seasoned egg, wood-ear mushroom, nori and plenty of green onion in a striking round bowl. The rich tsukemen (¥1,050) has a strong pork-bone dip, and the mazesoba, with a different kind of punch, comes with white rice; pair a bowl with the meat-and-egg-yolk rice bowl on hungry days. Summer brought a chilled chuka soba with pork soft-bone chashu. The owner and staff keep the mood bright. One diner found the tsukemen just average. Buy a ticket first; closed Mondays; cash only.

places.notes: [Ramen · a ramen-and-fried-rice lunch counter near Tanimachi 4-chome] An eight-seat lunch-only counter in Uchihonmachi, open since 2011, where the fried rice draws as big a line as the noodles. The classic order is the half-and-half set (¥1,400 with a large fried rice), picking a ramen: the rich kote shiro shoyu one regular always orders, a shio scallop, a spicy miso full of vegetables and minced meat, or dan dan noodles with a subtle Sichuan-pepper note that come with a side of rice. From 13:00 the menu expands to the kuro-tama fried rice, dark-soy and packed with chashu, worth a 20-minute wait to fans. The omelette and seafood fried rices are huge. It's smoky from the woks, and one diner found the service brusque. Lunch Tuesday to Saturday only; cash only.

places.notes: [Sushi · a relaxed one-chef sushi counter in Higashi-Shinsaibashi] A sushi counter where the chef works alone and quietly, a rare place in Minami to order serious sushi à la carte as well as by the course. Start with a platter of six appetizers and about five kinds of sashimi, then nigiri on small, red-and-white-vinegar rice that lets the fish lead: sweet shrimp straight from the tank, chutoro (one regular's pick of the tuna), eel, raw anago with a crunchy bite, standout ikura and a beautifully presented sea urchin. Tamago is Kansai-style, and dessert is a homemade pudding. Diners call the balance of quality and price unusually good for this level. With one chef, order slow dishes early. Closed Sundays.

places.notes: [Japanese · a quiet nine-seat kushiage counter by Namba Station] A small second-floor counter a minute from Namba exit 13, open since 2024 in a quieter corner of Namba, good for an unhurried dinner or a low-key business meal. The Harusai course (about ¥5,000) brings 12 of the chef's skewers, classics and seasonal ones, fried to order and handed over one at a time; details like asparagus cut into easy bites show the care. Add a quail egg if you have room. It ends unusually with a Japanese-style pho and ice cream. The draft beer is poured with real attention to the foam. The owner-chef is friendly and creative, and staff are attentive. Open for lunch too.

places.notes: [Japanese · mentaiko-and-tororo hot pot to 1 am in Higashi-Shinsaibashi] A calm hot-pot izakaya in Higashi-Shinsaibashi, open since 2021 and featured on TV, open until 01:00 every night. The signature is the Hakata mentaiko tororo nabe: pork belly, chicken, fish balls and tofu in a good broth, crowned at the table with a heap of creamy grated yam and salty, spicy mentaiko, then finished as a cheese risotto. Sides are drinking food with flair: avocado yukke, a theatrically long toro-taku roll wrapped in thick nori, potato salad with truffle flakes, fresh oysters. All-you-can-drink is ¥1,500, so three drinks or more makes it worth it; one table spent just over ¥6,000 each. Staff finish the pot for you. A second branch, Bettei, is upstairs.

Many diners order the tsukemen (¥1,450): glossy, smooth whole-grain flat noodles worth tasting plain, and a dip that balances soy with sweetness, gentle heat and acidity, with three kinds of well-cooked chashu; one regular has been 63 times. The Choro raa men (¥950) is a clear broth of clam and jidori chicken with strong umami and an elegant, gentle finish, in original shio (the staff's suggestion) or shellfish shoyu; pick melt-soft braised pork or rare chashu, and regular or smooth whole-grain noodles. At lunch the bigger "Choro-mori" portion and a small rice are free. Half the fun is the self-serve butter, grilled nori and Okuizumo sansho: add them midway, then drop the rice, the rest of the egg and a pat of butter into the broth for a risotto. The chuka soba (¥1,000) is a deep, slightly oily broth of niboshi, katsuobushi and kombu; choose rich or light soy (rich is the punchier pick). House-made medium-thin noodles, flecked with whole wheat, pick up the broth well, and the two rare chashu (beef chuck roll and chicken breast) are tender. For something bigger, one regular swears by the mazesoba, oyster with nori or horumon with sweet-spicy colon (¥1,400), finished with rice like a risotto. The owner is attentive. One diner found the light version unremarkable. Lunch Monday to Saturday, until sold out.

places.notes: [Ramen · a ramen-and-set-meal diner by Tanimachi 6-chome] A casual ramen diner near Tanimachi 6-chome, open since 2012, where you can have a quick lunch set or settle in for beer, gyoza and fries at night, with the TV on. The lunch ramen set (¥990) pairs a rich soy tonkotsu with gyoza and rice. The spicy miso (¥1,140 with rice) is mild and creamy rather than fiery, with crunchy mizuna. There are chicken paitan bowls in shio or shoyu, rich and punchy, and a garlic-butter chicken ramen with thin noodles as a ¥1,600 set. Smaller mini-ramen sets suit lighter appetites, and garlic powder on the counter perks things up. One diner found the noodles a little soft. Short waits at lunch; open late most nights.

places.notes: [Sushi · sushi and tempura in one omakase, drinks included, in Higashi-Shinsaibashi] A seven-seat wooden counter in Higashi-Shinsaibashi, open since October 2025, whose omakase combines Edomae sushi with fresh tempura and makes the price easy: ¥15,000 with free-flow soft drinks, or ¥18,000 with alcohol. The chef has more than 25 years of experience. Expect a clear hamo soup, sawara sashimi, a striking mackerel "prosciutto," then crisp tempura of abalone, anago or nodoguro and maitake with yuzu-kosho salt, and a chawanmushi topped with Hokkaido sea urchin, before nigiri on lightly pressed red-vinegar rice, each fish prepared its own way and served at the right temperature: otoro, akami, generous uni. Diners note the knife work at the counter and a calm atmosphere for special occasions. Book ahead.

places.notes: [Yakiniku · thick-cut beef sliced to order at a Namba counter] A lively 14-seat yakiniku counter a minute from Namba Station, open since 2024, where staff cut the meat to order and season it in front of you. The thick-cut series is the reason to come: premium salted tongue with lemon and a thick outside skirt with wasabi soy, juicy and generously portioned. Start with kakuteki or cucumber kimchi, order rice even if you usually don't, and finish with a soupy curry ochazuke or curry zosui. The ¥5,000 recommended course is good value. One diner found the menu a little limited. The counter fills quickly, so book on Tabelog. Smoking allowed; open nightly until midnight.

places.notes: [Japanese · a one-chef counter kappo hidden under Dotonbori] A ten-seat counter in a basement in the heart of Dotonbori, open since 2013 and run by one chef, with a back door onto a terrace over the Dotonbori River. The cooking is creative seasonal Japanese served on fine tableware: chilled chawanmushi with eggplant in summer, sashimi such as bluefin tuna, and in autumn a sanma rice one diner called amazing. One regular never looks at the menu and simply leaves it to the chef; à la carte works too. The sake list is wide, with rarities like a sparkling sake from Okayama, and the value draws praise. Despite the location it feels calm, not touristy, and the counter invites chat with the chef and neighbors. Lunch on Wednesday and Friday to Sunday is an omakase (¥5,800, two or more, book by the day before). Closed Mondays.

places.notes: [Japanese · grill-your-own dried fish over charcoal off Dotonbori] A basement izakaya under a green lantern in Dotonbori 2-chome, open since 2002, where you grill Shizuoka dried fish and vegetables yourself over a tabletop charcoal brazier. The assorted platter brings mackerel, horse mackerel and shishamo; shiitake come out bursting with juice, and there's a surprisingly good beef platter of thick tongue, wagyu short rib and tenderloin. Summer adds hamo with grated daikon and ponzu. Order the kamameshi when you sit down, since it's cooked to order and takes over 30 minutes; the salmon and ikura is the pick. Ingredients are mostly domestic, and the sake and shochu lists are strong. The room is calm, with a counter and tatami tables. Book a day ahead for weekend lunch or a 17:00 start.

The Chinese-style fried rice comes from a recipe shared by Nakamura, a friend of the owner's mother. One regular has lost count of visits; the draw is drinking food from the griddle: kasu hari (abura kasu with crisp mizuna, ¥770), ten cheese, sautéed scallops, and okonomiyaki such as pork and egg crowned with a runny fried egg. Finish with salt yakisoba with crisp pork fat, or a curry yakisoba. It's often full of reservations, so book or call ahead. Open until 03:00; closed Sundays; cash only; smoking allowed.

places.notes: [Ramen · chicken paitan and clam shoyu, with wagyu sushi, by Tanimachi 4-chome] A lunch-only shop on the ground floor of the Dia Palace building in Uchihonmachi (the clam-and-chicken ramen shop Choro is upstairs), open since November 2024. Every regular bowl is ¥900. The paitan, the shop says, is a "triple soup" of three chickens, Yamagata pork and Kuroge wagyu tendon; one diner smelled a neighbor's bowl and called the aroma "comparable to tonkotsu ramen." For something lighter, the chicken and clam shoyu comes with thin noodles and yuzu. Add the ¥400 wagyu roast sushi, seared in front of you, or the ¥300 seared chashu-mayo rice bowl. A soy-milk cold tantanmen with yodare-dori chicken ran in summer 2026 and drew raves, though one diner found it bland. Lunch only, closed Sunday and Monday, cash only; one diner found it closed before last order.

places.notes: [Ramen · miso ramen specialist facing Utsubo Park] A branch of a miso-only ramen chain in front of Utsubo Park, open since 2021 with plenty of tables. The base is the chain's Hokkaido 100-year miso, a salty aged red miso it sears to draw out depth; one diner found it rich and robust, "perfect for when you're craving a rich bowl." If that's too strong for you, the silver miso uses a milder Kyushu barley miso, though one diner found it too mild. The gold miso is seared with white wine, almond and sansho; a spicy miso (¥980) comes in three heats. Lunch sets run about ¥900 with fried rice or plain rice, though one diner found the set ramen too simple and another warned off the fried rice. There's a kids' miso ramen too. Lunch can draw a short line.

places.notes: [Ramen · chicken paitan and big chashu set meals in Uchihonmachi] A small counter of about 10 seats a few minutes from Sakaisuji-Honmachi, running since 2011 and specializing in chicken paitan. The ajitama paitan (¥1,000) is rich yet relatively light, with thick-cut pork-belly chashu; at lunch you get a free large serving of noodles or rice. The other draw is the chashu set meal: 150 g or 250 g of chashu with mayonnaise and black pepper, a neatly rounded mound of rice, kimchi and soup, ¥1,300 for the large. There are also a classic ramen one diner found nostalgic, and Taiwanese mazesoba. Buy tickets at the machine outside; it takes ¥1,000 notes only. Snug, so not for groups. Cash only.

The signature shoyu ramen (¥950) is a clear, gentle broth with a hint of sweetness in the soy, with chashu, menma, red onion and chili; flat noodles are ¥100 more, and the garlic comes on the side; one diner found it changed the bowl a lot. You choose noodle firmness and add-ons like yuzu peel and onion. The "umakara" (¥990) adds a stronger chili kick to that sweet shoyu. There's also a seafood shoyu, a tantanmen one diner came back for four times (chilled in summer), and a miso ramen. Free rice at lunch.

The tonkotsu ramen (¥700) is a milky but light, creamy pork-bone soup with very little odor, on straight thin Kyushu-style noodles cooked to the firmness you ask for. Everything else is a variation on that base: tonkotsu shoyu, sliced-garlic, butter, spicy, a tomato ramen and tantanmen. At lunch, ¥800 gets any regular ramen with mentaiko rice, diced chashu rice or plain rice, though the rice sometimes runs out. One diner found the staff attentive in explaining things to overseas visitors. It's light rather than heavy, so one diner wished it were more filling. Cards and QR accepted.

places.notes: [Ramen · thick chicken paitan from a one-chef counter by Uehommachi] A clean, eight-seat counter a few minutes from Uehommachi where one chef cooks fast, open since 2020. The chicken paitan (¥850) is thick and velvety, "rich yet not overwhelming" to one diner, with smooth straight thin noodles, tender chashu, long menma, red onion and bonito flakes. Stir in the spicy miso on the side little by little; it's hot. For more, there's an even richer, thicker paitan; a chuka soba one diner prefers; and a warm mazesoba. In summer, a chilled sea bream shio ramen with yuzu salt sells in limited numbers. Finish the soup with ¥100 rice. Mark your order on the sheet at the counter and pay cash after. One diner hit clumps of salt. Lunch only on Wednesday and Saturday.

places.notes: [Ramen · tantanmen in several flavors near Sakaisuji-Honmachi] A tantanmen shop behind a neon sign, opened in October 2025, that one diner learned is a sister shop of the Honmachi Chinese restaurant Koyouju. Start with the "Moto-Aji" original (¥950): a rich, only mildly spicy soup under a generous minced-meat sauce, bean sprouts and greens, on fairly thin noodles; one diner couldn't stop drinking the soup, which changes as the meat sauce mixes in. There are also "Shin-Aji" and miso versions, a shoyu tanmen and a sour-spicy suanshu tanmen; in summer a chilled spicy tantanmen (¥1,200) ran, though one diner wanted more heat. It also works as a casual Chinese spot: one diner had mapo tofu, pork and bean-sprout stir-fry, a half tantanmen and two lemon sours at 8 pm for under ¥2,500. Counter, tables and a terrace. Cards and QR accepted.

places.notes: [Sushi · red-vinegar sushi omakase at an eight-seat counter with a Namba night view] An eighth-floor, eight-seat counter of single-board hinoki in Soemoncho, open since February 2025, a sister shop of Sushi Akazu in Shinsaibashi. The omakase (¥19,800 in September 2026) runs in two seatings and builds around firm rice seasoned with aged red vinegar; one diner who worried it wouldn't suit loved it. Expect Hokkaido oysters in ponzu, a tuna trio of otoro, chutoro and marinated akami, steamed abalone whose liver sauce you finish over a little rice, sea urchin crowned with caviar, soft simmered anago, then a smoked-daikon toro-taku hand roll and a pudding-like tamago that plays dessert. One diner mentions the friendly chef, others the Minami night view, and two call it an anniversary or date place. BYO costs ¥5,000 a bottle.

The ¥14,800 omakase runs to about 18 dishes: sea bream under a Tosa-vinegar jelly finished over binchotan, aori squid flash-frozen and finely scored, seven-day shima aji, dry-aged chutoro on rice kept warmer at 42°C so the fat melts, Densuke anago swished as shabu-shabu, and the signature botan ebi topped with shrimp roe and sea urchin. A fish-bone soup simmered for hours and a vanilla pudding close it. Diners praise the explanations and playful touches; one was surprised with a birthday plate. One diner noticed many overseas guests. There's a 5% service charge. Lunch on weekends.

places.notes: [Shabu-shabu · Okinawan Agu pork shabu-shabu in Higashi-Shinsaibashi] A clean, reservation-only shabu-shabu room near Shinsaibashi that serves Okinawa's Agu pork, sliced and arranged like a rose; repeat diners come back for meat that is sweet and "not greasy at all." The ¥5,280 course opens with crunchy mozuku vinegar, then the hot pot, with homemade ponzu heaped with green onion, a sesame sauce and yuzu-kosho; wrap the pork around green onion or pickled island garlic. Staff explain the pot and serve the first round. Finish with zosui or Okinawa soba made with Ishigaki noodles, and add the sweet purple sweet potato tempura. One repeat diner always buys the ponzu to take home. Order a course or the hot pot per person, or a per-head charge applies. There's a second branch in Namba.

places.notes: [Standing bar · horumon and game, from kangaroo to badger, by Nippombashi] A retro standing bar behind a plastic-sheet door just off Sennichimae-dori, picked for Tabelog's tachinomi 100 in 2025, where 1980s and 90s J-pop plays on a big screen and you mix your own highball from bottled soda. The owner runs the shop with two female staff members. The draw is fresh offal and game: Matsusaka beef garlic small intestine (¥580), a seared Miyazaki beef yukhoe with egg yolk (¥980), and a kangaroo tenderloin steak (¥720) diners find tender, juicy and not gamey. Venison and wild boar are staples; pheasant, badger (as a winter hot pot), camel and sea lion turn up when in stock, camel announced on the shop's Instagram. Liver and the rarer cuts go fast, so come at opening; there can be a line. The weekend curry wins praise from the few who order it. Portions are small and prices exclude tax. Cash only.

places.notes: [Late-night diner · omurice and izakaya snacks from midnight to 8 am in Higashi-Shinsaibashi] A ten-seat U-shaped counter with no big sign, behind a curtain and sliding door in Higashi-Shinsaibashi, that keeps reverse hours: midnight to 8 am, Tuesday to Sunday. The owner calls it a casual izakaya, so order a drink, but the dish to get is the omurice (¥780), the most popular to one diner: fragrant ketchup rice under rich egg with a tangy, thick ketchup. The macaroni salad with a hint of curry, octopus-shaped red sausages and pork kimchi go with a lemon chuhai; there's also marinated mackerel and octopus sashimi. One diner found it packed at 5:30 am; another has come for over 10 years. Spend runs about ¥1,400. Cash only.

places.notes: [Ramen · cafe-style ramen with coffee on the ground floor of My Dome Osaka] A big, calm, 100-seat ramen cafe on the ground floor of the My Dome Osaka exhibition hall, opened in August 2025 by the company behind Choro. The bowls are light: a chicken-based shoyu on straight thin noodles with thin slices of duck chashu, a niboshi shoyu (¥950) and a miso, with seasonal changes. The popular lunch set pairs shoyu ramen with yakimeshi and a drip coffee for ¥1,000; others come with lu rou fan or seasoned rice, and there's a kara-age set (¥900) and Basque cheesecake. Two diners found the shoyu on the salty side. With Wi-Fi, outlets, raised tatami seating and a kids' menu, it suits families and laptop lunches. Order at the touch-panel ticket machine and clear your own table.

places.notes: [Ramen · chicken-tonkotsu paitan, tsukemen and abura soba by Tanimachi 4-chome] A small counter of about seven seats near Tanimachi 4-chome, with tables upstairs when it fills after noon, running since 2018. The ramen (¥900) is a chicken and pork-bone paitan that one diner found hearty, with short medium-thin noodles and thin, well-seasoned pork-belly chashu; add the A set (+¥150) for two kara-age and rice. The tsukemen (¥980) pairs medium-thick chewy noodles with a chicken, pork-bone and seafood dip, light in body but oily on top, with a little acidity. The abura soba (¥890) comes regular or Japanese-style, dressed in soy and shrimp oil over thick glossy noodles; at lunch ¥1,070 adds kara-age and rice. One diner found the menma flat and the welcome cool. Dinner on weekends depends on the soup.

places.notes: [Ramen · herb-scented shio ramen at lunch in an Italian restaurant, Awajimachi] A stylish room between Honmachi and Yodoyabashi that serves Italian food at night and turns into a ramen shop at lunch, open since March 2025. The shio ramen (¥1,000) is the bowl to get: a rich chicken and aromatic-vegetable broth drawn out with herbs and spices, which one diner likened to Italian dressing, with rare chashu and thin noodles. A lemon wedge comes on the side; squeeze it in midway for a brighter, almost pho-like finish. Add umeboshi or yuzu-kosho for more changes. One diner brought a 2026 Kansai ramen guide that gave the shio a semi-grand prize. There's also a shoyu, and a chashu rice bowl that sells out. A small noodle portion is very small. Lunch only; a line formed after noon one April day.

places.notes: [Ramen · thick chicken-and-vegetable "doro" soba near Kitahama] A small office-district counter between Kitahama and Sakaisuji-Honmachi, open since 2020 and, one diner says, one of the chain's last two shops along with Nara, serving doro soba: a soup of chicken and vegetables simmered until they dissolve, so thick it clings to the noodles "like a purée." Two diners were surprised how easy it is to drink and how clean the finish is; one found the flavor ordinary beneath the texture. Choose your richness, from the basic bowl up to the extra-thick Oni Kyoku (¥1,600), or a spicy version (¥1,500). Toppings of fried green onion and eringi add aroma, and pink pickled ginger from the counter sweetens and shifts the soup. At lunch there's a doro soba set with a mini chashu rice bowl, or add a mini kara-age bowl for ¥100. Buy a ticket first; staff help if you're unsure. Cash only.

places.notes: [Ramen · niboshi chuka soba with back fat, on Tabelog's Ramen 100 since 2017, in Kyomachibori] A seven-seat counter near Awaza, open since 2012 and picked for Tabelog's Ramen 100 every year from 2017 to 2025, with early-morning hours from Thursday to Sunday and late nights most days. The niboshi ramen (¥950) is gentler than the name suggests: a mild soy base with floating back fat and a pleasant niboshi bitterness, on medium-thick curly noodles; one diner thought of Yamagata ramen. The special niboshi mazesoba (¥1,300) is the other draw: sweet-savory soy and concentrated niboshi over wide, chewy curly noodles from Kyoto's Menya Teigaku, piled with block and rare chashu; one diner said the regular version would do. There can be a line at night, with chairs outside. Cards, e-money and QR accepted. A second shop is in Nakazakicho.

places.notes: [Ramen · shoyu on medium-thick curly noodles and karasumi mazesoba, by Shitennoji] A tiny eight-seat shop near Shitennoji, open since 2022 and picked for Tabelog's Ramen 100 in 2024 and 2025. The noodles are the point: robust, flat, medium-thick and curly, which one diner was "a bit moved" to find. The shoyu ramen is light with niboshi umami (¥1,250 with wontons and egg); the rich shoyu adds a strong garlic hit, aosa seaweed and fish powder to stir in. For heat, the Inazuma chuka soba and mazesoba layer chili, sansho and black pepper over sweet soy and back fat. A repeat diner's favorite is the chilled mazesoba with karasumi, green onion and niboshi, finished with a warm egg sauce, though the shio with beef tendon, clams and niboshi may top it. Seats are few, so expect a short wait at noon. Pay first, cash only.

places.notes: [Ramen · rich tonkotsu with free rice at lunch near Higobashi] A second-floor ramen shop near Higobashi with flashy decor, open since 2012 and the main branch of its name. The tonkotsu ramen (¥950) is a rich, slightly grainy pork-bone soup with a pleasant pork aroma, deep but not too salty, on thick, firm noodles; one diner tasted seafood in it too. Two chashu come with it: a smoky, sweet-fatted belly block and a meaty loin. At lunch the rice is free and self-serve, with pickled greens, tsukudani and takana; one diner had two bowls, and when it sold out the staff found some leftovers. Add garlic and chili powder from the table. The black tonkotsu seemed the more popular order to one diner. Open until midnight Monday to Thursday, lunch only Friday to Sunday.

Arrive by 11:30 for a free mini rice bowl. The chicken nikomi ramen (¥900) is a thick, creamy chicken paitan with a sweet chicken-fat finish that doesn't feel heavy afterward; pick thin or medium-thick noodles. The chicken and seafood (¥900) is flavorful but not too heavy. For +¥300 the full toppings bury the noodles in grilled and rare chashu, egg, nori and green onion. Tsukemen and a chicken shoyu round out the menu. After 13:30 you get almond tofu or a black coffee on the house. Cash only.

places.notes: [Sweets · made-to-order ohagi with a two-hour line, by Nippombashi] A small, long-standing ohagi shop off Sennichimae-dori (often called Tamaseiya), picked for Tabelog's sweets lists from 2017 to 2026, that opens at 14:00 four days a week and closes when it sells out. There's one thing to buy: a box of six small ohagi (¥1,170), choosing up to two of smooth red bean, chunky red bean and kinako, made fresh after you order, so the line is slow; October diners waited one and three-quarter to two hours, and about 40 people were queued by opening. The anko is gently sweet with a touch of salt, the kinako fine, the rice soft and lightly crushed, and even people who dislike ohagi like them. Eat the kinako ones the same day; anko keeps until the next morning. Takeaway only, cash only.

places.notes: [Italian · uni pasta, carpaccio and wine in a tiny Ura-Namba bar] A small, nearly always full Italian bar at the end of a backstreet in Ura-Namba, open since 2009 and one of several PIENO shops. It shares the main shop's menu, so start with the three-fish carpaccio (¥1,298) and the fig, mascarpone and prosciutto spring rolls, add the oyster ajillo or a skirt steak, and finish with the signature uni cream pasta (¥1,188). Pasta comes firm; one diner came back ten years on for the unchanged Genovese. Handwritten specials change daily, the wine list explains itself, and the sangria is homemade. One diner spent about ¥5,000 with drinks, another about ¥8,000 with two bottles of red between two. It's cramped, so skip it with big luggage and reserve for Friday or Saturday evenings.

places.notes: [Izakaya · obanzai counter with a ¥900 niku dashimaki lunch in Ura-Namba] A twelve-seat counter in the Ura-Namba backstreets, open since 2020, that is two places in one. At lunch the line forms before opening for the ¥900 set: pick one of six mains, most famously the niku dashimaki, a fluffy, freshly rolled dashi omelet topped with sweet-savory beef, with obanzai, a little sashimi, a big bowl of tonjiru and rice refills; or swap the rice for a draft beer. Staff take your order in the line. At night it's an easier, friendly izakaya: the "five" obanzai platter that one regular says usually comes with six, thick-cut ham katsu, chikuwa tempura with shibazuke tartare, the dashimaki again, and highballs. It's the main shop of its name. PayPay or cash.

places.notes: [Tempura · counter tempura courses with a shaved-ice finish in Shinsaibashi] A calm twelve-seat tempura counter on Shinsaibashi-suji, open since 2018, the second shop of Tempura Osakaya Kusatetsu in Fukushima. The chef, Shin Tamura, trained at the Nikko Hotel and has 32 years in Japanese cuisine. Courses begin with a look at the day's ingredients, then two shrimp, fried one piece at a time in front of you, with three salts and tentsuyu and a suggestion for each. In autumn there's matsutake as tempura or a dobin-mushi with scallop and ginkgo, and one diner called the Beni Haruka sweet potato the best tempura sweet potato ever eaten. Finish with tendon, curry or rice with ikura, then a fluffy shaved ice and dandelion coffee. Lunch on Friday to Sunday is the way in: courses from ¥7,700 with a drink, or ¥10,000; reviewers' spend ran up to ¥15,000–20,000. Explanations are thorough. 10% service charge.

places.notes: [Yakitori · Hakata mizutaki and yakitori down a Higashi-Shinsaibashi alley] A busy chicken restaurant tucked down an alley in Higashi-Shinsaibashi, running since 2007 and often hard to book. The hot pot is the reason to come: a Hakata mizutaki whose rich, creamy collagen broth arrives as a solid block and melts in the pot, deep and gentle with tender chicken; finish with zosui or noodles, and reserve it ahead. Around it, there's a five-kind chicken sashimi plate with no off flavors, tataki, salt-grilled skewers, tsukune with egg yolk, fried gizzards and fried tulip wings the size of a KFC piece. Portions are big. Service is quick and the room loud enough that one diner couldn't hear the table. Seating is capped at 2½ hours when busy; ¥660 otoshi.

places.notes: [Ramen · Agu pork and Tanba black chicken shoyu and shio, with inventive limited bowls, by Kujo] A nine-seat counter near Kujo, open since 2019 and picked for Tabelog's Ramen 100 in 2024 and 2025, with lines at the 11:00 opening. A husband-and-wife team runs it; the owner trained at ramen shops before opening. The base is an additive-free double soup of Agu pork and Tanba black chicken with a layered fish dashi; the ajitama shoyu (¥1,250) floats Agu back fat over flat noodles from Tsurumi Seimen, with juicy Agu belly chashu. The shio is clear and mellow, its umami building as you go. For the simplest taste of broth and noodle, there's a kake-style shio or shoyu soba with only onion. Repeat diners come for the limited bowls: a stir-fried chicken-shoulder noodle tossed in a cast-iron pan, an Onomichi-style back-fat shoyu, chilled ramen in summer. Add the seasonal takikomi rice. Ticket machine, cash only; closed Mondays.

places.notes: [Ramen · rich miso on thick curly noodles near Kitahama] A fifteen-seat counter in the Kitahama office district, open since 2020 and run by the same people as the nearby Tsukemen Ide, with a lunch line that some diners call routine. The miso ramen (¥1,000) is rich and slightly gritty, with a pork-bone base beneath, on thick, chewy curly noodles of whole wheat, brightened by chopped purple onion and white negi with yuzu peel. Two variations stand out: the spicy miso, with five heat levels and the first three free, where the miso stays the star; and the "Wasan sansho" miso (¥1,100), whose aroma greets you at the door and gives a refreshing finish. Buy your ticket inside before you line up. Cards and PayPay accepted.

places.notes: [Ramen · thick pork-bone and seafood tsukemen in Kitahama since 2011] A busy fifteen-seat tsukemen shop in the Kitahama office district, open since 2011, where lunch means buying a ticket, a short wait outside and often a shared table. Finish with soup-wari from the table. Add all the toppings (¥600) or a rice bowl of shredded pork or niku-miso. There's also a curry tsukemen. One diner found it simply average. Its sister shop, Miso Noodle Koji, is a few blocks west. Cards and PayPay accepted.

places.notes: [Ramen · whipped chicken paitan by Taisho Station] A bright, clean seven-seat counter a block from Taisho Station, open since September 2024 and serving the chicken paitan that one diner hadn't found anywhere else in Taisho. The soup is whipped until frothy and creamy but not too heavy, on thin straight noodles, with two chashu: rare pork shoulder and a roasted or grilled pork belly. Choose shio, shoyu (the soy comes through strongly) or a spicy version; one diner found the extra noodles salty. Order rice (¥100) and you get takana and spicy mentaiko free, or go for the rare chashu bowl with egg yolk. In summer there are chilled bowls such as a sea bream and clam shio with tempura, which can sell out at lunch; one August evening there was a line of six. Closed Wednesdays; Tuesday is lunch only.

The tori soba (¥900) is a piping-hot soy broth of long-simmered parent-hen bones with Kochi and Osaka soy and a bright hit of yuzu, on medium-thin straight egg noodles; one diner found the yuzu overpowering. The BLACK version packs garlic and black pepper; RED brings heat; the yuzu shio and a garlicky tori mazesoba fill out the menu. Finish with a chicken chazuke (¥550) or a mini chashu bowl. The limited chicken paitan often sells out. Cash only.

Indian staff keep the room running efficiently. The recommended Tenryu ramen is a rich tonkotsu shoyu with melt-in-the-mouth chashu; the classic bowl floats a layer of fine back fat over a pork-bone soup that is rich but not heavy, with two thick slices of pork belly. The shio tonkotsu is the lighter choice. Pair it with gyoza or the ramen and fried rice set (¥1,150), or order extra noodles. One nine-visit regular says every ramen here is good. Close to Shinsekai and busy with visitors, but not a tourist trap, one diner felt. Cash only; closed Wednesdays.

One repeat diner always orders the pork modern-yaki with a fried egg before a Shinkigeki show; the suji-negi-tama of slow-cooked beef tendon and green onion is another favorite. Start with the assorted basashi, five kinds or seven with heart and tongue, from lean thigh and tenderloin to the rich mane fat, then a sakura yukhoe or tataki. One diner comes almost monthly and books Friday and Saturday well ahead. Smoking is allowed, so no one under 20.

Live eels are prepared on the spot and grilled Kansai-style without steaming over fierce heat, so the skin comes out crisp, like a potato chip in the shirayaki, while the flesh stays fluffy and juicy. The ¥7,700 course walks through it all: a creamy yuba sesame tofu, rare eel shabu-shabu in ponzu, crisp shirayaki and kabayaki side by side, then an unaju of a whole eel with liver soup; three kinds of sansho let you play with the finish. A young chef opened this eight-seat counter after seven years at a Michelin two-star restaurant. The cooking is refined rather than flashy: the seven-dish course with drinks (¥11,000) runs from a mizuna and beef appetizer through a sashimi platter with sea urchin and crab, a chewy lotus-root dumpling in kuzu sauce and Saikyo-grilled flounder to seasonal tempura and a clay-pot rice, with leftovers turned into onigiri for tomorrow. places.notes: [Ramen · clear jidori shoyu and shio, and inventive summer chilled bowls, by Kujo] A small, slightly hidden counter three minutes from Kujo, open since 2023 and usually run by one cook who chats with guests and has adjusted a recipe in response to guest feedback. The owner previously ran Naniwa Tonkotsu Ramen Taisho Bashi Manten near Taisho Station before going independent. The broth is a clear soup of Tajima chicken and Tanba black chicken with real kombu and a delicate seafood dashi; the shoyu ramen is deep enough to drink to the last drop, with firm straight noodles and pink rare chashu. Pair it with the tamago-kake gohan, made with a branded egg. Summer brings the stars: a chilled shio ramen (¥1,200) with tomato ice cubes and two chashu, and a weekend chilled hamo ramen with sudachi, best tried on the spoon first. With one person cooking, expect waits when it's busy. Order and pay in cash up front.

places.notes: [Ramen · beginner-friendly Jiro-style ramen in Edobori] A thirteen-seat counter near Higobashi, open since November 2024, serving Jiro-style ramen without the rituals: you buy a ticket, enter in order and skip the topping call. The standard 200 g bowl has a sharp soy flavor balanced by the sweetness of noodles and vegetables, which go up to double-extra; the fat is unseasoned, so eat it with the noodles, and the pork is firm and lean. The soupless ramen (¥1,100) is a repeat diner's order, the cold TKM coats the noodles in egg, and the soupless tantanmen with an onsen egg is properly spicy. Pile on mayonnaise, pork scraps or a raw egg if you want the full effect. Lunch rarely has a wait. Cash only.

It breaks from Edomae: each piece comes with its own house sauce or condiments and hidden knife work, like aori squid scored so finely it turns fluffy, topped with sea urchin. The ¥22,000 course might open with grilled kuruma shrimp under karasumi, run through flounder, yuzu-scented sea bream and a sweet potato chawanmushi, then grilled mackerel with ume and condiments, tuna and anago. Save room for the add-ons: a toro-taku roll and an "adult" ebi-mayo one diner calls a must, though one diner found the ¥10,000 uni hand roll and the overall bill steep, and the extras not offered clearly. Closed Wednesdays.

places.notes: [Ramen · chicken stewed ramen and lunch sets, izakaya by night, by Tenmabashi] A fifteen-seat basement counter on Tanimachi-suji, five minutes from Tenmabashi, serving ramen at lunch and turning into an all-you-can-eat-and-drink izakaya in the evening; by name and one diner's account, it is a branch of Okamoto Shoten near Kitahama. The chicken stewed ramen (¥950, with chashu and egg) looks rich and frothy but drinks smooth, with chicken sweetness. The menu is long: sets pair a bowl with a mini rice bowl, chicken curry or kara-age, and there's seafood shoyu with rare chashu, chicken paitan tsukemen and a spicy seafood ramen that one diner found heavy and short on seafood. Another found the ramen average but good value. From 13:30 a mini rice bowl is free. Cash or PayPay; smoking allowed.

The ramen (¥850) is a double soup of seafood and chicken paitan, slightly thick, rich but easy to drink, with the seafood coming through as you slurp the thin, firm, low-hydration Menya Teigaku noodles. Tender pork-belly chashu comes in thick slices in the chashu ramen (¥1,000). Finish with Dive Rice: kimchi rice you drop into the last of the soup. Rice is half price at lunch. Pay as you order. Cards and QR accepted.

places.notes: [Ramen · kombu-shellfish chuka soba and seasonal white soups, with wok fried rice, by Kujo] A clean counter by Kujo Station, open here since April 2025 after moving from Namba, where you can watch the fried rice tossed in the wok and the bowls carefully plated. The most popular bowl is the chuka soba: a kombu and shellfish broth with a strong wheat aroma from the noodles and two kinds of chashu, one a grilled pork belly. The white tonkotsu soba changes every three months; autumn 2026 is salmon and miso in a frothy soup with sautéed vegetables (¥1,180). Summer brings a chilled tantanmen with cream cheese and lemon. The fried rice, fluffy with burnt soy and optional butter, draws its own fans (one diner warns it can taste a bit salty), and the set (¥1,580) pairs it with a bowl. Warm service. Buy a ticket at the entrance; cash only. Closed Thursdays.

The style is aged Edomae: sea bream aged six days in kombu with sudachi salt, yellowtail aged five, marinated bluefin, on slightly firm rice seasoned with red vinegar. Lunch is the deal: a ten-piece omakase (¥4,500) with shijimi soup, chawanmushi, red miso soup and free tea. In the evening, fifteen-piece courses run ¥6,800–8,300; the top one, only served here, adds kinmedai, kinki, snow crab and sea urchin. A 10% service charge applies from July 2026. Lunch is popular, so reserve.

places.notes: [Sushi · ¥4,400 omakase that ends in seafood ramen, Higashi-Shinsaibashi] An eight-seat counter of the 881 Group, open since January 2026 on a hard-to-find third floor (take the emergency stairs from the second; the door has no sign). The listing says the chef trained at Michelin-rated and well-known sushi restaurants in Ginza. There's one course, ¥4,400, in two seatings at 17:30 and 20:00: soft-shell turtle soup, rare katsuo, then nigiri worked by aging, kombu-curing and vinegaring, such as four-day saba, kombu suzuki, sardine and nodoguro, plus a mackerel bozushi, steamed anago and a tuna and herring-roe hand roll. It finishes with a seafood shio ramen in the size you choose, then sweet tamago. All-you-can-drink is ¥2,200 more. Several diners rate the value outstanding. Lively, casual and good for a first sushi counter. Card only.

places.notes: [Sushi · ¥18,000 aged-sushi course with drinks included, Higashi-Shinsaibashi] A calm ten-seat counter on a fourth floor, open since November 2025, with one all-in course (¥18,000) that includes alcohol or soft drinks. The rice is seasoned firmly with red vinegar and carries aged toppings, such as four-day sea bream, kombu-cured kisu and tuna from the Osaka supplier Teramoto Shoten, served as chutoro, marinated bluefin and otoro. Between pieces come creative plates: a mascarpone chawanmushi that eats like carbonara, Densuke anago shabu-shabu, abalone liver sauce and an uni don with two kinds of sea urchin. A fried mehikari roll and milk pudding close it out. Two seatings nightly, weekend lunch, reserve by the day before; 5% service charge.

The courses start with chicken plates (peperoncino, a tsukune hamburger, chicken prosciutto, and sashimi on the Sai course) before the hot pot, which staff cook for you. Gunma black chicken is tender in a rich but not heavy broth, with soft cabbage, grated yam and house yuzu-kosho. Finish with broth poured over rice, zosui or tea rice. One diner liked the pasta with lettuce enough to want seconds. Courses run from the small Hashi upward. Seen off at the elevator. Cards accepted; closed Sundays.

places.notes: [Ramen · weekly-changing ramen in a Kitahama basement bar] A hidden basement counter near Kitahama, open since September 2025: by day it serves ramen, by night it is the whiskey bar BULLSEYE. The ramen is the creation of a former curry chef. The menu changes every week (check Instagram) and leans on seafood broths and spice. Past bowls include a chilled seafood-broth clear shio with grilled pork and chicken breast, a chilled clam ramen whose deep, clear broth one diner found astonishing, a chilled tororo ramen with grilled gizzards, and a shrimp paitan with a hint of curry. Many come with a mini takikomi rice; pour the leftover broth over it. One diner disliked the seasoning powder on a cold bowl. One person ran it on an August visit, and bowls took 10–15 minutes. PayPay only.

places.notes: [Ramen · emulsified Jiro-style tonkotsu by Tsuruhashi] An eight-seat counter a few minutes from Tsuruhashi, open since 2019, which one diner with more than twenty visits calls the best Jiro-style ramen in Kansai. Unlike the usual soy-heavy Jiro bowl, the soup is a creamy, emulsified tonkotsu, slightly sweet and not too salty, so even extra back fat goes down easily. Noodles are medium-thick, flat and straight, smooth rather than chewy. Pick the noodle weight (150–300 g) and your garlic, vegetables and fat on the touch panel, so there's no call to learn; extra vegetables can water the soup down. There's also miso, soupless and tsukemen. Vinegar or fish powder from the table changes the flavor. Expect a line at opening; keep the narrow sidewalk clear. Cash only. Kept clean.
