places.notes: [Ramen · Hakata tonkotsu and tomato tonkotsu by Tenmabashi] A Hakata-style tonkotsu shop a minute from Tenmabashi exit 4, open since 2015, with a counter and one long shared table. The Jun Ton is the straight Hakata bowl: pork head bones, knuckles and back fat simmered for 15 hours into a clean, odor-free soup, on very thin, low-hydration noodles ordered firm or harder, with belly and thigh chashu. The pick of one long-time diner is the Tomaton, tonkotsu with a spicy tomato and garlic sauce that one compares to soup pasta, though two others found it ordinary. Half kaedama is ¥140. Spicy takana is free; one diner had to ask for it. Ticket machine; cash only. Closed Tuesdays.

Three bowls: the standard Kami Tora ramen (¥890), rich pork bone on thin noodles; the black, with fragrant roasted black garlic oil and wood ear; and the red Akatora, a spicy miso tonkotsu that one diner found not hot at all. Order the noodles firm, ask for extra fat, and add kaedama (¥100) whenever you like. Takana, pickled ginger and garlic are on the table. Gyoza with the house Akuma sauce and a chashu rice bowl round it out. One diner found the soup too intense, another wished it were hotter. Ticket machine outside; cash only.

places.notes: [Chinese · neighborhood champon, gyoza and fried rice by Tamatsukuri] A small local Chinese diner just south of Nagahori-dori near Tamatsukuri, open since 2012, run by an elderly couple with the TV on. The chef has nearly half a century of experience. The menu runs to fifteen noodle dishes, and the champon stands out: a big, piping-hot bowl of chicken-and-soy soup piled with pork, shrimp and vegetables over chewy noodles. Sets are cheap: champon with half fried rice for ¥750–1,000. The fried rice is fluffy, with roast ham, sausage and bacon. The gyoza have handmade wrappers and a ginger-heavy filling (five for ¥350). There's also gomoku ramen, a tonkotsu Kyushu ramen, yakisoba and kara-age. Order out loud and pay after. Cash only; smoking area inside.

The Mazesoba Rekka is the fiery version. For soup, the torichuka is a sweet chicken broth with large chicken pieces and tenkasu on curly noodles, and the Yonezawa ramen is lighter on thin noodles. Busy at lunch. Cards and PayPay accepted.

The batter has a rich dashi base. The classic is the Mugi Special; the mentaiko mochi cheese is the other standby, best with crispy edges and an egg yolk stirred in. Customize with chikuwa, corn and Baby Star, or try rotating monja such as Komtang or Shin Ramyeon. Tonpei-yaki, okonomiyaki and simple sides (avocado sashimi, diced cucumber) fill the gaps. Open until 2:00, or 5:00 on Fridays and Saturdays. Smoking allowed.

places.notes: [Ramen · fried rice and light chuka soba by Tenmabashi] A small shop right by Tenmabashi Station, open since 2024, whose banner and name put the fried rice first. Buy a ticket downstairs (cash, no big notes), then climb a steep, narrow staircase to the seats. The usual order is the set (¥1,280–1,290): a light shoyu chuka soba on thin, straight noodles with a soba-like bite, rare chashu and thick menma, plus half a plate of fragrant, fluffy fried rice. Opinions split: several diners call the fried rice the reason to come, while others found both mild, and one saw the set cost ¥980 a week earlier. Water and dish return are self-service.

places.notes: [Ramen · chicken paitan and seasonal chilled bowls by Tsuruhashi] An eleven-seat shop two minutes from Tsuruhashi, open since 2020 until 00:30. The base is a chicken paitan, rich but refreshing, in shoyu or shio, plus a clean, light shio. The shoyu tsukemen is sharp and salty, and one diner ranks it among Japan's top three. Kimchi is free and good, and chicken plates with beer make it an evening stop too. Short lines at lunch. Cards and QR accepted.

places.notes: [Ramen · creamy clam shio ramen in Via Abeno Walk] A busy shio ramen shop in the Via Abeno Walk mall near Tennoji, open since 2021. Seasonal tsumami (lightly grilled sawara, tuna three ways, hairy crab) lead into generous, fresh nigiri on small rice balls, the rice switched between red and white vinegar to suit each topping, with kabosu as a recurring accent. Over thirty sakes are on hand, and staff pick one to your taste. The atmosphere is neither stiff nor casual, and the chef chats easily. Expect ¥15,000–30,000 with drinks. Reserve; closed Wednesdays and Sundays.

The owner, a woman, trained at Men FACTORY JAWS; the Ganso Chuka Soba was developed by the owner's father, who served it at a street stall. The Ganso Chuka Soba (¥890) is a surprisingly clear, low-oil soy broth of Tosa Hachikin chicken that clings to thin, smooth noodles; the Akayoroshi soba (¥1,200) goes the other way, heavy on garlic and vegetables, finished with rice like a risotto. Tomato, sesame and horumon ramen round it out. At night it's an izakaya with obanzai lined up on the counter and oden, and the ramen makes a gentle finish. Open until 2:00 on Fridays and Saturdays. The white salmon ramen floats an espuma over a creamy broth, then piles on smoked salmon, thin chashu, croutons, crisp burdock chips and balsamic, over slightly wavy flat noodles; the salmon tantanmen is the spicy signature. The Genovese mazesoba, rich with basil and cheese, is a good second dish, and the salmon rice set comes alive with broth poured over. One diner found the white salmon broth more salty than salmony. Order at the kiosk, pick your garlic, back fat and vegetables, and collect a bowl of extra-thick, chewy noodles under sprouts, cabbage, heaps of green onion and thick chashu. The shio Jiro is powerfully salty; the soupless version is heartier still. Cheddar cheese is the surprise topping that works, and black oolong tea comes free. It's milder than many Jiro shops, which suits newcomers. Under ¥1,000 for a regular. Open until 23:00.

The seasonal soup is a treat: canola-flower miso in spring, chilled dashi with yuba over nyumen in summer, red miso in autumn. There's also mazesoba, Taiwan mazesoba, tsukemen and a monthly limited bowl (October's was a salty "junk" mazesoba with fried garlic and a fried egg). Add half fried rice or gyoza. Order on your phone. One diner found the large mazesoba heavy, another waited 15 minutes between rice and ramen.

The house Tomio niboshi soba (¥1,200) is balanced rather than brutal; the rich niboshi chuka soba goes thick and cement-grey with a pleasant bitterness for true fans. One diner found the portion small.

The young owner-chef, Iwao, is passionate and experienced, and the chef's wife is also at the shop. Formerly Karato, now Junsei, it serves one omakase course (¥22,000) set each day by the ingredients: caviar layered with karasumi, aged wagyu tartare, 48-month Iberico jamón sliced at the counter, a fresh corn soup, homemade pasta, sea urchin on brioche, then a charcoal-finished fish and a beef curry with a Kobe pork cutlet. Choose your dessert from five; fruit juices such as pear and melon make a non-alcoholic pairing. Dishes are explained carefully. Reservation only; closed Mondays.

The assorted sashimi of wild fish is the reason to come, cut with care; after that the menu runs from autumn eggplant in hairy crab sauce, matsutake dobin-mushi and crab-filled lotus root manju to Kue hot pot in winter, plus a few surprise Korean and Chinese dishes such as cold noodles and sweet and sour pork. places.notes: [French · counter French with Wakayama ingredients, Nagahoribashi] A white, calm second-floor counter near Nagahoribashi, easy to miss from the street, that builds its French courses around Wakayama produce: Kumano beef, Nanko plums, Kaneyama miso and Binchotan charcoal for meat finished on a shichirin in the open kitchen. The chef is from Wakayama Prefecture, and the shop is featured in the Michelin Guide Kyoto-Osaka 2025. Meals open with a miniature garden that changes with the season. Lunch (around ¥10,000) might bring carrot mousse with ikura, an octopus quenelle in clam chowder and Iwate duck with Kaneyama miso; dinner runs to the Kumano Beef & Foie Gras Course with a wine pairing. Save room for the warm brown-sugar financiers, and try the homemade plum soda. Courses by reservation; 10% service.

places.notes: [Udon · a noodle factory's own udon shop by Kuromon Market] A clean, calm little udon shop just outside Kuromon Market, run by a noodle maker founded in 1910, open only a few days a week. The shop belongs to a noodle maker with more than 100 years of history and has appeared on many TV shows and in magazines. The owner, a woman, runs the shop with the owner's husband; both are very kind. The thing to order is the kamaage udon (¥680): thin homemade noodles in their own hot water, buried under bonito flakes, which you season with Yuasa soy sauce and fresh-ground sesame — a dish that began as the factory's staff meal. The cold mentaiko nama-shoyu udon (¥830) is a good summer choice, and you can pick thin, extra-thin or thick noodles or kishimen. Add the free homemade tenkasu and green onion. Cash only; open Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday and Saturday.

The knife work stands out, changing how each piece of fish feels and melts, and a wall of wine faces the counter, so wine and sake pair easily with the nigiri. Weekend lunch is the gentle way in at ¥6,600 for omakase nigiri. Conversation at the counter is relaxed and friendly. One diner found the rice a bit dry and one the chawanmushi weak. Closed Mondays.

The order is ji pai, a big, thin cutlet of pounded chicken breast fried crisp and juicy, in salt-pepper or the sweet special sauce, as a bento over rice with lightly seasoned vegetables, thick fried tofu and egg. Read them before you go: dinner carries a ¥330 coperto and a per-person minimum order, and the kitchen can be slow on busy nights. In return you get carefully made pasta, a good wine list chosen with the staff, and dishes like fresh fish carpaccio, tripe stew, duck, Sangen pork and a steak of satisfyingly red meat. Lunch is the easy way in: pasta with salad, bread and an Italian omelette for ¥1,300–1,600, three days a week. Closed Mondays.

places.notes: [Sushi · sushi omakase with a champagne pairing, Minami-Senba] A sophisticated ten-seat sushi counter inside a champagne-themed hotel near Nagahoribashi, built around one idea: sushi with champagne. The head chef, Kim, previously worked at the two-star Kuruma Sushi and at Sushi Shiro. The omakase runs to small dishes and about a dozen nigiri, with standouts like abalone steamed for six hours in its liver sauce (mixed with a little sushi rice at the end), sweet uni, medium-fatty tuna and anago with a rich sauce. places.notes: [Pizza · a one-person Neapolitan pizza counter, Shinmachi] A clean, thirteen-seat counter near Nishi-Ohashi where the owner, working solo as pizzaiolo, stretches, tops and fires every pizza in a blazing wood oven in front of you, alongside a steady run of takeout orders. It has held a Michelin Bib Gourmand five years running, was ranked 27th in 50 Top Pizza Asia-Pacific 2023, and was named one of the top 100 pizza restaurants in 2017, 2018, 2019 and 2021. Buy a ticket from the machine; the Margherita is ¥1,000 and arrives in a few minutes, toasted outside and chewy within, uncut so you slice it yourself. Try the Marinara or the Ricotta e Cipolla too. No reservations and cash only; go right at opening, as lunch lines form fast. Closed Mondays and Tuesdays.

The curry is light and soupy, built on dashi rather than heat: choose a chicken-broth base with Shodoshima soy sauce or a katsuobushi dashi with soy milk, then chicken-and-pork or fish keema, and mix in the sides, such as a crunchy gizzard achar. Closed Tuesdays.

places.notes: [Italian · a refined Italian of seasonal courses, Shinmachi] A calm twelve-seat Italian near Nishi-Ohashi, pale blue outside and gray stone and concrete within, where courses of unexpected ingredient pairings arrive on carefully chosen tableware. The chef has 20 years in Italian cooking, and one diner says the chef came out of Ponte Vecchio; the owner is a certified sommelier who picks the monthly sake pairings. The chef trained at a well-known restaurant in Kobe and runs PRESTAU with the chef's wife. The monthly lunch course (¥7,700) is the way in: a squid-ink risotto with cuttlefish and sudachi, delicate sardine with turnip, homemade conchiglie in beef-tongue ragù and charcoal-grilled duck, with a delicate rather than bold hand on seasoning. Desserts come in three stages. Dislikes are handled if mentioned ahead. One diner found drink service slow. Closed Mondays and one Sunday a month.

places.notes: [Ramen · rich chicken paitan by Daikokucho Station] A friendly ramen shop seconds from Daikokucho Station, open since late 2024 with a table for four as well as the counter. The young owner has a great smile, and a lively head chef works alongside. The signature is a rich, frothy chicken paitan; the special bowl adds grilled chashu, steamed chicken, an egg and red onion. The paitan also comes as a miso ramen, light enough to finish, and there's a back-fat shoyu with thin tip menma that is lighter than it looks. places.notes: [Ramen · a chashu-heavy neighborhood ramen shop, Zaimokucho] A small, old-fashioned ramen counter near Matsuyamachi, now under a new owner and busy even mid-afternoon. The draw is chashu: the chashu ramen (¥1,200–1,300) carries about five thick, tender slices over thin, soft noodles, in shio, shoyu or miso, with garlic and spicy miso on the counter to sharpen it. For something different, the Harapeko Kizuna-men is a bowl of mixed noodles with chopped chashu and green onion; mix it from the bottom, then add vinegar and chili oil as the owner suggests. Dinner is courses only: a November 2025 seven-course meal ran from seasonal oysters through charcoal-grilled anago and handmade squid-ink tagliolini to Wagyu sirloin cap with truffle sauce, and the house specialty is a Kawachi duck carpaccio. After 21:30 it opens an à la carte menu and works as a bar until 1 am, good for squid-ink pasta and dessert as a second stop. Two diners praise the plating, one the chef's funny conversation; another found the course price on the high side. About ¥8,000–15,000; ¥550 service charge.

The star is the puppy bun (¥330), custard in the head and chocolate or hojicha cream in the body, with a Shiba Inu version (weekends only, per one diner) and a pink one that one diner took to hold strawberry jam. Also a dango Danish (¥300), a mitarashi dango bun, a clover-shaped Kyoto matcha anpan, a melon bread with a face and a yakisoba bun under a fried quail egg. There's a tea of the day to taste, and Japanese tea ordered with bread is ¥200 off. Buns are small and cheap, so it's easy to try two or three. Claim a seat upstairs before ordering.

The master's second son also works in the room. Several diners say the meat is lean, tender and free of gamey smell. The ¥2,500 lunch course brings a freshly fried venison cutlet, a low-temperature roast and venison fried rice; at night try the venison carpaccio, a juicy roast with salt and fried onions, rillettes on baguette, and the deer bread, roast venison on salty garlic toast. Newer dishes include crisp pleatless venison gyoza and a peppery venison mazesoba with egg yolk. A seven-dish venison yaki-shabu course (¥7,500) needs booking; one diner wished the cuts were explained. One diner noted a generous wine pour. ¥500 dinner charge.

The draw is the Dubai chocolate mochi (¥740), chewy outside with pistachio and a crunchy filling, which often sells out (check the shop's Instagram stories). Also a crackly brûlée cheesecake with ice cream (¥980), strawberry-matcha and Earl Grey shortcakes, a pumpkin Basque cheesecake and bear-shaped sablés. There's another branch in Amerikamura with a slightly different menu. One diner waited a long time for an order; another found the cookies a little stale.

places.notes: [Izakaya · a quiet sake-and-fish izakaya by Kintetsu Nippombashi] A calm 17-seat izakaya a minute from Kintetsu Nippombashi, run by two people, with fish the owner buys at the market and a deep drink list: over 40 sakes kept in a dedicated fridge, 80-plus shochu and 15-plus umeshu. Start with the sashimi platter, then the rolled omelet, brought out on a hot teppan with extra dashi poured on so it bubbles at the table. Diners also praise the fried hatahata, homemade zaru tofu, whitebait with grated daikon and ponzu, mackerel pressed sushi and monkfish liver with nara-zuke. Dishes can take a while, and one diner found many sakes out of stock. Closed Mondays.

More than 30 skewer cuts, many rare, come from Tanba chicken, Tokushima young chicken and Daisen Jidori, each grilled over charcoal, and some get unusual house finishes such as escargot butter or black truffle oil. The omakase is good value; add vegetable skewers, the garlic edamame and a comforting egg soup with thin noodles to finish. One diner found the duck tataki weaker than the rest. Reservations by Japanese mobile number only. Closed Wednesdays and Thursdays; smoking allowed.

The batter is fluffy enough to melt, the sauce measured; get the negiyaki with seasoned beef tendon, a mixed okonomiyaki or a buta-tama with a runny egg, and maybe squid yakisoba. Diners use it to dodge the queue at the main shop, though there's often a short line here too (orders are taken while you wait), and it takes time to cook. Takeout is popular. Weekdays it breaks between 14:30 and 17:00.

places.notes: [Yakitori · a charcoal skewer bar for chicken and pork, Higashi-Shinsaibashi] A casual charcoal skewer bar on the ground floor of GROOVE Shinsaibashi East, open from 16:00 to midnight, with an 8-seat counter that suits solo drinkers since skewers can be ordered one at a time. Alongside juicy yakitori it grills pork skewers and a spicy offal, and the soft-cartilage kara-age and doteyaki are worth ordering; one diner loved the sweet potato with honey mayo. Seasoning runs strong and rich, made for drinking, with ¥500 draft beer and highballs poured to the brim. A chopstick lottery comes with handwritten notes. Service opinions split: two diners found staff cheerful, two found them curt or pushy.

places.notes: [Sake bar · a wood-toned sake bar with creative small plates, Higashi-Shinsaibashi] A stylish fourth-floor sake bar in GROOVE Shinsaibashi East, warm wood inside, with a sake list that changes each visit, plus gin, shochu and whisky. The food is more than snacks: taro dumplings with beef and burdock in a nameko sauce, spring cabbage and prosciutto croquettes, Kagoshima chicken sashimi, fatty bluefin and seared mackerel, and in spring a run of firefly-squid dishes ending in clay-pot rice. The deep-fried house curry bread is a good take-home. Book a course for better value than ordering à la carte. Pretty sake cups and tableware. Rules: one non-alcoholic drinker per group, two-hour limit when busy. Closed Thursdays.

Ten small balls come per serving, soft and gooey rather than crisp, with a strong dashi flavor and big pieces of octopus. One diner calls the classic sauce-and-mayo (¥600) the most popular; another was told that Koga Ryu was the first to put mayonnaise on takoyaki. The negi versions come buried under green onion, with sauce (¥700) or ponzu. Eat upstairs or take them to the park. Two diners say Osaka locals pointed them here instead of Dotonbori. PayPay or cash only.

places.notes: [Soba · soba-shabu and meat dipping soba on Takashimaya's restaurant floor, Namba] The Takashimaya branch of Naniwa Soba, a small Osaka soba chain (four shops) on the seventh-floor restaurant level, with colorful seats. The signature, trademarked, is soba-shabu: Wagyu swished through the house dashi and eaten with fresh soba, as a course from ¥5,000. For a simpler meal, one repeat visitor always picks the meat dipping soba (¥1,300), pork in a lightly spicy chili-oil dip that becomes a rich soup when you add soba water at the end. Also chilled sudachi soba, ume-and-yam soba and an oyakodon set; diners praise the delicate Kansai-style broth. Open to 21:30 or 22:00, later than many department-store restaurants.

places.notes: [Mexican · a late-night taco and tequila bar since 2001, Higashi-Shinsaibashi] A small Mexican bar near Shinsaibashi, open since 2001 and late into the night, with a neon 'Tacos' sign, a terrace and a Latin, clink-glasses mood. Tacos come on handmade tortillas: chorizo with tangy salsa, tender braised pork rib (¥880), pulled pork with beans, or cheese-filled. Start with the shrimp-and-avocado cocktail de camarón (¥1,320) and a crisp garlic-mushroom quesadilla. About 30 salsas sit ready for heat-seekers, and the tequila and mezcal list is deep; one diner who doesn't care for tequila found the tequila soda easy to drink. One diner found the chicken taco's mayo-like sauce unexpected. Book ahead: food can run out late. Closed Mondays.

The açaí is thick and creamy, piled with fruit and honey, and you can build your own with granola, kiwi, coconut, nuts or mango; the Greek yogurt with comb honey is rich and filling. Bowls run about ¥1,680, which diners call a little pricey. Two diners called it the best açaí bowl ever, but one found a smaller, unripe-mango bowl on a return visit. Tabelog lists vegan options. Hours are unclear (the listing shows evenings to 4 am, reviewers came at lunch), so check before you go.

places.notes: [Pizza · a cheap oven-baked pizza bar, Higashi-Shinsaibashi] A small Italian-bar-style pizza place in the Higashi-Shinsaibashi drinking streets, known for cheap, chewy, rustic pizzas that are on the small side, so a group can order several. Diners like the Margherita, a basil pizza, the quattro formaggi with honey and a mentaiko pizza, with ahijo and prosciutto to start and inexpensive wine. There's a one-drink rule. Pizzas were ¥500–600 in older reviews; recent prices aren't reported. Service reports range from attentive (pizzas sent one at a time so each stays hot) to curt, and one diner found the backless stools hard going after an hour. Most reviews are older; the latest is June 2025.

Each piece arrives already seasoned, with salt, citrus or plum paste instead of soy sauce. The ¥20,000 omakase runs like a small kaiseki: appetizer, three sashimi, grilled fish and chawanmushi before ten nigiri from squid and striped jack to chutoro, sea urchin and eel; there's also a ¥12,000 sushi course and lunch courses that diners call good value. Past highlights include tuna cooked in a salt crust, well-judged kohada and bonito with salt. You can ask for less rice. Closed Mondays.

Okonomiyaki comes in several styles, pork, oyster, a mixed modern and even Hiroshima-style, served on individual pans; around it, yam-yaki, cheese tonpei-yaki, shrimp mayo, shrimp toast and a salty, well-liked soba-meshi, plus salt-grilled offal and thick beef tongue. One diner didn't care for the sauce. The owner, a woman, runs the kitchen alone, so it can be slow, but diners like the warm touches (a message card on the table, a candy on the way out) and fair prices. Tabelog lists vegan options; ask.

The thing to order is the thick-cut tongue wrapped in green onion, garlic and ginger, which the shop calls its own creation; grill it well. The Ning set (¥9,680) is a tour of 11 cuts, and the branch-only special misuji is worth adding. Also tongue yukhoe, yukhoe on gimbap and a gelato that surprised one diner with its quality. One diner had a grill that wouldn't heat on one side and found the beer too icy. 90-minute seating.

places.notes: [Tempura · a 7-seat tempura course counter, Higashi-Shinsaibashi] A quiet seven-seat tempura counter a few minutes from Shinsaibashi, where each piece is fried and handed over in front of you. The ¥12,100 dinner course opens with seasonal sashimi (steamed abalone with liver sauce, snow-crab sashimi), then light, crisp tempura, the shrimp especially juicy, with a fresh salad mid-way and a tempura rice bowl or tempura in tea broth to finish. In winter the showpiece is a female crab packed back into its shell and fried whole. Diners praise the warm, joking hospitality and a list of rare sake and wine. A summer lunch set ran ¥1,650–1,980 in 2026. Book ahead; closed Sundays.

Black Wagyu is seared to your chosen doneness and cut, and one diner recommends wasabi; a fuller course adds Ise lobster and abalone, at about ¥24,000. Lunch runs about ¥3,000–4,000, and à la carte is possible when seats are free. Good for anniversaries: one diner got a surprise cake. Open daily, lunch and dinner.

It roasts its own beans and brews each cup to order: ask the owner for a recommendation (one diner was steered to a freshly roasted Mandheling), or try the mocha with its grapefruit-like acidity or the strong blend. The baked cheesecake is the standard partner, smooth and well balanced; coffee jelly is on the menu too. Not everyone was won over: one diner found the coffee ordinary, the dish-washing loud and the stay limited to 60 minutes. Cash only.

The ¥5,500 course is the way in: appetizers, crisp bacalhau croquettes, Tanba chicken piri-piri, a seafood cataplana, then rice or risotto to finish and a freshly baked pastel de nata. Two diners single out the octopus and the port wine, and you can pick a bottle downstairs and pay corkage. Staff are good at pairing wines. One diner missed Vinho Verde. It fills up, so book. Closed Sundays and Mondays.

places.notes: [Café · an espresso café-bar from noon to 2 am, Amerikamura] A casual espresso bar on the north edge of Amerikamura, by the Hariju building, open from noon until 2 am and as much a day-drinking spot as a café. Order a double espresso, strong and well-roasted, or a cappuccino doppio, at prices one diner called cheap for a city café (¥363–583 in 2024). The homemade tiramisu, light and not too sweet, is the reason two diners came back; paninis and doria cover meals. Tables are well spaced and the style is laid-back: you're left alone. Smoking is allowed inside, there's no restroom, and one diner found the room getting cluttered. Terrace seats.

Courses move from small appetizers to seafood (live abalone grilled in front of you, Ise lobster, scallops), four seasonal vegetables, and black Wagyu with a choice of sauces and salts, then garlic rice or a rich black beef curry. Lunch courses are the value play; one long-time diner noted lunch prices have risen and the 80 g steak now feels small. Chefs are happy to chat. Closed Tuesdays.

The meal opens with chilled kuzu somen sharpened with sudachi, then small seasonal dishes and uni piled on clay-pot rice before the tempura, which diners call light and gentle on the stomach. The standout is sweet shrimp from Amakusa with crisp fried heads; vegetables shine too. A rich curry is an optional finish. One repeat visitor keeps bringing guests to impress. Expect ¥15,000–30,000 with pairings. Reservation only; skip the perfume.

The mapo tofu (¥1,200) is the signature, meaty, spicy and numbing; the beef-tendon version has its own fan. Also the yodare-dori, whose sauce one diner wanted to drink, grilled shumai of Jinan mochi pork (2 for ¥500), black-vinegar sweet-and-sour pork, shrimp chili and seafood noodles in thick sauce. Pair with a Shaoxing highball or baijiu jasmine highball. The owner travels to research and source ingredients, and the room is friendly. ¥300 charge, one drink, adults only.

The burgers are by a former French chef, mixing French technique into burgers. The burgers are big: some diners use a knife and fork, one prefers to wrap them in paper and bite. The fries get nearly as much praise, crisp with a refined sweetness; one diner called them the best fries ever. Get the Classic, the Comple, or the B set (¥2,500 with fries and a drink); a three-patty stack is there if you're hungry. Ten seats; it closes when the burgers sell out.

places.notes: [Japanese · a hidden 5th-floor koryori for seasonal small plates and sake, Nagahoribashi] A calm Japanese room on the fifth floor of a building near Nagahoribashi, hard to find but often full, serving Osaka-style small plates with sake and shochu. The head chef trained at Naniwa Kappo Kameji in Nishi-Shinsaibashi. Dinner starts with a run of small dishes and a rich dashi that two diners single out, then a generous sashimi platter. places.notes: [Okonomiyaki · Kishiwada-style kashimin-yaki and late drinks, Ura-Namba] A narrow, counter-only bar in Ura-Namba, the second shop of a kashimin-yaki specialist, serving the Senshu cousin of okonomiyaki that's rare in central Osaka. The owner is Nakagawa of the comedy duo Randies, who still serves customers, and the walls are covered with comedians’ autographs. A thin crepe is topped with crunchy cabbage, little pieces of chicken and minced beef fat, which melts into the batter for a rich but surprisingly light cake; the original is ¥650, so groups order several (green onion, cheese curry, mochi and cheese). Also the hefty western-style modern with noodles, a garlicky udon-soba-offal 'uso-yaki', soba-meshi with natto and good drinking snacks. Open to 2 am; no cards; smoking allowed.

You choose your own cup and saucer from the shelf (fine porcelain, one diner noted), and any coffee that doesn't fit is served on the side. Diners single out an Ethiopian for its balance of aroma and acidity and an Indonesian 'dark' that drinks clean with chocolate notes. Ordering can be slow when it's busy. Dog-friendly. Cash only; open until 23:00 on weekdays.

The owner speaks English. Breakfast and lunch are bagel sandwiches packed with fillings (bacon, egg and cheese ¥980; ham and avocado; salmon, prosciutto and cream cheese), messy but filling; one diner found the bagel itself a bit hard. Coffee is hand-dripped from three beans, ground per cup, and takeaway cups get a hand-drawn illustration. The lattes stand out, especially a thick caramel latte; sweets include a tiramisu on a waffle base. Cramped inside, and it can be nearly full on weekend afternoons.

Window seats look straight onto the tended temple garden. The sweets are made in-house: a daily sweets set (¥1,650) such as a rich cheesecake with caramel and almonds, or a seasonal wagashi tray of red bean, chestnut, ice cream and chrysanthemum monaka, good with the properly made matcha. Summer brings an ume-syrup kakigori topped with a pickled plum. Prices run high for drinks (matcha about ¥1,400), which one diner put down to the view. Cash only.

places.notes: [Café · a Taiwanese-style soy milk café for breakfast, Namba] A cheerful little café near Edion Arena decorated with cartoon soybeans, serving soy milk made the Taiwanese way: lighter and more refreshing than Japanese soy milk, with a stronger bean taste. Choose plain, oolong-tea, black sesame or mixed berry (¥660), and set the sweetness level yourself; one diner found 25% just right. A fluffy, juicy Taiwanese meat bun (¥320) makes it breakfast, and the bun-plus-soy-milk combo was ¥500. Summer adds shaved ice with tapioca, and you get sunflower seeds to crack while you sit. Opens at 8:00; closed Mondays.

The gelato case changes daily (¥420), with flavors such as salt vanilla, dried fig and cheese, pumpkin, hojicha and Earl Grey chocolate. There's a little eat-in space; weekend afternoons bring short lines. Closed Wednesdays.

A matcha Basque cheesecake and a hojicha baked cheesecake are just as rich. Lattes are unsweetened, so the matcha comes through (the 'Zuiun' is ¥850), with mango and strawberry versions too. Diners call prices high and touristy, and one waited a long time, but matcha lovers rate it. Order first, then sit.

The pudding is firm and eggy with a slightly bitter caramel, and the seasonal menu goes all in: an autumn sweet-potato pudding with ice cream (¥780), a purple sweet-potato Mont Blanc mille-feuille layered with mochi and custard, a cinnamon sweet-potato tart. Expect a line: about 15 people were waiting before opening one Saturday, and the line runs up the stairs; don't queue in front of the Kumon next door. When the stand is busy, orders can take a while.

places.notes: [Creative · natural wine and seasonal plates from an open kitchen, Namba] A wood-toned second-floor restaurant beside the railway near Nankai Namba, open until midnight, where the cooking is ingredient-led and the wine list leans natural. Courses (from ¥8,000, plus an anniversary course) run from a playful 'American dog' in jet-black binchotan-charcoal batter to buri carpaccio, charcoal-grilled sawara, a sweet-potato soup with stracciatella, sansho Bolognese and low-temperature Kyoto Hiyoshi pork, ending with black figs and canelé. You can also go à la carte: crab miso toast, a porcini omelette, grilled vegetable salad and a pork sauté that won over one seafood eater. Good non-alcoholic drinks too. It suits celebrations, and a birthday plate can be arranged. Sofa seats are first-come even if you've booked. Table charge ¥550. Closed Sundays.

Look carefully, as the sign is small next to its neighbors. Smoking is allowed on the terrace, which one diner found uncomfortable. No credit cards; e-money and QR are fine. places.notes: [Pasta · homemade meat sauce on chewy fresh pasta, Minami-Senba] A small counter pasta shop near Shinsaibashi built around its meat sauce, slow-simmered from the beef cut senbon-suji. The classic version is rich and clings well to chewy fresh pasta without any meaty smell; the listing also highlights a cream meat sauce with Australian grain-fed beef meatballs, and there are limited sauces like a dashi meat sauce topped with bonito flakes, a monthly avocado cream, carbonara and arrabbiata. Choose fresh or whole-wheat noodles. Weekday lunch includes a free large size and a side of soup, and drinks are just +¥200. Ordering is by QR code. One diner found the oyster and karasumi pasta bland and disliked being pushed to add the shop on LINE. Six terrace seats allow smoking and pets.

places.notes: [Chinese · numbing Sichuan mapo tofu and set meals, Yotsubashi] A small, calm Sichuan eatery in the basement of a building you reach straight from Yotsubashi Station's Exit 2 stairs. The owner formerly ran Meigen, a popular Chinese restaurant in Honmachi, so its signature mapo tofu lives on here; the listing also cites experience at Osaka's Koshin. Every lunch set is ¥1,000, and mapo tofu is the house signature: boldly Sichuan, with a generous hit of numbing pepper that one diner calls addictive and another found too spicy to finish. Unusually, set meals continue at night, like a ¥1,500 two-item platter of mapo tofu and yurinchi with refillable soup and rice. In the evening there are small plates for drinking too: dry dandan noodles (small ¥500), steamed chicken with Hong Kong sauce (¥300), a spicy shrimp mayo and century egg tofu with sesame sauce. One person runs the place, so expect to wait a little for orders. Closed Sundays; Saturday dinner is by reservation only.

places.notes: [Sweets · light mousse cakes and chocolate, Kita-Horie] A small, stylish patisserie a minute from Nishi-Ohashi Station, with a showcase of seasonal cakes and just four counter seats to eat in. One diner notes that most cakes are mousse-based and made airy, so fruit and chocolate come through without heaviness: the Écrin (¥700) layers strawberry and mascarpone mousse around a passion fruit centre, and one diner compared its texture to a premium Aero bar. In autumn there is a chestnut roll (roulé au marron, ¥680) with Hokkaido cream and a Japanese-chestnut Mont Blanc; the soufflé au chocolat (¥680) is surprisingly light. Kouign-amann to take away, and café au lait (¥600) or a creamy cappuccino to drink. Eat-in seats can't be booked, so come soon after the 11:00 opening; cakes can be reserved by phone. Closed Mondays and Tuesdays.

places.notes: [Café · a retro tea room with a home-style daily lunch plate, Minami-Senba] A dimly lit café near Nagahoribashi that feels like an old Western-style house or British tea room, with antique furniture and stained glass. A reviewer describes it as run by a lovely elderly couple. It opens only Tuesday to Thursday for lunch and serves one thing: the daily 'Honeysuckle rice' plate (¥1,100, ¥1,300 with a drink), a main such as a light Japanese-style hamburg steak with grated daikon and ponzu plus several small vegetable sides, white or mixed-grain rice and soup. Several diners value it as a balanced, home-style meal that changes every day; a mini parfait or cake can be added. One diner was served hot water on arrival in winter. Cash only, and smoking is allowed inside.

One diner called the gelato natural, another found flavors not seen elsewhere: tangy mango, café latte, latte noir, pistachio, matcha, Earl Grey, strawberry and walnut, with the DUO giving two in a cone. One diner had the Earl Grey Blanc (¥1,300), full of bergamot aroma; there's a matcha affogato too. There are no tasting spoons, so decide at the case. Dogs are welcome inside, and there's a small terrace. Closed Thursdays.

places.notes: [Café · seasonal fruit parfaits and pot tea, Minami-Horie] A small European-style tea salon facing Minami-Horie Park, known for elaborate seasonal fruit parfaits: peach Melba with a whole peach in summer, melon, blood orange or ruby grapefruit with brûlée, Shine Muscat and grape in autumn (¥2,600, or ¥2,900 with a drink). The owner-chef, who makes the seasonal desserts, is from France. One diner swapped in the deep-steamed sencha gelato (+¥50) and found it lighter than matcha. The tea list is long and comes by the pot. For a fuller visit, the afternoon tea set adds sandwiches (the cream cheese is the star for one diner), scones and a dessert; crepes with pistachio ice cream sell out some days. House rules: each guest orders at least one food item, parfaits come as a drink set, and pricier drinks cost extra. One diner found the bowls smaller than in the photos. Cash only; reservations taken; closed Mondays and Tuesdays.

Drinks include a strawberry milk soda with fruit pieces, royal milk tea and an aromatic café au lait, and a message can be added to an order. places.notes: [Teppanyaki · seafood and steak courses at the counter, Shinmachi] A second-floor teppanyaki counter two minutes from Yotsubashi Station where seafood gets as much attention as the beef. A reviewer believes it is run by a couple. Courses are priced by the seafood you pick: diners describe sashimi such as itoyori or fatty sea bream with white soy and ginger, lobster in a rich Américaine sauce and abalone cooked in front of you, with a whisky flambé for show; the top course ends on a tender Chateaubriand that one diner ate with just salt, then garlic rice and a gentle white-miso fish soup. Platters are shown before cooking, and each abalone order comes with a decorated shell to take home. Wide wine list. Counter seats are course-only; lunch must be booked online three days ahead. Closed Mondays and two more days a month.

places.notes: [Japanese · tempura bowls at lunch and seasonal courses at night, Minami-Senba] A cozy 10-seat Japanese restaurant hidden at the back of a building just off Shinsaibashi-suji. The shop says it is run by a couple both born in the Year of the Rabbit. Weekday lunch is a short run of tempura bowls and set meals, from a ¥700 tempura bowl to a two-shrimp special bowl (¥1,000) with a light batter and a dashi-rich Kansai-style sauce; rice can be made large for free, miso soup comes alongside, and you pay first. Lunch ends when the rice runs out, and one diner saw it fill up soon after noon. At night it becomes a place for seasonal Japanese courses built on fish bought at Kuromon Market, with a good sake list; one diner was served a warming sake-lees soup on a cold night. Courses need booking by the day before; à la carte diners pay a ¥550 charge. Smoking is allowed. Closed Sundays.

You order à la carte and dishes arrive course-style: pork rillettes with red cabbage, lobster and scallops with salted onion mousse and lobster consommé jelly (¥3,960), the signature cabbage steak under a Gorgonzola sauce (mop it up with baguette), cod milt with Shimonita leeks, a 100 g Black Wagyu sirloin cap steak, then garlic rice or a mixed seafood okonomiyaki. Portions suit two, and one pair of diners was allowed to take leftovers home. Run by a couple, so service can be slow; one diner felt pressed to order a full run from appetizer to dessert. Book ahead; ¥550 appetizer charge; JCB or AMEX only.

places.notes: [Kushiage · Kitahorie, a one-person counter of creative skewers in rice flour and rice oil] A ten-seat Horie counter that has turned out creative kushiage for about ten years, with one person doing everything. The shop calls its style halfway between kushikatsu and tempura: market produce in a light rice-flour batter, fried in Wakayama rice oil and finished with a torch, so diners keep eating without feeling heavy. Skewers arrive one by one until you say stop, or in courses of 10 to 20: angel shrimp, wagyu, kisu with crab and mitsuba, Kawachi duck with porcini, a roast-beef-and-foie-gras finale, even an eel chazuke skewer and dessert. A tomato-and-mozzarella salad with hot fried zucchini opens, and the aosa dashi chazuke is a favourite way to finish. Unusually for kushiage, the shop says it can make the skewers gluten-free or vegetarian on request — say so when you book. One November 2025 diner found the batter hard and gritty; a September 2026 diner ranks it No. 1 for skewers.

There is one dish: chicken curry brought bubbling in a clay pot, with tender chicken, a soft-boiled egg and marinated tomatoes in a thin, soup-like curry that tastes of whole spices ground to order rather than curry powder. A card explains how to eat it: smell it, sip the clear top like soup, eat it with the spiced rice, then tip the rice and onion pickles into the pot and break the egg for a creamy porridge. To eat, queue from about 9:30, take a numbered ticket when they are handed out around 10:05, order and pay cash, and come back at your time slot; the day's servings go by mid-morning. Diners describe a gentle owner and pleasant staff; one found the flavour a little monotonous, and another thought one visit enough.

places.notes: [Teppanyaki · Minami-Senba, a nine-seat Wagyu counter near Nagahoribashi] A quiet, stylish counter of nine seats wrapped around the teppan, so every seat watches the grilling, with art pieces around the room. The owner-chef grills Black Wagyu (the shop names Yamagata beef) and seasonal vegetables in front of you; diners praise the vegetables as much as the meat, a rich potage served hot or cold, a small assortment of appetizers, and garlic rice to finish, with salt, ponzu or soy sauce for the beef. Lunch is the deal: a Black Wagyu set from ¥3,180, or a limited steak rice bowl. Dinner courses run ¥7,080 to ¥17,000. The service is homey: staff have arranged birthday plates and cakes, lent a shawl to a pregnant guest, and the chef likes to chat after the meal.

places.notes: [French-Japanese · Minami-Senba, a couple-run counter for French food you eat with chopsticks] A small counter between Shinsaibashi and Honmachi, open since 2014 and in Tabelog's Innovative 100 for 2025, where French techniques of taking a dish apart and rebuilding it meet Japanese dashi, miso and seasonal fish. The single omakase runs 12 or 13 dishes for ¥14,770 — think a root celery mousse with Ezo abalone and sea urchin, foie gras mousse with persimmon, isaki with burdock and a sea bream dashi foam, a beef fillet main that regulars call the best part, and a grilled matsutake risotto to finish — then five desserts, and you may choose all of them. The homemade focaccia comes with refills; diners warn to pace yourself. A couple runs the room warmly. Weekend lunch is a good-value way in. Pay cash: the card processor went under in July 2026.

places.notes: [Sushi · Minami-Senba, an alley-end Edomae counter where the drinks are included] At the far end of the Senba Uraroji alley, in a renovated machiya, an eight-seat wooden counter serves what diners call Osaka-style Edomae sushi: fish aged for days, cured with vinegar or kombu, or simmered, on mild red-vinegar rice. The dinner omakase (¥20,000 in summer 2026) includes free-flow drinks, sake among them, so drinkers find it a rare bargain. It runs to about 20 dishes: it opens with a toro-taku hand roll of aged tuna and miso-pickled daikon, peaks with a shabu-shabu of a 700 g Densuke anago, and ends with a sea urchin gunkan stuffed and heaped with urchin, miso soup from the anago broth, and watermelon. Portions are generous; ask for smaller nigiri if needed. The chef is friendly and chats across the counter. Reservation only; budget 2.5 hours.

Opened 13 December 2021 (Tabelog). · Bring out each fish with Edomae methods — aging, curing with vinegar or kombu, simmering — so each piece is a dish in itself (Tabelog and Senba Uraroji site, shop-provided). · Aged-fish omakase; Densuke anago shabu-shabu; sea urchin gunkan.

places.notes: [Italian · Shinmachi, a ten-year-old upstairs Italian with produce from Tango] A wood-lined second-floor room up a narrow staircase near Nishi-Ohashi, open since 2016, that cooks with fish, organic vegetables and meat sent from Tango, the owner's home region, and changes the menu with each day's delivery. From the counter you can watch the single chef at work; tables suit the courses (¥6,500 to ¥10,000): a September 2026 ¥6,500 course ran from a heart-shaped mousse and tuna with pickles through pizza, pasta with bottarga, grilled shimaaji and a dessert plate of panna cotta, pineapple sorbet and Shine Muscat grapes. À la carte, a four-time diner rates the summer chilled pasta with pesto and myoga above everything; there are also clam pasta and chicken gratin. The owner chooses the wines. It's often full, so book; lunch stopped in April 2026.

places.notes: [Okinawa soba · Minamisenba, a lunch counter with a line of office workers] A ten-seat counter in Minamisenba's office blocks that opened in 2024 as the area's first Okinawa soba specialist, and now often has a line at weekday lunch. The shop takes the broth seriously: katsuobushi and kombu with niboshi, dried clams, two kinds of Okinawan salt and a splash of awamori, poured clear and golden over flat, medium-thick noodles worked out with a noodle factory. Fresh shredded ginger stands in for the usual pickled kind. The big bowl is the Tengan soba (¥1,200), with crisp-grilled three-layer pork and tender salt-simmered cartilage soki; the salt soki soba (¥950) is the everyday order, and one diner on a 71st visit still adds the ¥100 back fat. In summer there's a chilled Churaumi soba. Add a small jushi or a Po-Tama onigiri, and season with koregusu or yuzu kosho from the counter. Lunch only, no cards (PayPay is fine), and it closes when the soup runs out. A second shop runs in Honmachi.

The star is the carne asada: lean steak cooked rare, eaten on its own first, then wrapped in a tortilla with chili con carne, jalapeño pickles, mashed potato and fresh salsa. Around it, Mexican-izakaya plates with a Japanese streak: spiced beans with sansho, spicy takuan, shibire chicken in a sansho sauce, chili-cheese quesadilla, pulled-chicken nachos. The October 2026 course (¥7,000 with all-you-can-drink) pairs red-meat and lamb steaks and ends with a curry. One diner found the menu short for a long stay and suggests it as one stop on a crawl. Drinkers only, no children, PayPay rather than cards.

places.notes: [Japanese · Shinmachi by Nishi-Ohashi, a regulars' counter for seasonal small dishes since 2013] A bright, clean Japanese restaurant a few minutes from Nishi-Ohashi Station, open since 2013, which sets out to serve seasonal food in a homely room without fuss. The menu is long and moves with the market: sashimi that one diner calls the highlight, kizushi that won another over at first bite, bamboo shoots simmered in dashi in spring, eggplant in summer, matsutake dobin-mushi in autumn, and plenty of small plates for sake, such as mentaiko with a little karasumi, or a white sesame and celery salad. Finish with the natto zosui, which a first-timer went home wanting to cook. Regulars, many older and local, keep it full, so book; one diner who waited was phoned the moment a table came free. Tabelog puts dinner at about ¥8,000–15,000 a head, plus 10% service.

places.notes: [Yakitori · Shinmachi, an omakase counter that looks like a sushi bar] Nothing outside says yakitori: inside is a quiet room with a coffered ceiling, natural-stone walls and a counter cut from a 200-year-old hinoki, more like a sushi or kaiseki bar. The owner-chef, born in Osaka and shaped by youth spent in Yamagata, trained at a well-known Kitashinchi yakitori restaurant before opening here in October 2025, and grills mainly Yamagata and Hinai jidori over Kishu binchotan, folding in Japanese and French technique. Two seatings a night run one course of about 15 dishes: a pâté de campagne in a monaka shell, a grilled-maitake consommé, skin-on thigh and neck, crunchy gizzard, wings smoked after grilling, truffle-cheese tsukune, a chawanmushi under porcini-and-truffle sauce, then karasumi somen or spiced curry and a pumpkin cheesecake on red bean paste. One diner describes a young grill master who greets and explains each dish, then grills with total focus at the centre of the counter. Pairings run to wine and champagne as well as sake.

Seasoning is gentle throughout (saikyo-miso Spanish mackerel, basil-grilled mackerel, herb-crusted salmon, a mild mapo tofu), and the health tea changes daily. Lunch is about ¥1,000 and fills up before noon; turnover is quick and takeaway is offered. In the evening the same kitchen serves vegetable-heavy set meals with four or eight side dishes. A January 2026 diner returning after five or six years found the master and partner still there, and a July 2024 diner notes the owner specializes in astrology.

About a dozen breads sit at the buffet, mostly sweet, and croissants and salt bread come out hot every 30 minutes, often brought to the table; diners single those two out. The premium plan adds mini desserts, French toast and fruit sandwiches. Seating is timed (80 minutes per Tabelog) and tight, a few tables went to the terrace on a busy holiday, and after noon some breads run out or dry. Reviews are mostly happy; one diner found ¥2,000 for a salad plus the bread add-on poor value. Bread is half price after 4 pm.

The tamago is filled with foie gras, squid and shrimp. Lunch is 10 pieces for ¥5,000 or a ¥12,500 omakase, served quickly by one person; dinner is a course. The pieces are small, and one April 2026 diner found the sweet soy glaze too strong; a long-time fan returns for the foie gras and mozzarella nigiri. A July 2022 diner who had eaten at Sushi Yoshi in Tsuruhashi some 20 years earlier found much the same menu here. Book by phone, from a Japanese mobile number if possible.

Start with the appetizer platter — hummus, orange-marinated beets, tapenade, a carpaccio, sometimes a smoky roasted-eggplant dip or an Aleppo-style red pepper and walnut paste — then the seafood bouillabaisse, saving the broth for the risotto that reviewers insist on. Lamb brochettes over spicy couscous are the official No. 1; the red-wine-braised beef cheek is said to take three days. Since spring 2026 lunch is a pita sandwich set with lentil soup, harissa and tzatziki from about ¥1,000. The wine list leans unusual. Diners call the owner cheerful and willing to talk food at the counter; the room was featured in an・an and Meets, per an October 2025 review. One cook means relaxed pacing, and the counter passage is narrow.

places.notes: [Chinese · Hakuromachi, a white, stylish room up the back stairs behind the W Osaka] Easy to miss: climb the stairs at the back of an older, well-renovated building and the second floor opens into a bright, modern room with a counter and tables. A January 2025 reviewer called it the second shop of Tokuchaina, and a September 2026 diner who usually goes to Tokuchaina came here for the first time. The cooking is Cantonese-leaning and gently seasoned, with market fish and seasonal vegetables: start with the assorted appetizer platter, then the mapo tofu sharpened with fermented black beans, a fresh-fish carpaccio, stir-fried squid with black beans, shrimp chili or the tom yum fried rice, and finish with a green-onion and char siu noodle soup. Natural wines and Shaoxing run alongside. Weekday lunch is a few sets (mapo tofu, yurinchi, shrimp chili and a weekly special); an April 2026 diner had the special soy-sauce noodles with four small sides for ¥1,200. Dishes come out at a leisurely pace, so order most of it at once.

Yamato beef from Nara is the point. The signature is the thick-cut Chateaubriand tongue, sliced and grilled at the counter; diners also order the Chateaubriand, outside skirt, the truffle yukke and the beef sashimi, and finish with garlic fried rice studded with Chateaubriand. The kitchen also cooks pasta, beef stew, tacos and a katsu sandwich, and a sommelier pours from over 100 wines. Omakase courses run ¥6,000 or ¥11,000. Several October 2026 diners found the service slow on busy nights; one table had a two-hour limit.

Tempura is fried in 100% rice oil and brought to you a few pieces at a time, so it arrives piping hot: lunch is a set with rice that is cooked continuously in small cookers and refilled free (white or barley), miso soup and homemade daikon pickles on the table. The favourite is the Tamago set, whose soft-boiled egg tempura goes over the rice; others go for 'angel shrimp' (from New Caledonia, one regular heard), kisu, sardines, cheese-stuffed chikuwa or a dorayaki tempura with butter. In the evening, ¥1,000 buys a beer with shrimp, eggplant and chicken tempura. The shop is the only restaurant of Patria Co., whose site names the manager as Takimoto Youhei, from Hokkaido; an August 2026 regular noticed new staff and a new potato salad.

places.notes: [Korean · Shinmachi, sundubu from 11 am to 11:30 pm] A clean, modern 17-seat room on Naniwa-suji, two minutes from Nishi-Ohashi Station, that opened in September 2025 as the second shop of a sundubu restaurant whose first is in Yuzato. The tofu is made in the shop every morning and the broth is wagyu bone and tail with a homemade tategi chili paste; diners call it rich and deep, with clams and a hint of sweetness under the heat. Pick one of eight sundubu (the horumon version is the favourite), a spice level from 0 up, and toppings. At lunch it comes with rice, a raw egg, Korean seaweed and kimchi and namul for about ¥1,000, and the room fills with office workers. Evenings turn into a Korean izakaya: soy- and spice-marinated shrimp that drew a 'What is this? So delicious!' from one table, wagyu yukhoe, chijimi, bulgogi, and makgeolli. The name is read Toshi, not Shun, as one diner learned. It stays open between lunch and dinner, a plus for one regular.

places.notes: [Ramen · Sakaisuji-Hommachi, chuka soba and free fried rice until 12:30 am] A lively 24-seat shop two minutes from Sakaisuji-Hommachi Station that opened in August 2026 with one hook: every bowl comes with a free mini fried rice, and ¥380 more makes it all-you-can-eat. The operator, an Osaka company that also runs CoCo Ichibanya and Ramen Daisensou franchises, set out to make the town chuka soba of a Showa childhood: house-made noodles and a clear, light broth in shoyu, shio or miso. Diners describe chicken-bone stock with chicken oil, a hint of shellfish and a slightly sweet soy, with thin straight noodles; one called it Tokyo-style with an Osaka twist. The fried rice has drawn YouTubers: refills come out in about two minutes, and diners report going back four or five times, but one late-night diner found it bland and the garlic ramen not hot. After 4 pm a list of Showa diner sides appears, from horse-mackerel fry to red sausages. Cash only at the ticket machine; open daily until 12:30 am.

places.notes: [Izakaya · Tanimachi 6-chome, the original Sonoda: chashu egg and drinks from 11 am] A lively Showa-retro diner at the end of the Karahori shopping street that opened in 2016, made Tabelog's Izakaya 100 in 2021 and has since spawned branches in Tokyo and Fukuoka. By day office workers pack in for ¥1,000 set meals with free rice refills; at any hour others settle in with a Kohaku Ebisu or a Baisu sour. The dish everyone orders is the chashu egg, tender chashu under a fried egg; then the menchi katsu under aurora sauce, meat tofu, nam-pla-pickled celery and chicken nanban. Many finish with the Chinese soba, a seafood-based shoyu with flat noodles, chashu and clams, which one diner called a bowl you wouldn't expect from a tavern. One diner thinks the site was once a butcher's. Cash only, no bookings, and smoking is allowed after 2 pm. A returning diner found the service slipping on a quiet September 2026 afternoon.

places.notes: [Ramen · Minamihonmachi, a yakiniku shop's lunchtime beef-tendon chuka soba] By night a yakiniku and horumon restaurant in the Minamihonmachi office district; at lunch, since September 2024, a ramen counter that puts the yakiniku kitchen's A5 wagyu beef tendon on chuka soba. There are three bowls: the dark, soy-based BLACK, the beef-bone WHITE and the chili-red RED. One diner expected beef and found seafood first: the BLACK is a sweet, seafood-scented shoyu that looks heavier than it tastes, with slow-simmered tendon, chopped onion and green onion, and an egg yolk to stir in. The RED is sweet and spicy with plenty of Korean chili. Noodles are medium and chewy. The plain BLACK was ¥780 in 2025; the Mashi Mashi with extra tendon and green onion ¥1,100, and a ¥350 bowl of tendon bokkake rice finishes the job. The newest review is from September 2025, so check the shop's Instagram first.
places.chef: Lunch-only ramen that opened on 9 September 2024 (Tabelog) inside the yakiniku and horumon restaurant 和ちゃん, which serves yakiniku at night (Instagram @yakiniku.kazuchan; 2025 reviews). A diner credits the bowls to the yakiniku chef (May 2025 review). · Ramen built on the same wagyu the yakiniku uses; the sign promises the ultimate ramen made with Japanese wagyu beef tendon (April 2025 reviews). · Wagyu beef-tendon chuka soba, BLACK, WHITE and RED.

places.notes: [Cake shop and café · Shinmachi, a one-person patisserie since 2007] A small cake shop between Nishi-Ohashi and Yotsubashi that has outlasted the area's fast-changing cafés since 2007, with a motto of sweets that are gentle on body and mind and an online store branded "additive-free sweets". The owner bakes, runs the café and cooks lunch alone, so things take a while: the fruit roll cake is rolled to order and the cream puffs and pies are filled after you ask. Diners single out the apple pie (one was told to try it both warmed and as it is), a moist roll with fresh chocolate cream, a mousse-like lemon pudding and a sweet caramel cheesecake. Light lunches change: a piping-hot bacon-and-mushroom gratin set (¥950, May 2026), and earlier a buckwheat-flour pizza. Prices are low; bring cash.

places.notes: [Kushikatsu and horumon · Shinmachi, a smoky Showa-style counter by the Orix Theater] A lively kushikatsu izakaya that moved from Kitahorie to a ground-floor spot near the Orix Theater, billing itself as a trip back to the good old Showa era. The batter is light and crisp; diners also go for the grilled offal skewers, a grilled liver with sesame oil and salt, a sweet-spicy Chiri-tori hot pot of beef horumon and vegetables in a square iron pan, and the specialty dote-yaki. Finish with ramen in the pot, cold kimchi noodles, or a cheese risotto. The sauce once came in a shared no-double-dipping pot (2025); by April 2026 it was poured over the plate. A May 2025 group found the owner very pleasant, and later diners felt it was a regulars' place that still made a newcomer feel warmly welcome. Every seat allows smoking, and a 2025 diner found the ventilation weak.

places.notes: [Baked sweets · Shinmachi, a madeleine shop with three hard-to-book seats] A tiny shop near the Orix Theater where the smell of fermented butter fills the room and the oven sits in full view. Almost everything is to take away — boxes of madeleines in a dozen flavours (fermented butter, French or Takachiho butter, carrot, chocolate, walnut, Gorgonzola) and the shop's shell cakes — and every purchase comes with one still warm from the oven. The three seats inside are reserved for a light, milky soft serve with a seasonal sauce, or a firm pudding on top of it. Two diners link it with Chihiro Kashiten a few streets away: a September 2026 diner calls it a sister shop, and an October 2026 diner says the logo looks familiar and the shop is run by the son of a former influencer who had sold shares in that shop. A line may wrap the block.

The shop site lists this one shop. Its relationship to ちひろ菓子店 (Chihiro Kashiten, skipped in b200 as a chain) is unclear: a September 2026 review calls it "a sister shop of Chihiro", while an October 2026 review says it is run by the son of a former influencer who had sold shares in the shop it resembles. places.notes: [Hawaiian · Hakuromachi, build-your-own poke bowls] A bright, wood-toned Hawaiian café between Sakaisuji-Hommachi and Nagahoribashi that has served custom poke bowls since 2019 and bills itself as the first in Osaka to do so. You tick an order sheet: a base of multigrain rice, salad or half and half, two mains such as tuna, salmon or tender roast beef, four sides like avocado, tobiko, edamame and egg yolk, then a sauce; extras push the bill up (one diner reached ¥1,350 in April 2025 and remembers when it was under ¥1,000). Beyond poke there is loco moco, garlic shrimp tender enough to eat shells and all, crisp mochiko chicken and a fruit-heavy açaí bowl, plus a terrace where dogs are welcome. Seating is limited, so weekday lunch can fill up; no reservations.
places.chef: Hawaiian diner that opened on 2 September 2019 (Tabelog), billed by the shop as Osaka's first custom poke bowl specialist (Tabelog, shop-provided). Run by Hawaiisukiyane Co. places.notes: [Wagashi · Shinmachi, a 150-year-old sweets shop run by a couple] A small Japanese-sweets shop founded in 1877 in Shinmachi, a former geisha district; the shop's sign survived the wartime fires and the shop was revived after the war. Today a married couple makes and sells everything, which is why the famous autumn chestnut steamed yokan (hand-peeled chestnuts, Hokkaido bean paste, ¥3,000 for a half) is reservation-only and gone by late December. Year-round there is Yūgiri monaka with the shell kept crisp until you buy it and a bear-shaped honey cream cheese monaka; in summer Warawazu mochi (somewhere between water yokan and mochi), bouncy mizu manju, fu manju and a fruit kanten where the watermelon is still crunchy; in September Osaka-style moon-viewing dango. One diner calls the cream-and-butter dorayaki the best ever. In August 2026 a diner waited behind a couple of customers. Closed Sunday and Monday.
places.chef: 小澤康雄・小澤ゆう子 · Owners (a married couple), who make and sell the sweets · The shop was founded in Meiji 10 (1877) in Shinmachi, once a hanamachi; the signboard escaped the wartime fires and, "like a baton passed to the third generation", let 御菓子司 廣井堂 be revived after the war. It is now run by the married couple 小澤康雄 and 小澤ゆう子, and the couple make and sell everything (shop site, read October 2026: "小澤康雄・小澤ゆう子 夫婦にて"; the chestnut yokan page says the two make and sell everything, so mass production is hard). · A small shop aiming for taste and service that please each customer; a writer once described it as "変わりゆく町の変わらない味" (the unchanging taste of a changing town) (shop site). · Chestnut steamed yokan; Yūgiri monaka; honey cream cheese monaka; Warawazu mochi.
places.gfd: Ask. No gluten information; many sweets are rice-based (daifuku, mochi, dango), but fu manju is made with wheat gluten, the baked sweets, pies and dorayaki are wheat-based, and the chestnut steamed yokan recipe is not stated. Ask about each sweet.
places.vgd: Ask. Much of the range is bean paste, rice and agar, but some sweets use egg-yolk bean paste, condensed milk, cream cheese, honey or butter and cream; ask about each sweet.

places.notes: [Burgers · Shinmachi, choose every layer] A calm, café-like burger shop in the stylish Shinmachi area that opened in 2016 billing itself as Japan's first custom-burger specialist. Pick a brown, white or whole-wheat bun (or lettuce instead), a beef patty, pork rib or chicken leg, one of ten house-made sauces and three vegetables, or order a set burger like the Tex-Mex with avocado and jalapeños or the ABC. Diners single out the patty: coarse-ground with steak-like chunks, cooked rare and juicy enough to soak the bun. The owner explained the menu to one first-time diner in May 2026. One diner found it pricey for the size. Sofas and a terrace; open until 9 pm Thursday to Saturday, and fine for just a drink.
